[p. 281]

﴿When the Event occurs﴾ ﴿there will be no denying its occurrence﴾.

Opening the surah with a temporal adverbial clause that carries a conditional sense is an striking opening, because it captures the mind by creating anticipation of what follows this temporal condition, together with the awe contained in the subject, which anticipates a great event that is about to take place.

"Idha" (إذا) is a temporal adverb (ظرف زمان), and it is connected to the implied verb (الكون المقدر) in the phrase "in gardens of delight" etc., and to His saying ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 28] etc., and to His saying ﴿amid scorching winds and boiling water﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 42] etc. "Idha" was given the meaning of a condition (ضمّن إذا معنى الشرط).

The clause ﴿there will be no denying its occurrence﴾ is an explanatory resumptive clause (استئناف بياني) arising from His saying ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ etc., and it is a parenthetical insertion (اعتراض) between the clause ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ and the clause ﴿Then the companions of the right hand﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 8] etc.

The answer (الجواب) is His saying ﴿Then the companions of the right hand — how blessed are the companions of the right hand!﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 8] ﴿And the companions of the left hand — how wretched are the companions of the left hand!﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 9]. It thus serves as the answer to the condition, and it also serves to detail the clause ﴿and you will be three kinds﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 7]. The "fa" (الفاء) is used with two meanings: linking the answer, and indicating consequence (التفريع). The clause ﴿there will be no denying its occurrence﴾ and what follows it is a parenthetical insertion.

Al-waqi'ah (الواقعة) originally means the event that happened, i.e., took place; one says "a matter occurred" (وقع أمر), meaning it took place. Just as one says "the truth of a report is its conformity to what is real (الواقع)", i.e., that the meaning understood from it agrees with what that meaning designates in existence, whether actual or anticipated according to that meaning. From this is the word for a battle: one says "the Battle of Dhi Qar" (واقعة ذي قار) and "the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah" (واقعة القادسية).

In making it feminine, they had in mind the meaning of "event" (الحادثة), "occurrence" (الكائنة), or "the Hour" (الساعة). This feminine form is very common in the language and runs on the tongues of the Arabs; they only intend by it the meaning of event, hour, or the like. Close to this is the expression "the circle has turned against him" (دارت عليه الدائرة). God says ﴿They say, "We fear that a misfortune may befall us"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 52], and "upon them is a circle of evil" (عليهم دائرة السوء).

Here, al-waqi'ah refers to the Resurrection (القيامة). This descriptive term became, by dominance, a proper name for it in the terminology of the Qur'an. God says ﴿So on that Day the Event will occur﴾ [al-Haqqah: 15], just as it was named al-Saakhkhah (الصاخة), al-Taamah (الطامة), and al-Aazifah (الآزفة),

[p. 282]

i.e., the Hour that is to occur. With this sense, the phrase ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ contains a fine paronomasia (تجنيس, tajnis).

Al-waqi'ah: the one described by occurrence, which is coming into being.

"Kadhibah" (كاذبة) may be an active participle from the unaugmented verb "kadhaba", and it is feminine in form to indicate that it is an attribute of an implied feminine noun, whose intended word here is "nafs" (soul), i.e., every lying soul will be negated. It may be from the intransitive "kadhaba", when one speaks contrary to what is actually the case. This is because those who deny the Resurrection say: "The Resurrection will not occur", and so they lie in this. When the Event occurs, all souls will believe in its occurrence, and so no soul will remain that denies it, i.e., regarding its matter or in reporting about it. All this implied meaning is indicated by the context.

It may also be from the transitive "kadhaba", like the expression "his own soul lied to him" (كذبته نفسه), meaning his soul told him a false tale, i.e., his opinion told him a lying account. This is because the belief of the one who denies resurrection is a belief that his deficient reason has made appealing to him; so it is as if his soul told him a tale and he then took it to be false. People also say: "His soul lied to him about the great matter" when he undertook it and failed; it is as if his soul, when it encouraged him to enter it, said to him, "You can handle it, so confront it and do not worry, for you will overcome it." When he then sees his inability, it is as if his soul had informed him of what would not happen, and so it deceived him, just as one says "his eye deceived him" when he imagines something seen which did not exist.

The meaning: When the Resurrection occurs, those who deny it will be certain of it; they will abandon their belief that it will not occur, and they will know that they went astray in their reasoning. This is a warning, threatening those who deny the Resurrection with the disgrace of failure and the foolishness of their opinion among the people of the gathering.

The application of the attribute of lying to all of this is a metaphor (استعارة), by likening the cause of a fruitless act to one who gives a false report, or by likening causation to speech. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "Lying is a kind of speech, so just as speech may be extended to what is not uttered, as in the verse of Abu al-Najm:

"The ropes said to the belly, 'Truly...'"

lying may likewise be extended to what is not uttered, as in:

"Because the cloth-bags and the sacks lied."

The lam in "li-waq'atiha" (لوقعتها) is the lam of time (لام التوقيت), as in ﴿Establish prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ [al-Isra': 78], and His saying ﴿So divorce them at their waiting period﴾ [al-Talaq: 1]. And the saying: "I wrote it for such-and-such a date of such-and-such a month." It means "at" (عند). Its origin is the lam of specification (لام الاختصاص), and its usage became common in specifying a timed matter with its time, as in His saying ﴿And when Moses came at Our appointed time﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. This is an extension of the meaning of specification to the point that its original sense was forgotten. In a hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked which deed is best, and he said: 'Prayer at its time.'" This usage is different from the usage in His saying ﴿They will have no food except from a bitter thorny plant﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 6].

Surah 56, verse 3:

﴿Abasing [some], exalting [others].﴾

Two predicates (khabarān) of an omitted subject (mubtada' mahdhuf), the pronoun referring to al-Waqi'ah (the Inevitable Event). That is: it is abasing and exalting, meaning that by it there occurs the abasing of peoples who were high and the exalting of peoples who were low. This is by the abasing of the tyrants and the corrupters who were in exaltation and lordship in the world, and by the exalting of the righteous who were in the world not regarding most of them. It is also abaser of places that were high, such as mountains and minarets, and exalter of what was low due to the overturning by the earthquakes of the earth.

The attribution of abasing and exalting to al-Waqi'ah is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), since it is the time of the manifestation of that. In His saying ﴿abasing, exalting﴾ there is the embellishment of antithesis (tibaq) along with i'rab (grammatical construction), by the affirmation of two opposites of one thing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 56, verse 4–7:

Page 284
﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking﴾ ﴿and the mountains are crumbled to powder﴾ ﴿and they become scattered dust particles﴾ ﴿and you become three kinds of people﴾.

﴿When the earth is shaken﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the clause ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 1], and it is a substitution of the part-inclusive type (badal al-ishtimal).

Al-Rajj (ر ج ج) means agitation and intense movement. So the meaning of ﴿ruijat﴾ (was shaken) is that a shaker shakes it, namely the tremors, the sinking into the ground, and similar things that befall it.

Its emphasis by the verbal noun (ta'kid bi-l-masdar) serves to indicate that it will certainly happen, and it also allows the nunation (tanwin), which conveys magnitude and awe.

Al-Bass (ب س س) is used in the sense of crumbling (al-taftit), which is the scattering of joined parts. From it comes al-basisah, one of the names of sawiq (roasted barley flour). The meaning is that the mountains are ground to powder and blown away. This is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they ask you about the mountains. Say, "My Lord will blow them away with a blowing"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 105] ﴿and leave it a level, smooth plain﴾ [Ta-Ha: 106].

Al-Bass is also used for driving livestock; one says bassa al-ghanam, when he drove the sheep. In the hadith, "Then a people will come driving (yabissuna) their wealth and families, while Medina is better for them, if they only knew," it has the same meaning as His saying, ﴿and the day We set the mountains in motion﴾ [al-Kahf: 47], and His saying ﴿and the mountains are set in motion﴾ [al-Naba': 20]. Its emphasis by His saying "bassan" is like the emphasis in His saying "rajjan," for conveying magnitude through the nunation.

The consequence expressed by ﴿then they become scattered dust particles﴾ following ﴿and the mountains are crumbled﴾ is fitting with the meaning of bass, because when the mountains are set in motion, they move in a way that breaks them into pieces and scatters them, that is, a movement of scattering and collision.

Al-Habā' is the fine dust that appears in the rays of the sunlight. It was discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿And We will make it scattered dust particles﴾ [al-Furqan: 23] in Surah al-Furqan.

Al-Munbatt is the active participle of inbatta, the intransitive form of battahu, meaning he scattered it. This intransitive form was chosen for its suitability with His saying ﴿and the mountains are crumbled﴾, in that the passive form has a meaning similar to the intransitive. The phrase ﴿they become scattered dust particles﴾ is an eloquent simile, meaning: they became like scattered dust.

The address in ﴿and you become three kinds of people﴾ is to all people, and this is a transition (takhallus) to the purpose of the surah, which is admonition.

Page 285
Al-Azwaj means the categories. The word zawj (pair/kind) is used for a category or type, as in His saying: ﴿In them is every fruit, two kinds (zawjan)﴾. The reason is that when a category is mentioned, its counterpart is generally mentioned with it, so it becomes a pair.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 56, verses 8–12:

﴿So the companions of the right hand: what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ ﴿And the companions of the left hand: what are the companions of the left hand?﴾ ﴿And the foremost, the foremost.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones brought near,﴾ ﴿in Gardens of Bliss.﴾ You have already learned, at the explanation of His saying, ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 1], the aspect of the complement of *idha* (when). Since His saying, ﴿And you will be three kinds﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 7], is coordinated with the clauses to which *idha* was prefixed in His saying, ﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 4], it is the focal point of the purpose of the timing by the second *idha*, which is the substitute for the first *idha*. Both contain the meaning of a conditional, so this is as if it had the meaning of a response. You may make the *fa'* (so) serve to connect the response with the detail after the summary. The clause ﴿So the companions of the right hand﴾ is then the response of the second *idha*, leading to its being the response of the first *idha*, because the second is a substitute (*badal*) for it. Therefore it is permissible for this to be the response of the first *idha*, and the *fa'* is then used in both of its meanings, as was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿There is no denying its occurrence﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 2].

The detail has indicated that the categories are three. One category among them is the companions of the right hand, who are those placed on the right side in the Garden or at the gathering place. The right (*al-yamin*) is, in common usage, the side of care and honour, and it is derived from *al-yumn*, i.e., blessing.

The second category is the companions of the left hand (*al-mash'ama*). It is a name of a side derived from *al-shu'm* (ill omen), which is the opposite of *al-yumn*; it is harm and the absence of benefit. In the following verse they are called the companions of the right and the companions of the left (*al-shimal*). Thus the left is made the opposite of the right, just as *al-mash'ama* is made here the opposite of *al-maymana*, indicating that their state is a state of ill omen and evil. All of this is metaphorical (*musta'ar*) for what is known in the speech of the Arabs regarding the use of these two expressions for this figurative meaning (*kinaya*), which has spread until it has become equal to the explicit sense. Its origin came from augury and divination by birds (*al-zajr wa al-i'afa*), since they used to expect the attainment of some good from their aims through a bird or wild animal passing from the right of the diviner to his left, and they used to expect evil from its passing in the opposite manner. Its detail has been mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿They said, "Indeed you used to come to us from the right"﴾ [al-Saffat: 28] in Surat al-Saffat, and some of it has been mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿They saw in Moses and those with him an omen (*yattayyaru*)﴾ [al-A'raf: 131] in Surat al-A'raf, and at His saying, ﴿They said, "Indeed we have taken an omen (*tatayyarna*) from you"﴾ [Ya-Sin: 18] in Surat Ya-Sin.

For this reason, here it has dispensed with informing about both groups with a predicate that describes some of their states, by mentioning what is a summary of their two states, from what is suggested by the expressions *al-maymana* and *al-mash'ama* which are attributed to their companions. This is through the manner of the interrogative used for expressing wonder at the state of the two groups in happiness and misery. It is a wonder left in its ambiguity here, so that the soul of the listener may go in every possible direction, toward good and toward evil. Thus *ma* in both places is an interrogative noun.

﴿Companions of the right hand﴾ and ﴿and companions of the left hand﴾ are two predicates about *ma* in both places, like His saying, ﴿The Inevitable Reality, what is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ [al-Haqqa: 1–2] and His saying, ﴿The Striking Calamity, what is the Striking Calamity?﴾ [al-Qari'a: 1–2].

The mention of the two expressions *ashab al-maymana* and *ashab al-mash'ama* after the two interrogatives, rather than bringing their pronouns, is because the context of wonder and exposure requires explicit mention, in the same way as His saying, ﴿And what will make you know what it is?﴾ [al-Qari'a: 10].

His saying ﴿and the foremost﴾: this is the third category in the count, and they are the most excellent of the three categories. Describing them with precedence requires that they precede their like among the good-doers, whom He referred to as companions of the right hand. So they are foremost toward good, for people do not compete except for obtaining a precious thing that is desired by all people. As for evil and harm, they shrink back from it.

The true meaning of *al-sabq* (precedence) is one person arriving at a place before another person arrives. It is used here by way of metaphor (*isti'ara*), and the poet al-Nabigha combined both meanings in his saying:

You outstripped the men who strive eagerly for glory,
as the horse outstrips and hunts before the rest of the herd.

Therefore it is permissible that ﴿the foremost﴾ be used for hastening and rushing toward good in religion, as in His saying, ﴿And the foremost, the first of the emigrants and the helpers﴾ [al-Tawba: 100] in Surat Bara'a. It is also permissible that it be used for competing to attain good, as in His saying, ﴿Those hasten to good works, and they are foremost in them﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 61] in Surat al-Mu'minun.

His second saying ﴿the foremost﴾ may be taken as a predicate about the first ﴿the foremost﴾, just as He gave information about the companions of the right hand by saying ﴿what are the companions of the right hand?﴾, because it indicates a description of them with something whose true nature cannot be grasped, such that expression cannot convey it by any description other than this one, since it is the furthest that expression can reach. So if the listener wishes to imagine their qualities, he must reflect on their condition. This follows the manner of His saying, ﴿And those are the successful﴾ [al-Baqara: 5]. It is also permissible to take it as an emphasis of the first. Thus the upshot of the clause ﴿what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ and its counterpart, and the clause ﴿the foremost, the foremost﴾, is the expression of wonder at their state, and its method is metonymy (*kinaya*). But there is a difference between the two metonymies: one was through the manner of asking about the description, and the other through the manner of the impossibility of expressing it by anything other than that description.

The meaning is: their state has reached the furthest point of excellence and elevation, such that the speaker finds no predicate by which to inform about them that is more indicative of their rank than the name *al-sabiqun* (the foremost). Thus this predicate is more eloquent in indicating the nobility of their rank than informing with the interrogative *ma* of wonder in His saying, ﴿what are the companions of the right hand?﴾. This is like the saying of Abu al-Tammah al-Qaynī:

And I am of those people who are the people themselves;
when a chief among them dies, his companion stands up.

Along with that, the derivation of their title from *al-sabq* indicates that they have reached the utmost of what seekers seek.

The omission of the complement of *al-sabiqun* in the verse is for the purpose of making the description *al-sabiqun* stand in the position of a title for them, and in order to convey generality, meaning that they are foremost in every field toward which pure souls race, like His saying, ﴿And for that let those who compete compete﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 26]. Thus these are the foremost to faith in the messengers, and they are those who accompanied the messengers and prophets and received their laws from them. This category exists in all eras since antiquity, and it continues among the nations down to the Muhammadan community, and it is not a category that has ended and preceded the Muhammadan community.

The *al-sabiqun* were delayed in mention after the companions of the right hand in order to arouse the listeners' eagerness to know their category, after the other two of the three categories had been mentioned, as an encouragement to emulate them.

His saying ﴿Those are the ones brought near in Gardens of Bliss﴾ is a resumptive explanatory sentence (*isti'naf bayani*), because it answers what the saying ﴿and the foremost, the foremost﴾ provokes of the listener's question about the effect of the praise given to them.

On this basis, this became the beginning of a detailed account of the recompense of the three categories, in the manner of *al-nashr ba'da al-laff* (spreading after folding), a spreading that is somewhat disordered, a disorder required by the connection of meanings in relation to each category mentioned most recently, then by giving priority to what is more important in relation to the remaining two categories. Thus some of the speech holds onto the hems of other parts of it.

The *muqarrab* (one brought near) is more eloquent than *gharib* (one who is far), because its form indicates selection and choosing. This nearness is figurative (*majazi*): it has been likened to nearness in the sense of close association with someone near and concern for his affairs, since the one who is obedient, striving in obedience, is like one who draws near to God, that is, one who seeks nearness to Him. When he reaches a high rank in that, God brings him near, that is, treats him as one brought near and beloved. As has come in the hadith: "My servant does not cease to draw near to Me through voluntary acts until I love him; when I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes, and his foot with which he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely give him, and if he seeks refuge in Me, I will surely protect him." All these attributes are figurative, approximating the meaning of drawing near.

He did not mention the complement of *al-muqarrabun*, because it is evident that they are brought near to God, that is, by His care and preference. Likewise the time and place of the drawing near were not mentioned, for the purpose of generalizing all times and places, both those counted in this world and the Hereafter.

Making the subject a demonstrative pronoun (*ism al-isharah*) is an alert that they are deserving of what is reported about them, because of the description mentioned before the demonstrative, namely that they are foremost. This is in the manner of what was mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 5] in Surat al-Baqara.

His saying ﴿in Gardens of Bliss﴾ is a second predicate about ﴿those brought near﴾, or a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from it. Its placement after the description ﴿brought near﴾ indicates that its content is among the effects of the nearness mentioned.

The detail has indicated that the categories are three. One category among them is the companions of the right hand, who are those placed on the right side in the Garden or at the gathering place. The right (*al-yamin*) is, in common usage, the side of care and honour, and it is derived from *al-yumn*, i.e., blessing.

The second category is the companions of the left hand (*al-mash'ama*). **Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 56, verses 13–14:**

﴿A multitude from the earliest peoples﴾ ﴿and a few from the later ones﴾ is an *i'tiraḍ* (a parenthetical clause) placed between the phrase *"in gardens of delight"* and the phrase ﴿on couches interwoven﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 15].

*Thullatun* ("a multitude") is the predicate of an omitted subject, whose implied sense is "they are a multitude." The implied pronoun refers back to *al-sabiqun* ("the foremost"), so the meaning is: the foremost are a multitude from the earliest peoples and a few from the later ones.

This parenthetical clause is intended to honour the category of the foremost and to exalt them, by way of *kinayah* (indirect allusion). The words *thullah* and *qalil* ("few"), which imply that they are a small number from among many, entail that they are a rare and precious category, since in common usage precious things are few. Compare the words of al-Samaw'al, and others said it too:

*They taunt us that our number is small,*
*So I said to them: "Indeed the noble are few."*

Along with this, the Muslims are given the good news that their share in this category is like the share of the believers of earlier times, the companions of the messengers. This is because the Muslims had heard in the Qur'an and in the hadiths of the Messenger (ﷺ) the praise of the steadfastness of the earlier believers alongside the messengers and their striving. Perhaps it occurred to their minds that such a quality could not be attained after them, so God gave them the good news that they too have a share of it, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Muhammad is but a messenger; messengers have passed away before him. So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 144], up to His saying ﴿And how many a prophet fought, and with him many devoted followers; and they did not weaken for what afflicted them in the way of God, nor did they falter, nor did they submit. And God loves the patient﴾ [Al 'Imran: 146], and other verses. This is to spur the Muslims on and to kindle their resolve to take on what would join them to the likes of the earlier foremost, so that they would multiply these deeds. In a hadith: "Among those before you, a saw would be placed on one of them and he would be sawn through to his bone, yet that would not turn him away from his religion."

*Al-thullah*, with a *damma* on the *tha'* and no other vowel, is the name for a group of people in general, whether few or many. This is the statement of al-Farra', the lexicographers, al-Raghib, the author of *Lisan al-'Arab*, the author of *al-Qamus*, and al-Zamakhshari in *al-Asas*. Al-Zamakhshari, however, said in *al-Kashshaf* that *thullah* is a large nation of people. This is best understood as his intention to explain its meaning in this verse, not its lexical definition.

Because this parenthetical clause carries a sense of honour, the Qur'an placed mention of it before describing their bliss, to point to the great quality of that bliss, which suits their description as *al-sabiqun*. This contrasts with what comes later concerning the companions of the right.

The meaning of *al-awwalin* ("the earliest") is a people who precede others in time. The "first" is the one who precedes in some attribute, such as existence or conditions, over the one who is "last" or "second." Thus "firstness" is a relative matter, clarified by the context wherever it occurs.

It is apparent that *al-awwalun* here refers to the earlier nations before Islam, based on what has preceded: that the address in His saying ﴿and you were three kinds﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 7] is addressed to all people under the heading that they are people. This is because the departed who precede a nation, tribe, or sect are called "the earliest," as al-Farazdaq said:

*And Muhalhil of the poets, he is the first.*

And He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿or our earliest fathers?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 45]. They are those who are succeeded by others and who are alive, or are considered as alive; and they are called "the later ones."

The people of Islam have been described as "the later ones" in the hadith on the virtue of Friday: "We are the last, but the first on the Day of Resurrection, although they were given the Book before us," and so on. Since the foremost have been described with what indicates that they are those who race to good, and their state on the Day of Resurrection has been described immediately after that, it is known that they are the best of the righteous among the followers of divine religions, from the time of Adam until the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ). These are the ones of whom He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿with those whom God has blessed: the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous﴾ [al-Nisa': 69].

Therefore, there is no doubt that *al-awwalin* means all the earlier nations, and most of those nations were people of obstinacy and disbelief, and the believers among them were few, as many verses of the Qur'an indicate.

The believers of some nations were described by their peoples as "the oppressed," "the lowly," and "the few."

There is no doubt that *al-akhirin* ("the later ones") means the last nation, which is the Muslims.

Thus the foremost are of two groups: a group from the past nations, whose total number in the ages gone by is large, such as the companions of Musa (peace be upon him) who accompanied him in the wilderness, the companions of the prophets of the Children of Israel, and the disciples (*al-hawariyyun*). And a small group from the Islamic nation, namely those who hastened to enter Islam and accompanied the Prophet (ﷺ), as God said: ﴿And the foremost, the first of the emigrants and the helpers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 100]. Since this verse was revealed before the Hijrah, its meaning can only be fully realized among the Muslims who were in Mecca.

The *min* ("from") is partitive, as is clear. This implies that the foremost in past times and in the era of Islam, present and future, are a part of the whole. Partitiveness entails relative fewness, and the word *thullah* indicates this, while the word *qalil* ("few") is explicit in it.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 56, verses 13–14:**

﴿A multitude from the earliest peoples﴾ ﴿and a few from the later ones﴾ is an *i'tiraḍ* (a parenthetical clause) placed between the phrase *"in gardens of delight"* and the phrase ﴿on couches interwoven﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 15].

*Thullatun* ("a multitude") is the predicate of an omitted subject, whose implied sense is "they are a multitude." The implied pronoun refers back to *al-sabiqun* ("the foremost"), so the meaning is: the foremost are a multitude from the earliest peoples and a few from the later ones.

This parenthetical clause is intended to honour the category of the foremost and to exalt them, by way of *kinayah* (indirect allusion). The words *thullah* and *qalil* ("few"), which imply that they are a small number from among many, entail that they are a rare and precious category, since in common usage precious things are few. Compare the words of al-Samaw'al, and others said it too:

*They taunt us that our number is small,*
*So I said to them: "Indeed the noble are few."*

Along with this, the Muslims are given the good news that their share in this category is like the share of the believers of earlier times, the companions of the messengers. This is because the Muslims had heard in the Qur'an and in the hadiths of the Messenger (ﷺ) the praise of the steadfastness of the earlier believers alongside the messengers and their striving. Perhaps it occurred to their minds that such a quality could not be attained after them, so God gave them the good news that they too have a share of it, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Muhammad is but a messenger; messengers have passed away before him. So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 144], up to His saying ﴿And how many a prophet fought, and with him many devoted followers; and they did not weaken for what afflicted them in the way of God, nor did they falter, nor did they submit. And God loves the patient﴾ [Al 'Imran: 146], and other verses. This is to spur the Muslims on and to kindle their resolve to take on what would join them to the likes of the earlier foremost, so that they would multiply these deeds. In a hadith: "Among those before you, a saw would be placed on one of them and he would be sawn through to his bone, yet that would not turn him away from his religion."

*Al-thullah*, with a *damma* on the *tha'* and no other vowel, is the name for a group of people in general, whether few or many. This is the statement of al-Farra', the lexicographers, al-Raghib, the author of *Lisan al-'Arab*, the author of *al-Qamus*, and al-Zamakhshari in *al-Asas*. Al-Zamakhshari, however, said in *al-Kashshaf* that *thullah* is a large nation of people. This is best understood as his intention to explain its meaning in this verse, not its lexical definition.

This is because the departed who precede a nation, tribe, or sect are called "the earliest," as al-Farazdaq said:

*And Muhalhil of the poets, he is the first.*

On the verses 15–26 of Surah al-Waqi'ah

The prepositional phrase is a third predicate ("khabar thalith") of ﴿أُولَئِكَ المُقَرَّبُونَ﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 11], or a second circumstantial clause (hal thaniyah) of the demonstrative noun. This is good news of some of the bliss they will have, of the kind that souls long for in this worldly life, so as to spur them towards this destination and strive to attain it through righteous deeds. Limiting the description to what is mentioned here does not imply that the bliss is confined to what is mentioned, for Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿وفِيها ما تَشْتَهِيهِ الأنْفُسُ وتَلَذُّ الأعْيُنُ﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 71] ("And therein is whatever the souls desire and what delights the eyes").

Al-Surur (the couches) is the plural of sarir, a long, wide seat upon which the reclining or reposing person sits. It has four legs and stands about a cubit above the ground. It is made of various kinds of wood; kings make it of gold, silver, ivory, and precious wood such as ebony, while the great and affluent make it of pure iron or iron decorated or coloured with gold. The sarir is the seat of nobles and kings. Its mention in His saying ﴿عَلى سُرُرٍ مُتَقابِلِينَ﴾ was discussed in Surah al-Saffat.

Mawdunah: that whose parts are interlaced with one another, as the rings of coats of mail are linked. Its surface is woven (tuwadan) in the space between its four legs, where cushions or rugs are laid for sitting and reclining, so that the bedding is soft and neither pains the one reclining nor the one sitting. Some commentators explained mawdunah as marmulah, meaning woven with strands of gold.

Al-Ittika' (reclining) is reclining with the side inclined away and leaning on the elbow; it was discussed in Surah al-Rahman.

Al-Taqabul (facing one another) is part of the completeness of the bliss, for in it is the intimacy of seeing companions and conversing with them.

His saying ﴿يَطُوفُ عَلَيْهِمْ وِلْدانٌ مُخَلَّدُونَ﴾ explains the phrase "in gardens of bliss," and something close to it was discussed in Surah al-Saffat.

Al-tawaf is walking repeatedly around something, and it implies constant attendance upon it. The youths are described as mukhalladun, meaning they remain constantly in attendance upon them, serving them, and never cease from that. Since they have become accustomed to seeing them, it is a blessing that they remain with them. Mukhalladun has also been explained as "made eternal in the attribute of youths," that is, in youth and freshness: they are not like the youths of this world who soon become young men, then middle-aged, then elders.

Abu 'Ubaydah explained it as "adorned with earrings." The earring is called khuld and khalad, its plural is khildah, like qirdah, a Himyarite dialect which all the Arabs used; they used to beautify their boys with earrings in the ears.

Al-Akwab is the plural of kub, a vessel for wine without handle or spout, round in shape, with a wide opening for drinking; it is like a cup.

Al-Abariq is the plural of ibriq, a vessel in which wine is carried for drinkers and then poured into the akwab. The ibriq has a spout and a handle.

Al-Ka's is a vessel for wine like the kub, except that it is elongated and narrow at the drinking mouth. It was discussed in Surah al-Saffat.

Al-ka's is a generic noun that applies to one or many, so its singular form here does not denote unity, for what is meant is many cups, as the plural of akwab and abariq implies. When the vessels for carrying wine are many, the cups of the drinkers are more numerous. The singular form was preferred because the word ku'us carries heaviness, with a pointed hamzah in its middle together with the heaviness of the plural form.

Al-Ma'in means flowing, and what is meant by it is wine which, because of its abundance, flows through the channels as water flows, and is not scarce and precious as it is in this world. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وأنْهارٌ مِن خَمْرٍ لَذَّةٍ لِلشّارِبِينَ﴾ [Muhammad: 15] ("And rivers of wine, delicious to the drinkers").

Al-Ma'in does not mean water, because the ka's is not a vessel for water; its vessels are the cups. It was mentioned in Surah al-Saffat: ﴿يُطافُ عَلَيْهِمْ بِكَأْسٍ مِن مَعِينٍ﴾ [al-Saffat: 45], ﴿بَيْضاءَ لَذَّةٍ لِلشّارِبِينَ﴾ [al-Saffat: 46], ﴿لا فِيها غَوْلٌ ولا هم عَنْها يُنْزَفُونَ﴾ [al-Saffat: 47], and these are the attributes of wine.

Al-tasdi' is to be afflicted with headache, which is the pain in the head caused by the intoxication that results from drunkenness; that is, wine does not afflict them with headache.

The meaning of ʿanha is "passing beyond it," that is, no headache arising from it befalls them. Thus it is free of that, unlike the wines of this world. So ʿan is used here in the sense of causality.

﴿ولا يُنْزِفُونَ﴾ is conjoined to ﴿لا يُصَدَّعُونَ عَنْها﴾, so a complement is understood for it, indicated by the complement of ﴿لا يُصَدَّعُونَ﴾. In Surah al-Saffat He said ﴿ولا هم عَنْها يُنْزَفُونَ﴾ [al-Saffat: 47], meaning no loss of intellect befalls them because of it, as occurs to drinkers in this world.

Al-nazf is the confusion of the intellect. Its verb is passive: nuzifa 'aqluhu, like 'uniya, so he is manzuf.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (yunzafun) with a fatha on the zay, from anzafa, whose hamzah is causative. Hafs, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a kasra on the zay, from anzafa, intransitive, meaning he became drunk and his intellect departed.

Al-fakihah: fruits and herbs such as almonds and pistachios; it was discussed in Surah al-Rahman. The conjunction of fakihah to akwab means: and they attend them with fruit. That is more conducive to ease and more delightful than passing it from hand to hand, for if they desire to pick it with their hands, the branches bend down to them, since a person may desire to take a fruit from its branch.

Ma yatakhayyarun: the kind that they choose and desire; that is, they attend them with fruits of the kinds they choose, so the verb yatakhayyarun indicates the intensity of choosing.

Lahm al-tayr (the flesh of birds) is the most excellent, most desirable and most valued of meats.

The conjunction of ﴿ولَحْمِ طَيْرٍ﴾ to fakihah is like the conjunction of fakihah to akwab.

Al-ishtiha' is the verbal noun of ishtaha, a derivation from shahwah, which is the love of attaining a desired thing, whether sensory or immaterial. It is said shahiyy like radiyy, and sha as da'a. The more common usage is ishtaha, and the infixed form here conveys intensification.

The mention of fruit before meat may be because fruits are more precious. By this the difference between fakihah and lahm tayr becomes clear: choice is assigned to the first, desire to the second. Also, desire is more closely tied to food than to fruits, so the pleasure of breaking the appetite with food is a pleasure beyond the pleasure of its good taste, while abundance of choice in fruits is the pleasure of variety of kinds.

﴿وحَوَرٌ عِينٌ﴾ is conjoined to ﴿وِلْدانٌ مُخَلَّدُونَ﴾, meaning: and there shall attend them ḥūr ʿīn.

Al-ḥūr al-ʿīn: women possessing ḥawar, which was discussed in Surah al-Rahman, and possessing ʿayn, which is breadth of the eye, discussed in Surah al-Saffat.

Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Ja'far read (wa-ḥūrin ʿīnin) with kasra in both words, so that ḥūr is conjoined to akwab by conjunction of meaning, as in the line: "and they have made the eyebrows and eyes elegant," meaning "and they have blackened the eyes." Or it is conjoined to (jannat): that is, "and in ḥūr ʿīn," meaning they are in ḥūr ʿīn or surrounded by them and encircled by them.

What is meant is the spouses of the foremost ones in Paradise, and they are those restricted within tents.

Al-amthal are likenesses. The entry of the particle of comparison kaf upon amthal is for emphasis, like His saying ﴿لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ﴾ [al-Shura: 11]. The meaning: they are like pearls, hidden.

Al-lu'lu' is pearl; its explanation was given under His saying ﴿يُحَلَّوْنَ فِيها مِن أساوِرَ مِن ذَهَبٍ ولُؤْلُؤًا﴾ [al-Hajj: 23] in Surah al-Hajj.

Al-maknun is that which is stored and hidden because of its preciousness; it was discussed in Surah al-Saffat.

(Jaza'an) is in the accusative as an object of purpose, governed by an implied verb indicated by al-muqarrabun, meaning: We gave them that as a reward. It may also be that jaza'an is a verbal noun that comes in place of its verb, the sense being: We rewarded them with reward.

On both readings the clause is a parenthetical insertion, serving to show their honour, in that the kinds of bliss they were granted were made a reward for a deed they had performed. This completes their being among the muqarrabun.

Then He completed the description of the bliss with His saying ﴿لا يَسْمَعُونَ فِيها لَغْوًا ولا تَأْثِيمًا﴾. This is a spiritual blessing, for the soul's freedom from hearing what it does not love to hear, and from hearing what it hates to hear, and from harm, is a blessing that brings ease of mind and occupies it with hearing what is beloved.

Al-laghw is speech that is not regarded, such as idle talk, and speech that has no purpose.

Al-ta'thim is blame and denunciation; it is the verbal noun of atthama, when one attributes sin to another.

The pronoun in (fiha) refers to (jannat al-na'im).

He followed the mention of this blessing with the mention of another blessing from among the favours, namely, what is heard that conveys honour, for honouring is a spiritual pleasure which gives the soul dignity and pride: ﴿إلّا قِيلًا سَلامًا سَلامًا﴾. This is an exception from ﴿لَغْوًا ولا تَأْثِيمًا﴾, by way of affirming a thing through what resembles its well-known opposite, which in rhetoric is called "affirming praise through what resembles dispraise." It has a great place in eloquence, as in the saying of al-Nabighah:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords have notches from the clashing of battalions."

So the exception is connected in appearance, and this is what is expressed as the disconnected exception according to the sense of the meaning. On this basis, qilan is in the accusative as an exception, not as a substitute for (laghwan).

The first (salaman) is the object of (qilan), that is, this utterance whose implied form is "we greet with peace," so it is a quoted clause after the verb "say."

The second (salaman) is a repetition of the first, a repetition not for emphasis but to indicate succession: peace following peace, like His saying ﴿كَلّا إذا دُكَّتِ الأرْضُ دَكًّا دَكًّا﴾ [al-Fajr: 21] and the saying "I read grammar chapter by chapter." Or it is intended to indicate the great number of those who greet, and so it signals, together with honour, that they are exalted and venerated. The difference between the two interpretations is that the first indicates repetition by repetition of times, and the second indicates repetition by repetition of those greeting.

This utterance they receive from the angels appointed over Paradise, as He the Exalted said: ﴿والمَلائِكَةُ يَدْخُلُونَ عَلَيْهِمْ مِن كُلِّ بابٍ سَلامٌ عَلَيْكم بِما صَبَرْتُمْ﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23], and some of them receive it from others, as He the Exalted said: ﴿وتَحِيَّتُهم فِيها سَلامٌ﴾ [Yunus: 10].

The word (salaman) came in the accusative rather than the nominative, although the nominative indicates intensification more strongly, as they mentioned regarding His saying ﴿قالُوا سَلامًا قالَ سَلامٌ﴾ [Hud: 69] in Surah Hud and Surah al-Dhariyat, because it was intended to make it a substitute for (qilan).

That is more conducive to ease and more delightful than passing it from hand to hand, for if they desire to pick it with their hands, the branches bend down to them, since a person may desire to take a fruit from its branch.

Lahm al-tayr (the flesh of birds) is the most excellent, most desirable and most valued of meats.

What is meant is the spouses of the foremost ones in Paradise, and they are those restricted within tents.

That is more conducive to ease and more delightful than passing it from hand to hand, for if they desire to pick it with their hands, the branches bend down to them, since a person may desire to take a fruit from its branch.

Ma yatakhayyarun: the kind that they choose and desire; that is, they attend them with fruits of the kinds they choose, so the verb yatakhayyarun indicates the intensity of choosing.

Lahm al-tayr (the flesh of birds) is the most excellent, most desirable and most valued of meats.

Al-ishtiha' is the verbal noun of ishtaha, a derivation from shahwah, which is the love of attaining a desired thing, whether sensory or immaterial. It is said shahiyy like radiyy, and sha as da'a. The more common usage is ishtaha, and the infixed form here conveys intensification.

The mention of fruit before meat may be because fruits are more precious. By this the difference between fakihah and lahm tayr becomes clear: choice is assigned to the first, desire to the second. Also, desire is more closely tied to food than to fruits, so the pleasure of breaking the appetite with food is a pleasure beyond the pleasure of its good taste, while abundance of choice in fruits is the pleasure of variety of kinds.

Or it is conjoined to (jannat): that is, "and in ḥūr ʿīn," meaning they are in ḥūr ʿīn or surrounded by them and encircled by them.

What is meant is the spouses of the foremost ones in Paradise, and they are those restricted within tents.

Al-laghw is speech that is not regarded, such as idle talk, and speech that has no purpose.

Al-ta'thim is blame and denunciation; it is the verbal noun of atthama, when one attributes sin to another.

The pronoun in (fiha) refers to (jannat al-na'im).

He followed the mention of this blessing with the mention of another blessing from among the favours, namely, what is heard that conveys honour, for honouring is a spiritual pleasure which gives the soul dignity and pride: ﴿إلّا قِيلًا سَلامًا سَلامًا﴾. Its surface is woven (tuwadan) in the space between its four legs, where cushions or rugs are laid for sitting and reclining, so that the bedding is soft and neither pains the one reclining nor the one sitting. Some commentators explained mawdunah as marmulah, meaning woven with strands of gold.

Al-Ittika' (reclining) is reclining with the side inclined away and leaning on the elbow; it was discussed in Surah al-Rahman.

Al-Taqabul (facing one another) is part of the completeness of the bliss, for in it is the intimacy of seeing companions and conversing with them.

Al-Ka's is a vessel for wine like the kub, except that it is elongated and narrow at the drinking mouth. It was discussed in Surah al-Saffat.

Some commentators explained mawdunah as marmulah, meaning woven with strands of gold.

Al-Ittika' (reclining) is reclining with the side inclined away and leaning on the elbow; it was discussed in Surah al-Rahman.

Al-Taqabul (facing one another) is part of the completeness of the bliss, for in it is the intimacy of seeing companions and conversing with them.

Al-nazf is the confusion of the intellect. Its verb is passive: nuzifa 'aqluhu, like 'uniya, so he is manzuf.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (yunzafun) with a fatha on the zay, from anzafa, whose hamzah is causative. Hafs, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a kasra on the zay, from anzafa, intransitive, meaning he became drunk and his intellect departed.

Ma yatakhayyarun: the kind that they choose and desire; that is, they attend them with fruits of the kinds they choose, so the verb yatakhayyarun indicates the intensity of choosing.

Lahm al-tayr (the flesh of birds) is the most excellent, most desirable and most valued of meats.

He combined the two descriptions because the fruit of this world is never free of one of the two opposites of these descriptions: its owners withhold it, and if they do not withhold it, it has a season in which it comes to an end.

The furush (couches) is the plural of firash, with a kasra on the fa', and it is what is spread out. It was discussed in Surah al-Rahman. ﴿Raised﴾ (marfu'ah) is a description of furush, meaning raised upon bedsteads (al-asirrah), that is, not spread on the ground.

It is also possible that by furush is meant the bedsteads, by the naming of a thing with the name of what it rests in.

[Page 301]

When the mention of the couches (*furush*) came up, and they are among the things prepared for reclining and lying down at rest in the dwelling, the thought comes to mind immediately that the wide-eyed maidens (*al-hur al-'in*) are seated with them on those couches, so the listener longs to hear their description. Thus the sentence ﴿Indeed, We created them with a special creation﴾ serves as an explanation, because the thought that arises is like a question about the attributes of these female companions.

The feminine pronoun in *anshi'nahunna* (﴿We created them﴾) refers to something not mentioned in the speech, but which is present in the minds of the listeners, like the verse of Abu Tammam at the beginning of one of his odes:

*They are the women who cut their hands, Yusuf's companions and their like.*

Another example is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿until she was hidden behind the veil﴾ [Sad: 32]. This is the best way to explain the verse, so the word *furush* in the verse is used in both of its meanings, and it is *marfu'* (raised), used in its literal and figurative senses, that is, in the physical raising and the metaphorical raising.

*Al-insha'* (creation) means bringing into existence and originating, and so it includes the restoration of what existed and then ceased. God has called restoration *insha'* in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Then God brings forth the final creation﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 20]. Accordingly, the wives of the believers who were their spouses in this world for those who enter Paradise are included, and it also includes the bringing into existence of new women (*unuf*), created in Paradise for the bliss of its people.

His saying ﴿and We made them virgins﴾ includes both categories.

*Al-'urub* is the plural of *'arud*, with a fatha on the 'ayn. It is said *'arabahu* with a fatha and then a kasra, and it is pluralized as *'arabat* in the same manner, and it is a term specific to women. The statements of the lexicographers differ on its explanation, and the best thing that brings them together is that *al-'urub* is the woman who makes herself lovable to a man, or who has the quality of one who makes herself lovable, even if she does not intend to be lovable, such as by laughing excessively in the presence of a man, or joking, or playing, or speaking submissively, or lisping in speech without a cause, or flirting with a man, or being easy-going in his company, or behaving coquettishly and showing opposition to a man's desires in play rather than seriously, or showing displeasure at him in the same way, like being angry without anger but rather as a means of sitting heavily upon the man. Nabih ibn al-Hajjaj said:

*That is my 'arisa angry, wanting to part from me. Did you intend separation, or coquetry?*

The witness is in his saying *am li-dalal* (or for coquetry). God, Exalted is He, said:

﴿So do not be soft in speech, lest one in whose heart is a disease should covet, but speak with a noble word﴾ [al-Ahzab: 32], and He said ﴿and let them not stamp their feet so that what they conceal of their adornment may be known﴾ [al-Nur: 31].

They only explained it as "one who makes herself lovable" because when they saw these actions attract a man's love for the woman, they thought that the woman does them in order to gain the man's love. For this reason, some of them explained *al-'arub* as "the one in heat" (*al-mughtalima*), but that is only one state of some of the *'urub*. It is reported from 'Ikrimah that *al-'urub* is "the one who flatters" (*al-malaqah*).

*Al-'urub* is a name for these meanings, whether combined or separated. They treated it as a name that indicates qualities, not as a derived form from verbs, and therefore they did not mention a verb or a verbal noun for it. In origin it is derived from *al-i'rab* and *al-ta'rib*, which is speaking with obscene speech.

*Al-'irabah*, with a kasra on the 'ayn, is a noun from *al-ta'rib*, and its verb is *'arrabat* and *a'rabat*. It is therefore mostly attributed to the pronoun of the woman. It seems they regarded it as an expression of what should not be disclosed openly. Then this derivation was forgotten, and *al-'urub* was treated like non-derived nouns. It is also said *'arabah*, like *'arub*. The plural of *al-'urub* is *'urub*, and the plural of *'arabah* is *'arabat*.

In the dialect of the people of Makkah, the female who makes herself lovable is called *al-'arabah* and *al-shakilah*. In the dialect of the people of Madinah she is called *al-ghanijah*, and in the dialect of Iraq *al-shakilah*, meaning one possessing *shakl* (with a fatha on the kaf), which is coquetry and *al-ta'arrub*.

*Al-atrab* is the plural of *tirb*, with a kasra on the taa' (the upper dotted letter) and a sukun on the ra'. It is the woman whose age is equal to the age of the women to whom she is attached. It has been said that *tirb* is specific to women, and that a man of equal age is called *qarn wildah*.

So the meaning is that they are made to be of equal age, with no difference between them, that is, they are in the same youthful age, so their beauty is not different in all aspects of beauty. On this basis, the women of Paradise are described as *atrab*, each one of them being equal to the others.

Hamzah, Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, and Khalaf read *'urban* with a sukun on the ra' (a light sukun), and this is the consistent form in the dialect of Tamim for this word.

The *lam* in ﴿for the companions of the right hand﴾ is claimed by both *anshi'nahunna* and *ja'alnahunna*, to convey emphasis on the concern for the companions of the right hand, which is derived from the context in His saying ﴿and the companions of the right hand, what of the companions of the right hand?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 27], and the rest of the verse.

[Page 303]

Know that what is given to the companions of the right hand is not contrary to the kinds of what is given to the foremost (*al-sabiqun*), nor is what is given to the foremost contrary to what is given to the companions of the right hand. The shade, the poured water, and the fact that their spouses are *'urban atraban* are not mentioned in the same way for the foremost, though it is certainly theirs, since they do not fall short of the companions of the right hand. Likewise, what is mentioned for the foremost, such as the youths (*wildan*), their cups (*akwab*) and their ewers (*abariq*), the flesh of birds, the fact that their spouses are *hur 'in*, and that they hear nothing but the word "Peace, peace," is not mentioned in the same way for the companions of the right hand, even though the people of Paradise have what the souls desire and the eyes delight in. Many verses mention that they were given things that are not mentioned as given to them in this verse, such as His saying ﴿and their greeting therein is peace﴾ [Yunus: 10]. So the purpose is not to distribute the bliss or to restrict it, but the purpose is to enumerate it and to arouse longing for it, although it is known from the context that the foremost are higher in rank than the companions of the right hand. What indicates the difference between the two ranks is that He mentioned the bliss of the foremost as "a recompense for what they used to do," for the reason we have explained in it, and this was not mentioned in the bliss of the companions of the right hand. The gist of the purpose of all this is to honor both groups.

Many verses mention that they were given things that are not mentioned as given to them in this verse, such as His saying ﴿and their greeting therein is peace﴾ [Yunus: 10]. So the purpose is not to distribute the bliss or to restrict it, but the purpose is to enumerate it and to arouse longing for it, although it is known from the context that the foremost are higher in rank than the companions of the right hand. What indicates the difference between the two ranks is that He mentioned the bliss of the foremost as "a recompense for what they used to do," for the reason we have explained in it, and this was not mentioned in the bliss of the companions of the right hand. The gist of the purpose of all this is to honor both groups.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 56, verses 39–40:

﴿A multitude from the earlier peoples﴾ ﴿and a multitude from the later peoples﴾, i.e., the companions of the right hand: a multitude from the earlier peoples and a multitude from the later peoples. The discussion of this is like the discussion of His words ﴿A multitude from the earlier peoples﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 13] ﴿and a few from the later peoples﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 14], so refer back to it.

In the tafsir of al-Qurtubi, it is related from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq that both multitudes are from the Muhammadan community: a multitude from its earliest part and a multitude from its remainder. He did not point out the chain of transmission (sanad) of this report.

The reason it is placed after the mention of their bliss is to indicate that the honour and rarity of this category are below the honour of the category of the foremost (al-sabiqun). The foremost are more honoured, and this implication is one of the consequences of the structures derived from the arrangement of the composition of the speech.

﴿And the companions of the left: what are the companions of the left?﴾ ﴿In scorching wind and boiling water﴾ ﴿And a shade of black smoke﴾ ﴿Neither cool nor pleasant﴾

This leads to the third of the three categories, namely the people of *al-mashaqqah* (opposition and hostility). The discussion of the phrase ﴿what are the companions of the left?﴾ and of the position of the clause ﴿in scorching wind﴾ after it is the same as the discussion of ﴿and the companions of the right: what are the companions of the right?﴾ (al-Waqi'ah: 27) ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾ (al-Waqi'ah: 28).

*Al-sumum* (السموم) is a very hot wind with no moisture in it. It is apparently derived from *al-summ* (poison), which is what destroys when it touches the body.

*Al-hamim* (الحميم) is water that is extremely hot.

*Al-yahmum* (اليحموم) is black smoke. It is on the pattern *yaf'ul* and is derived from *al-hummam* (حمم), on the pattern *Surad*, which is a name for charcoal. *Al-hummah* is a single piece of charcoal. The pattern *yaf'ul* here comes as a noun in which this derivation is intended, and this is not a productive pattern.

The particle *min* (مِن) in ﴿min yahmum﴾ is explicative (bayaniyyah), since the word *zill* (shade) here refers to the very substance of *al-yahmum*, that is, the black smoke.

The word *zill* is described as ﴿min yahmum﴾ to indicate that it is the shade of the smoke of the flame of Hell. Dense smoke casts a shade, since its density blocks the light of the sun. Only the shade of the smoke is mentioned because it is set in contrast with the extended shade prepared for the companions of the right, in His saying ﴿and extended shade﴾ (al-Waqi'ah: 30). That is, the companions of the left have no shade except the shade of *al-yahmum*. This is of the nature of *tahakkum* (mockery, sarcastic usage).

To realize the meaning of mockery, this shade is described by something that denies coolness from it and denies its nobility. The coolness of a shade is what it provides in its place by repelling the heat of the sun. The nobility of a shade consists of the good qualities found in shades, such as its being safe from the blowing of hot winds, the safety of the place it shades from insects and filth, and the safety of its ground from stones and the like. This is because *al-karim* (noble) in every kind is the one that combines the greatest number of the good qualities of its kind, as was mentioned in His saying ﴿Indeed, there has been delivered to me a noble letter﴾ (al-Naml: 29) in Surat al-Naml.

Thus the shade of *al-yahmum* is described with a specific description, namely the negation of coolness from it, and this is followed by a general description, namely the negation of the nobility of shades from it. In describing it by the negation of the good qualities of shades, there is a reminder to the listeners of what the companions of the left have been deprived of, perhaps so that they will beware of the causes of falling into deprivation. To convey this reminder, he turned away from describing the shade by heat and harm to describing it by the negation of coolness and the negation of nobility.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 56, verses 45–48:

﴿Indeed, they were before that affluent.﴾ ﴿And they used to persist in the great violation.﴾ ﴿And they used to say, "When we have died and become dust and bones, will we indeed be resurrected?﴾ ﴿Or our forefathers of old?"﴾

This is a justification (ta'lil) for the punishment that the People of the Left (ashab al-shimal) receive. It is therefore necessary that what this justification includes was among the states of their disbelief, and that it had an effect in bringing the punishment upon them, as indicated by the conjunction of "And they used to persist in the great violation" and "And they used to say," etc., upon it.

As for their persistence in violation and their denial of resurrection, there is no doubt that they are a cause of the punishment, because God threatened them for it and they did not desist from it. What remains to be considered is His saying, "Indeed, they were before that affluent," for affluence in living is not in itself a crime, and many a believer has lived in affluence, and not every disbeliever is affluent in his living. So affluence is not an independent cause for the requital with which they were treated.

The interpretation of this justification is then either: that affluence is a cause by way of its combination with what is mentioned after it, namely that their persistence in violation and their denial of resurrection were two great crimes, because they were surrounded by ingratitude for the blessing of affluence which God had bestowed upon them, in the manner of His saying, "And you make your provision that you deny" [al-Waqi'ah: 82]. Thus affluence is a part of the cause, not an independent cause. And in this there is something of the meaning of His saying, "Leave Me with the deniers, possessors of blessing, and give them respite a little" [al-Muzzammil: 11].

Or it is intended that affluence in living attached their hearts to the world and made them content with it, so that this became something that filled their thoughts with the denial of the Hereafter. Thus the intended affluence is that to which this denial is an accompaniment and with which it is closely bound. Its equivalent is His saying, "And those who disbelieve enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat, and the Fire is their abode" [Muhammad: 12].

(Page 306)
Al-Mutrafin is explained as meaning "arrogant towards accepting the truth." Al-mutraf is the passive participle of atrafahu, i.e., made him one possessing "turfah" (with a dammah on the ta' and a sukun on the ra'), meaning abundant blessing. Its form is passive because the real agent of the affluence is not known, as is the case with verbs that are constructed with the figurative rational attribution (al-isnad al-majazi al-'aqli), for which there is no real rational counterpart. It is not to be estimated as "God made him affluent," because the Arabs did not estimate it that way; this is of the type of "a speaker said" and "a questioner asked."

The People of the Left were described as affluent because none of them is free of affluence at least in some of his states and times, from the blessings of food, drink, women and wine, all of which deserve gratitude to their Giver; and they had mixed these with associating partners in all their circumstances. Or, because when they restricted their gaze to thinking about the fleeting life, this diverted them from reflecting and reasoning about the soundness of what the Messenger (ﷺ) called them to. This is the basis for making affluence in the world one of the causes of their being requited with the mentioned requital.

The reference in His saying "before that" is to "scorching wind and boiling water" [al-Waqi'ah: 42] and "a shade of black smoke" [al-Waqi'ah: 43], interpreting them as what has been mentioned; i.e., they were before this day, which is what they were in the worldly life.

Al-hinth: sin, disobedience, and what one is strictly blamed for. From it is the saying "he broke his oath (hanatha fi yaminihi)," i.e., he neglected what he swore to, thereby bringing hardship upon himself.

It is possible that al-hinth is the breaking of an oath, for they used to swear that there would be no resurrection. God said, "And they swore by God with their most emphatic oaths that God will not raise up one who dies" [al-Nahl: 38]. That is among the great violation. And God said, "And they swore by God with their most emphatic oaths that if a sign came to them, they would surely believe in it" [al-An'am: 109]; and the sign of the inimitability of the Qur'an had come to them, yet they did not believe in it.

Al-'azim: strong within its kind, i.e., a severe sin; and the great violation is associating partners with God. In the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "I said: 'O Messenger of God, which sin is greatest?' He said: 'That you set up a rival to God while He created you.'" And God said, "Indeed, association is a great injustice" [Luqman: 13].

(Page 307)
The meaning of yusirrun: they persist in it, not accepting any moving away from it, i.e., they do not place for the call any consideration of examining the invalidity of the creed of associating partners.

The form of the present tense in yusirrun and yaqulun indicates the repetition of the persistence and the saying from them. The mention of the verb kanu is to convey that this was their habit.

What is meant by His saying "And they used to say: when we have died and become dust, etc." is that they believed in the impossibility of resurrection after that condition.

They argue in this that saying that implies they believe resurrection is impossible.

The interrogation is one of denial, a metonymy for deeming it impossible and far-fetched. A parallel to "when we have died and become dust, etc." has been mentioned in Surat al-Saffat.

The majority read "a-idha mitna" with both interrogatives retained, i.e., "when we have died, shall we indeed [be raised]?" Nafi', al-Kisa'i and Abu Ja'far read with the interrogative in "a-idha mitna" and the declarative in "inna lamab'uthun."

The majority read "a-wa-aba'una" with a fatha on the waw, as a conjunctive waw that conjoins an interrogative to an interrogative; the interrogative hamza was placed before the conjunction because interrogation takes precedence, and the interrogative was repeated for emphasis on far-fetchedness. What is meant by "saying" in His saying "And they used to say" etc. is that they believed in the fulfilment of the content of that interrogation.

Al-Mutrafin is explained as meaning "arrogant towards accepting the truth." Al-mutraf is the passive participle of atrafahu, i.e., made him one possessing "turfah" (with a dammah on the ta' and a sukun on the ra'), meaning abundant blessing. Its form is passive because the real agent of the affluence is not known, as is the case with verbs that are constructed with the figurative rational attribution (al-isnad al-majazi al-'aqli), for which there is no real rational counterpart. It is not to be estimated as "God made him affluent," because the Arabs did not estimate it that way; this is of the type of "a speaker said" and "a questioner asked."

The People of the Left were described as affluent because none of them is free of affluence at least in some of his states and times, from the blessings of food, drink, women and wine, all of which deserve gratitude to their Giver; and they had mixed these with associating partners in all their circumstances. Or, because when they restricted their gaze to thinking about the fleeting life, this diverted them from reflecting and reasoning about the soundness of what the Messenger (ﷺ) called them to. This is the basis for making affluence in the world one of the causes of their being requited with the mentioned requital.

Al-hinth: sin, disobedience, and what one is strictly blamed for. From it is the saying "he broke his oath (hanatha fi yaminihi)," i.e., he neglected what he swore to, thereby bringing hardship upon himself.

It is possible that al-hinth is the breaking of an oath, for they used to swear that there would be no resurrection. God said, "And they swore by God with their most emphatic oaths that God will not raise up one who dies" [al-Nahl: 38]. That is among the great violation. And God said, "And they swore by God with their most emphatic oaths that if a sign came to them, they would surely believe in it" [al-An'am: 109]; and the sign of the inimitability of the Qur'an had come to them, yet they did not believe in it.

Al-'azim: strong within its kind, i.e., a severe sin; and the great violation is associating partners with God. In the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "I said: 'O Messenger of God, which sin is greatest?' He said: 'That you set up a rival to God while He created you.'" And God said, "Indeed, association is a great injustice" [Luqman: 13].

What is meant by "saying" in His saying "And they used to say" etc. is that they believed in the fulfilment of the content of that interrogation.

[Page 308]

Having mentioned the punishment that the companions of the left will encounter, and its cause, which is their ingratitude for the blessing, and since the purpose of that was to warn the polytheists, and since their denial of the Resurrection was the thing that most reinforced their persistence in disbelief, God commanded His Messenger ﷺ to address them by affirming that the Resurrection will happen and that it includes them, their forefathers, and all people. That is, inform them that the first and the last, meaning they and their forefathers, will be raised on the appointed day with God. Thus the account of their condition on the day "the earth will be shaken" and what follows it has concluded.

The discourse opens with the command to speak, to draw attention to it, just as it opens similar passages with it in many verses, so that this is a conveyance from God, exalted is He.

Accordingly, His saying ﴿Say: Indeed, the first and the last﴾ and so on is a new, independent resumptive sentence (istinaf ibtida'i, a sentence beginning a fresh topic), connected to the context of relating their saying: ﴿When we have died and become dust…﴾ (the verse).

By "the first" is meant those to whom the description "first" applies in relation to those after them, and by "the last" those to whom another description applies in relation to those before them.

The meaning of "gathered" (majmu'un) is that they will be raised and assembled all together. The Resurrection is not in successive groups at different times, as the death of people was; rather, the first and the last will be raised on one day. This refutes what was implied by their statement ﴿Or our forefathers, the first ones?﴾ in their reasoning to deem the Resurrection unlikely: they regarded the earlier death of those who died before them as more evidence for the impossibility of their being raised, since centuries had passed over them and no group of them had been raised up to the time of this saying. So the meaning is: you [will be raised].

Emphasizing the report with "inna" (indeed) and the lam is to counter their denial of its content.

The word "mīqāt" (appointed time) here means time and term. Its original form is a noun of instrument for time, but they extended its use so that it is applied to the time itself, such that the mīm and the alif are no longer considered to indicate a separate meaning. They extended it further, applying it to a place for a particular act. This is probably derived from considering the precision and definition in fixing a time; among its examples are the mawaqit of the Hajj, which are places where the pilgrim enters the state of ihram for the Hajj at which he must not pass without being in that state. Among its uses is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas: "The Messenger of God ﷺ did not fix a specific limit (hadd) for wine."

It is also permissible to interpret it in this verse as the meaning of a time.

The verb "majmu'un" has been construed as implying the sense of "driven" (masuqun), so that the prepositional phrase introduced by "ila" (to) is governed by it, denoting the endpoint. Otherwise, the apparent construction of "majmu'un" would be with "fi" (in).

[Page 309]

The attaching of its prepositional object to it through "ila" conveys that they are driven toward it until they reach it, and thus it indicates a place. This is part of the concision (ijaz).

The annexation of "mīqāt" to "a known day" is because the gathering takes place on that day. Since the gathering occurring on that day is a gathering at that appointed time, there is an association between the time and the day that justifies annexing the time to it by the slightest association. This is more precise than making the annexation explicative (bayaniyya).

This is an allusion to the warning, with what they will encounter on that day which they denied.

Then indeed you, O you who are astray and deniers, [will eat from a tree of zaqqum]... This is part of what the Prophet (ﷺ) was ordered to say to them.

This ranked delay is like that in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say, "Yes, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected; then you will surely be informed of what you did"﴾ [al-Taghabun: 7]. Describing them as "astray, deniers" refers to their saying, "When we are dust, etc."

The describing of them as "astray" before "deniers" observes the order of occurrence, for they strayed from the truth and so denied resurrection, in order that they be wary of straying and reflect upon the proofs of resurrection. This is what the address with this warning of impending punishment requires.

Page 310
The tree of zaqqum is among the trees of punishment, as mentioned in Surat al-Dukhan.

Al-hamim is water of intense boiling, which was mentioned in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿For them is a drink of boiling water﴾ [al-An'am: 70] in Surat al-An'am, and was mentioned shortly before in this surah.

The purpose of His saying ﴿so you will fill your bellies from it﴾ is to depict their condition as horrifying in their recompense, in contrast to their state of luxury in the world, filling their bellies with food and drink, a filling that made them forget their attention to it and their drinking from reflection upon their destiny.

The horror is increased in the simile in His saying ﴿and drink as the thirsty camels drink﴾, as will come. Repeating the verb "drinking" serves emphasis and repeated evocation of that dreadful image. The meaning of "drinking upon it" may be that (ʿalā) here indicates elevation, i.e., they drink above it the boiling water; it is also permissible to understand from the particle (ʿalā) the sense of (maʿa, "with"), to express wonder at the horribleness of their state, i.e., they drink this burning water together with what they ate of the tree of zaqqum, which another verse describes as boiling in the bellies like the boiling of hamim, so that it conveys that they gulp it down and cannot refrain.

The (min) entering on "tree" (shajar) is for beginning (ibtida'iyyah), i.e., eating that is taken from the tree of zaqqum. The second (min), entering on "zaqqum", is explicative (bayaniyyah), because the tree is what is named zaqqum.

The feminine pronoun for the tree in His saying ﴿so you will fill your bellies from it﴾ is because pronouns for plurals of non-rational things usually come feminine.

As for the pronoun in ʿalayhi, it came in the masculine form because it refers to the eating derived from His saying "la-ākilūn" (you will eat), i.e., upon that eating, by interpreting the verbal noun as the passive participle, like "al-khalq" meaning "al-makhluq".

Al-Hīm is the plural of ahyam, which is the camel afflicted by al-hayam (with a dammah on the ha'), a disease affecting camels that causes fever in the intestines so that it never ceases drinking and is never satisfied; i.e., they drink from the boiling water a drinking that does not stop, so its pains are continuous.
