**Verse 56:** ﴿This is their hospitality on the Day of Judgment.﴾

This is an interjection between the sentences of the address, directed at listeners other than the ones addressed. So there is no shift (iltifat) in the third-person pronoun.

The reference of "this" (hadha) is to what was mentioned: eating al-zaqqum (the bitter tree of Hell) and drinking al-him (camels afflicted with extreme thirst).

Nuzul (ﻧُﺰُﻝ), with a ḍamma or sukūn on the zāy, means the food prepared for a guest. Here it is a tashbih tahakkumi (ironic comparison), like the ironic metaphor (istiʿara tahakkumiyya) in the verse of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:

*You alighted in the station of guests among us, so we hastened the hospitality before you could revile us.*

*We hosted you, and hastened your hospitality before dawn with a heavy millstone (club).*

And the verse of Abu al-Shaʿthar al-Dabbi, whose name is Musa ibn Suhaym:

*When a tyrant came to us as a guest with his army, we made the spears and the keen swords his hospitality.*

Page 312

"The Day of Judgment" (yawm al-din) means the Day of Recompense, i.e., this is their recompense for their deeds, similar to His words just before: a reward for what they used to do. Describing the Day of Judgment as the time of their nuzul indicates that what is termed "hospitality" is in fact a recompense for their deeds. This is tajrid (abstraction) of the ironic comparison, and it is an indicator (qarina) of the irony, as in the verse of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum: *a heavy millstone (club)*.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 56, verse 57:

﴿We created you, so why do you not believe?﴾

He followed the refutation of their denial of resurrection with an argument for its possibility and an approximation of the manner of the restoration (al-i'adah) which they deemed impossible. Thus he argued for the possibility of re-creation by pointing out that God created them the first time, so it is not far-fetched that He should recreate them. The Exalted said: ﴿As We originated the first creation, We will repeat it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 104], because they did not deny that, and the aim is not to establish that God created them.

This statement may be part of what he was commanded to say to them, and it may be an independent new statement (isti'naf). In both cases the address is directed to the listeners, so there is no iltifat (shift of pronoun) in the pronoun of "khalaqnakum."

The placing of the predicate-subject (al-musnad ilayhi) before the verbal predicate (al-musnad al-fi'li) serves a meaning that strengthens the judgment, as a response to their deeming it impossible that God be able to re-create them after the perishing of most of their bodies, when they have become dust and bones. This is thus a reminder to them of what they had forgotten: that God created them, and since they did not act upon the implication of that knowledge by deeming the re-creation impossible, they were treated as one who doubts that God created them. So the purpose of strengthening the judgment is to lead to what is to be derived from it, from His saying ﴿Have you considered what you emit?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 58] up to His saying ﴿We are not outstripped from replacing your likes﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 60]. The parallel to this verse in the composition of its structure and the sequence built upon it is His saying ﴿We created them and strengthened their makeup, and when We wish, We can substitute their likes, a complete substitution﴾ [al-Insan: 28] in Surat al-Insan.

Its position is that of an argument and a cause ('illah) for the content of the sentence ﴿Indeed, the former and the latter will surely be gathered﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 50]; for this reason it is not conjoined by a conjunction (lam tu'taf).

Page 313

Following upon this reminder is an exhortation to them to believe (tahdid 'alayhim al-tasdiq), that is, in the second creation, which is resurrection, since that is what they did not believe in.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (*al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr*) on Sūrah 56, verses 58–59:**

﴿Have you considered that which you emit?﴾ ﴿Is it you who create it, or are We the Creators?﴾ This is a *tafrīʿ* (a derivation, or consequence) of ﴿We created you﴾ [al-Wāqiʿah: 57], meaning: We created you with the creation that you have not seen, but you are certain that We created you. So reflect upon the creation of offspring, so that you may know that the re-creation resembles the initial creation. Five beings, differing in their states but united in their outcome, are mentioned, for in each of them there is the bringing into existence of something that was non-existent, and in all of them there is the gradual coming into being until life is established through them. The creation of offspring from lifeless water is begun, and perhaps this is the substance of life in your offspring in the wombs from the *nuṭaf* (drops of seminal fluid), an existence preceded by non-existence.

The interrogation is for *taqrīr* (affirmation, eliciting an admission), by specifying the creator of the embryo from the drop, for they cannot help but acknowledge that God is the Creator of the offspring from the drop, and this necessarily entails His power over what is of the same kind as re-creation.

The argument was begun by placing the clause ﴿Is it you who create it﴾ first, in addition to nullifying their doubt, for they analogised hidden matters to what is observed in their hearts: "We will not be restored after we have become dust and bones." Their proper course would have been to analogise from the formation of the embryo from the origin of the seminal drop, and so say: "Decayed bones do not become living beings." Otherwise, they never claimed at all that they were creators. Thus His saying ﴿Is it you who create it﴾ serves as a preparation for the argument that God is the Creator of foetuses by His power, and that this power is not limited to the second creation at the Resurrection.

The verb of seeing in ﴿Have you considered﴾ is of the class of *ẓanna* (to think, to deem), because it is not seeing with the eye. Al-Raḍī said: "In such a usage it is transferred from *raʾayta*, in the sense of 'you perceived' or 'you knew', as if it were said: 'Did you perceive its wondrous state, or did you know it? Inform me about it.' Thus it is not used except in asking about a wondrous state of something." End of quotation. That is, because the original meaning of the verb of seeing is among the actions of the limbs, not among the actions of the intellect.

[Page 314]

And ﴿what you emit﴾ is the first object (*mafʿūl awwal*) of the verb ﴿Have you considered﴾. In the transitivity of the verb *ara'aytum* to it there is generality, since the object of the verb of knowing is a state of what you emit. Thus the verb ﴿you saw﴾ does not fall directly upon ﴿what you emit﴾ itself.

Therefore the clause ﴿Is it you who create it﴾ is an explanation (*bayān*) of the clause ﴿Have you considered what you emit﴾, and the interrogative particle was repeated so that the explanation would correspond to what it explains.

By this interrogation the verb ﴿you considered﴾ becomes *suspended* (*muʿallaq*) from acting upon a second object, due to the presence of the cause of suspension, which is the interrogation. Al-Raḍī said: "When the second object begins with an interrogative word, it is preferable not to suspend the verb of the heart from the first object, as in: *ʿalimtu Zaydan a-yūminu huwa* ('I knew Zayd: does he believe?')." End of quotation.

The placement of the subject before the verbal predicate in ﴿Is it you who create it﴾ serves to add emphasis, because when they were placed in the position of one who claims that [they create], as you have understood, the clause negating it was formulated in a form indicating their claim, which establishes their control over the formation of offspring.

From the negation of creation from them and its affirmation for God, the meaning of *qaṣr* (restriction) of creation to God, Exalted is He, has arisen.

The particle ﴿or﴾ (*am*) is connected (*muttaṣilah*) and repeats the interrogative *hamzah*, and what follows it is coordinated, because it is usually the case that no predicate is mentioned for it, being sufficient that the predicate of the preceding coordinated element indicates the omitted predicate. Here, however, the predicate is repeated in His saying ﴿or are We the Creators﴾, in addition to affirming the attribution of creation to God in meaning, and to complete the rhyme (*fāṣilah*) and extend the pause itself. It is also permissible to take *am* as disjunctive (*munqaṭiʿah*), meaning *bal* ('rather'), because the interrogation is not genuine, so its purpose is not to seek the specification of the agent, and the speech would then be complete at His saying ﴿you create it﴾.

The meaning is: Do you suppose that you are the creators of the soul (*nasamah*) from what you emit?

Evidence from the causing of death among the living, showing that it is within God's power, is necessary because they are certain of it, witness it, and wish to avert it or delay it. The One who is able to create death after life is able to bring back to life after death, since the power to bring about a thing entails the power over its opposite. Therefore, whoever is able to create a living being from what has no life, and to cause it to die after life, is capable of managing both states of its giving life and causing death. Reviving after death is only a state of these two realities. Thus the proof of the possibility of resurrection becomes clear. This is similar to His saying, ﴿It is He who gave you life, then causes you to die, then gives you life again, then to Him you will be returned﴾ in Surat al-Mu'minun.

This is the reason for the expression ﴿We have decreed death among you﴾ rather than "We cause you to die." That is, death is placed according to a known and intended measure. The root of "qaddarnā" also carries a reminder of knowledge, power and will, so that the attention of minds turns to the many subtleties contained within this, especially in the decree of human death, which is a path to complete life if one takes its causes.

The word "baynakum" has another meaning: death comes upon them individually in turns and in succession, so none of them escapes it, and no category or age is specified for its arrival. The adverbial form "bayn" indicates that death is like a thing set for distribution, and none of them knows when his share of it will reach him. People are like those called to a division of wealth, fruit or livestock, where no one knows when his name will be called to take his portion, or when his lot will come to him, yet he is certain that he will receive it without doubt.

Thus in His saying ﴿baynakumu al-mawt﴾ there is an implicit metaphor (istiʿāra makniyya), since death is likened to something divided, and the comparandum is alluded to by the word "baynakum," which is commonly used for division. He, exalted, said ﴿that water is to be shared among them﴾ [al-Qamar: 28]. In this metaphor there is also an allusion (kināya) to death being a benefit and a good for people: in this world, so that the earth and provisions do not become too narrow for them, and in the Hereafter, for a fitting recompense.

The placement of the subject before the verbal predicate serves to affirm and strengthen the judgment. This emphasis returns to what the structure contains, namely the verb "qaddarnā" and the adverbial "baynakum," in their indication of the wisdom in the creation of death that we have mentioned.

* * *

﴿And We are not to be outdone﴾ ﴿in replacing your likenesses and bringing you into being in what you do not know﴾.

This is a consequence of the preceding inference that God is able to bring back to life after death. The apparent expectation would be to connect it with the conjunction "fa-" (indicating consequence) and to omit a separate conjunction, but it departs from both and connects with "wa" (and), as a conjunction of sentences. Thus it becomes an independent sentence, intended for its own sake, because its content yields the conclusion and also teaches a doctrinal matter. It thereby conveys information both explicitly and by implication. The explicit meaning is a reminder of the perfection of God's power, that no conqueror overcomes Him, that His power does not fall short of anything, and that He will replace them with another creation at the resurrection resembling their creation in this world. The implicit meaning is a threat of their annihilation and their replacement with another nation, like His saying ﴿If He wills, He can take you away and bring a new creation; that is not difficult for God﴾ [Ibrahim: 19]. Had the "fa-" been used, the meaning of the discourse would have been restricted to the two other meanings.

"Al-sabq" (being outstripped) is a figurative usage meaning being overpowered and rendered incapable, because being ahead implies that the one who is ahead overcomes the one who is behind. So the meaning is: "We are not to be overpowered." Furra ibn ʿAdāʾ al-Faqʿasī said:

"As if you had never been outstripped by time even once, when you attain what you were seeking."

The phrase ﴿on [condition] that We replace your likenesses﴾ is connected to "masbūqīn" (outstripped), because it is said: "He overpowered him in such-and-such," when he prevented him from attaining it. Its original sense is: "He overpowered him in such-and-such," meaning he gained control over such-and-such to the exclusion of the other. He, exalted, said ﴿And God is dominant over His affair﴾ [Yusuf: 21].

The pause may then fall on "umthālakum" (your likenesses).

It is also possible that ﴿on [condition] that We replace your likenesses﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "qaddarnā," meaning: "We have decreed death on the condition that We will bring you to life afterwards." This is an embedding (idmāj) that refutes their saying: "When we are dead and have become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected?" In this case "ʿalā" carries the sense of "maʿa" (with), and the circumstantial clause is a presumptive one (ḥāl muqaddara). This is like the preacher's saying: "On condition of demolition the building was raised, and on condition of exit the souls entered the bodies." The complement of "masbūqīn" would then be omitted and understood from context, meaning: "We are not overpowered regarding what We have decreed of your creation and your causing to die." The pause is then placed on "bi-masbūqīn."

The saying ﴿We have decreed death among you﴾ and so on also conveys, beyond this, a lesson concerning the state of death after life. In the alternation of those two states there is a lesson and reflection on the magnitude of God's power and His dispensing. From this aspect its relation is like that of His later saying, ﴿If We willed, We would have made it dry debris﴾, and His saying ﴿If We willed, We would make it bitter﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 70], and His saying ﴿We made it a reminder and a provision for the wayfarers﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 73].

The meaning of ﴿that We replace your likenesses﴾ is: We replace you with your likenesses; that is, We make your likenesses a substitute.

The verb "baddala" takes one direct object and reaches what is in the sense of a second object by means of the preposition "bi-," which is the most common, or by "min" of substitution. The object of "baddala" is suitable to be both the replaced and the replacement. It has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqara in His saying ﴿Would you exchange what is lower for what is better?﴾ [al-Baqara: 61], and in Surat al-Nisāʾ at His saying ﴿and do not substitute the bad for the good﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 2]. The estimated sense here is: "that We replace from among you your likenesses," so the complement of "nubaddila" is omitted and the object is retained, because the prepositional phrase is more suitable for omission.

"Al-amthāl" is the plural of "mithl" (with a kasra on the mīm and a sukūn on the thāʾ), meaning equivalent or counterpart. That is, We create selves resembling your selves that existed in this world, and We deposit your spirits in them. This indicates that the restoration is from non-existence, not from dispersal. The scholars of Sunna and kalām have differed concerning the determination of this.

It is also possible that it conveys the meaning of a threat of annihilation: that is, if We willed your annihilation, you could not have overcome Us. Then it is an embedding of the threat within the course of the argument, and it is of the kind of His saying ﴿If He wills, He can take you away and bring a new creation﴾ [Ibrahim: 19].

"Wa-nunshiʾakum" is conjoined to "nubaddila," meaning: We are not overpowered in bringing you into being.

This conjunction may be a conjunction of different essences, so that their bringing into being is something other than the replacement of their likenesses. That is, We are capable of both matters together. The replacement of their likenesses is the creation of other bodies in which spirits are deposited, while their bringing into being is the breathing of spirits into the dead bodies that are whole, and into the decayed bodies after restoring them by gathering their scattered parts or by producing their likenesses from their own substance, such as the coccyx bone. This refutes their dismissal of resurrection after the fixed forms of their doubt that prompted their denial of resurrection.

It may also be a conjunction of different attributes, in that what is meant by His saying ﴿and bring you into being in what you do not know﴾ is an indication, in a general manner, of the mode of the replacement.

He conjoined with "wa" rather than "fa" because this clause, by itself, is a depiction of God's power in His wisdom, after what His saying ﴿that We replace your likenesses﴾ has already conveyed, namely the affirmation that God is capable of resurrection.

The "mā" in His saying ﴿in what you do not know﴾ may refer to the manner, or the form, in which the bringing into being is conducted; that is, in a manner you do not know, since you have not encompassed knowledge of the hidden aspects of creation. This generality encompasses all the forms that possibility suggests for the resurrection of bodies for the placing of spirits within them.

The sense of containment derived from "fī" is a figurative containment, whose meaning is the strength of association, resembling the enclosing of the container around the contained, like His saying ﴿In whatever form He willed, He assembled you﴾ [al-Infiṭār: 7].

The meaning of "lā taʿlamūn" (you do not know) is that they do not know the details of those states.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 56, verse 62:

﴿And you have already known the first creation, so why do you not remember?﴾

He follows the proof of the possibility of resurrection, which rests on alerting [the listeners] to the capacity of divine power for it, and on closing the avenues of doubt, with a proof from analogical reasoning (qiyas al-tamthil), namely the comparison of the second creation with the first creation, which is known to them by necessity. So they are alerted, so that they may analogize the second creation to it, in that it is an originating from the effect of God's power and knowledge, and in that they do not comprehend the subtleties of how it comes about.

Page 319

The knowledge negated in His words ﴿fima la ta'lamun﴾ [in what you do not know] is detailed knowledge (al-'ilm al-tafsili), and the knowledge affirmed in His words ﴿And you have indeed known the first creation﴾ is general knowledge (al-'ilm al-ijmali). General knowledge is sufficient as an indication of detailed knowledge, since detail has no effect on belief.

There is also a tibaq (antithesis) figure of speech in the contrast between His words ﴿fima la ta'lamun﴾ and His words ﴿wa-laqad 'alimtum﴾.

Since their knowledge of the first creation was sufficient for them to refute their denial of the second creation, He made upon it a rebuke that He did not make for His words ﴿wa ma nahnu bi-masbuqina 'ala an nubaddila amthalakum wa nunshi'akum fima la ta'lamun﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 60], so He said ﴿fa-lawla tadhakkarun﴾, meaning: why do you not remember by this, so that you would refrain from denial? This is a declaration of their ignorance in leaving the analogy of like cases to like cases. Similar to it is His earlier words ﴿nahnu khalaqnakum fa-lawla tusaddiqun﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 57].

The present tense in His words (tadhakkarun) is used to alert that the door of remembrance is open; so if they missed remembering in the past, let them make up for it now.

The reciters: al-Jumhur read (al-nash'ah) with a sukun on the shin followed by an open hamzah, the verbal noun of nasha'a on the pattern of the single instance (fa'lah), denoting the single instance of the genus. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr alone read it with a fatha on the shin, followed by an alif and then a hamzah; it is a verbal noun on the pattern of fa'alah, contrary to analogical rule, and this was discussed earlier in Surat al-'Ankabut.

[Page 320]

This is a transition to another proof of the possibility of resurrection and of God's power to bring it about, through another kind of origination from non-existence.

The fa' (فَ, "then") here marks a consequence drawn from the preceding sentence, ﴿We created you, so why do you not believe?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 57], just as Allah built on it His saying ﴿Have you considered what you emit?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 58]. The purpose of these sentences is therefore unified, namely to argue for the possibility of resurrection. He intended to repeat and enumerate the argument by repeating the sentence ﴿Have you considered﴾ [afara'aytum], even though the object of the verb of seeing differs. A parallel will come later in His saying ﴿Have you considered the water that you drink?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 68], and His saying ﴿Have you considered the fire that you kindle?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 71].

If you wish, you may make the fa' mark merely a consequence of argument, not a consequence of the meaning of what it introduces relative to the meaning of what precedes it. Since the earlier argument has led to the general capability of divine power, it is also permissible that this sentence is intended as an illustration of a wondrous kind of the connections of power to bringing into existence, without intending an argument specifically for resurrection. Thus it is valid to make the fa' a consequence of the sentence ﴿Have you considered what you emit?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 58], insofar as it required the breadth of divine power.

The reason for moving from the argument from the creation of offspring to the argument from the growth of crops is the clear similarity between the formation of man and the formation of plants. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17].

The discussion of ﴿Have you considered what you till?﴾ is similar to the discussion of His saying ﴿Have you considered what you emit?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 58].

ما تَحْرُثُونَ (mā taḥrathūna, "what you till") is a relative construction (ism mawsul) with its clause, and its returning pronoun (ʿāʾid) is omitted.

al-Ḥarth (tillage) is splitting the earth in order to sow or plant in it.

The apparent meaning of ﴿what you till﴾ is the land itself. However, this does not fit the pronoun in ﴿you cause it to grow﴾ (tazraʿūnahu). Therefore the interpretation of ﴿what you till﴾ must be taken as meaning: what you till for (taḥrathūna lahu), that is, for its sake, by way of omission and transference (al-ḥadhf wal-īṣāl). What you till for is the plant. This is indicated by the pronoun of the object in ﴿Is it you who cause it to grow﴾ (ʾa-antum tazraʿūnahu), because the interrogation carries the sense of negation, and what is negated is what grows from the grain, not its seed.

The verb zaraʿa (to sow/cause to grow) is used in the sense of "to cause to grow" (anbata). al-Rāghib said: "al-zarʿ: causing to grow (al-inbāt), by His saying ﴿Is it you who cause it to grow or are We the Growers?﴾, so He negated the growing from them and attributed it to Himself." End of quotation, and he limited himself to this. The verb zaraʿa is also used in the sense of "to scatter the seed in the earth," as the author of Lisan al-ʿArab said: "zaraʿa al-ḥabba: scattered its seed (badhara-hu)." From this usage, the grain scattered in the earth is called zarīʿah. However, it is not appropriate to take the verse in this sense. The meaning is: have you considered the thing for whose sake you till the land, which is the plant—is it what you cause to grow? Rather, We are the ones who cause it to grow.

The clause ﴿Is it you who cause it to grow﴾ and what follows explains the clause ﴿Have you considered what you till﴾, as was mentioned regarding ﴿Is it you who cause it to grow﴾. The interrogation in ﴿Is it you who cause it to grow﴾ is a denying interrogation (istifhām inkārī), like that in His saying ﴿Is it you who create it?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 59].

The discussion of the position of am (ʾam, "or") in His saying ﴿or are We the Growers?﴾ is like the discussion of its counterpart in His saying ﴿or are We the Creators?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 59]; that is, ʾam is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿah) for a change of subject (iḍrāb).

Likewise, the discussion of placing the subject before the predicate verbal sentence in His saying ﴿Is it you who cause it to grow﴾ is like what is in His saying ﴿Is it you who create it?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 59].

Likewise, the discussion of negating the growing from them and affirming it for Allah the Exalted conveys the meaning of restriction (qaṣr) of growing to Allah the Exalted, that is, upon Allah rather than them. This is a restriction for emphasis (qaṣr mubālaghah), because human sowing is not considered of any significance.

From the verse there is taken an allusion to the illustration of the creation of bodies as a second creation, with a connection between decayed bodies and bodies renewed from them, by the growth of crops from the grain, which is connected to an ear of grain from which it was taken, and so it brings forth an ear like it.

End of quotation, and he limited himself to this. The verb zaraʿa is also used in the sense of "to scatter the seed in the earth," as the author of Lisan al-ʿArab said: "zaraʿa al-ḥabba: scattered its seed (badhara-hu)." From this usage, the grain scattered in the earth is called zarīʿah. However, it is not appropriate to take the verse in this sense. The meaning is: have you considered the thing for whose sake you till the land, which is the plant—is it what you cause to grow? Rather, We are the ones who cause it to grow.

The clause ﴿Is it you who cause it to grow﴾ and what follows explains the clause ﴿Have you considered what you till﴾, as was mentioned regarding ﴿Is it you who cause it to grow﴾. The interrogation in ﴿Is it you who cause it to grow﴾ is a denying interrogation (istifhām inkārī), like that in His saying ﴿Is it you who create it?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 59].

The discussion of the position of am (ʾam, "or") in His saying ﴿or are We the Growers?﴾ is like the discussion of its counterpart in His saying ﴿or are We the Creators?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 59]; that is, ʾam is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿah) for a change of subject (iḍrāb).

Likewise, the discussion of placing the subject before the predicate verbal sentence in His saying ﴿Is it you who cause it to grow﴾ is like what is in His saying ﴿Is it you who create it?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 59].

Likewise, the discussion of negating the growing from them and affirming it for Allah the Exalted conveys the meaning of restriction (qaṣr) of growing to Allah the Exalted, that is, upon Allah rather than them. This is a restriction for emphasis (qaṣr mubālaghah), because human sowing is not considered of any significance.

From the verse there is taken an allusion to the illustration of the creation of bodies as a second creation, with a connection between decayed bodies and bodies renewed from them, by the growth of crops from the grain, which is connected to an ear of grain from which it was taken, and so it brings forth an ear like it.

[p. 322]

The verb *ẓaltum* here means "you became," and all the commentators have understood it in this sense.

The meaning of the verb *tafakkahūna* has caused difficulty. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd reported that it means "you will marvel" (ta'jabūna). From 'Ikrima it is reported to mean "you will blame one another" (tatalawwamūn). From al-Hasan and Qatada it is reported to mean "you will regret" (tandamūn). Ibn Kaysan said it means "you will grieve" (taḥzanūn). Al-Kisa'i said: it expresses lament over what has been lost. He also said that it is among the words with contradictory meanings (al-aḍdād): the Arabs say *tafakkahtu*, meaning "I was made comfortable," and *tafakkahtu*, meaning "I was saddened." End of quotation.

The reason is that the verb *tafakkahūna* derives from the root f-k-h. The well-known sense of this root is delight and joy, but the context is one of the opposite of delight, and their statement ﴿إنّا لَمُغْرَمُونَ﴾ ﴿بَلْ نَحْنُ مَحْرُومُونَ﴾ supports this. Thus *al-fukaha* means delight and openness. Al-Kisa'i claimed that it is among the words with contradictory meanings, and this was adopted in the *Qamus* when it said: "*tafakkaha*: he ate fruit; and *tajannaba 'ani al-fākiha*: its opposite." What specifically pertains to the word is: "you throw away the fruit" in this manner. Perhaps its correct form is *al-fukāha 'an anfusikum* ("the delight of yourselves"), which is joy and gladness; a man is *fakih* if he is open-hearted and unconcerned with anything. End of quotation. He means that the *tafa''ala* pattern here expresses the reflexive (muṭāwa'a) of *fa''ala*, whose doubling indicates removal, as in *qashshara al-'ūd* ("he peeled the stick") and *qarrada al-ba'īr* ("he removed the mange from the camel"). The author of the *Qamus* affirmed this view and attributed it to Ibn 'Atiyya.

They took the clause ﴿إنّا لَمُغْرَمُونَ﴾ as an expression of remorse and grief, meaning: you know that the destruction of your crops is deprivation from God as a punishment for your disbelief. The meaning of *mughramūn* is from *gharam*, which is ruin, as in His words ﴿إنَّ عَذابَها كانَ غَرامًا﴾ ("Indeed, its punishment was ever a torment," 25:65). This is similar to what occurs in Surat al-Qalam in His words ﴿فَلَمّا رَأوْها قالُوا إنّا لَضالُّونَ﴾ ("And when they saw it, they said, 'Indeed, we have gone astray,'" 68:26), through His words ﴿إنّا كُنّا طاغِينَ﴾ ("Indeed, we were transgressors," 68:31).

Thus it is concluded that the meaning of the verse may run in accordance with the apparent sense of the root of the *fa''ala* form *tafakkahūna*, and that this would be mockery directed at them, taking them according to their habitual manners of jesting at God's signs. The indication of this mockery is what follows it, their words ﴿إنّا لَمُغْرَمُونَ﴾ ﴿بَلْ نَحْنُ مَحْرُومُونَ﴾.

It may also be that the verse is understood as making *tafakkahūna* mean "you will regret" and "you will grieve." For this reason the verb *tafakkahūna* here carries an effect that other words could not replace.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 56, verses 68–69:

﴿Have you considered the water which you drink?﴾ ﴿Is it you who brought it down from the cloud, or are We the ones who bring it down?﴾

This is in the manner of His saying ﴿Have you considered what you sow?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 63] and so on, as a continuation (tafri') and a question, with "considering" (ru'yah) being a verb of sight.

The reason for the transition is that the crop and the trees only grow by water. So the argument moves from the creation of plants to the argument from the creation of water, by which the crop and the trees have life. The description of the water as ﴿which you drink﴾ is an incorporation (idmaj) of a favour within the argument; that is, the sweet water which you drink, for drinking water is among the greatest blessings upon humankind, so that it is contrasted with His saying after it ﴿If We willed, We could make it salty; so why do you not give thanks?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 70].

The intended meaning is rain water, and for this reason He said ﴿Is it you who brought it down from the cloud﴾, and the intended meaning is: you brought it down upon your lands and your fields. Rain water is the majority of the drink of the Arabs addressed at that time, and for this reason the Arabs are called "the sons of the water of the sky" (banu ma' al-sama').

Al-muzn is the plural of the collective noun muznah, which is a cloud.

The aspect of the argument is the bringing into existence of that by which there is life after it was non-existent, by means of God Most High creating it in the clouds through the wisdom of the creation of water. Just as the argument was made from the bringing forth of the living from dead components in the creation of man and plants, the argument is made from the bringing into existence of that by which there is life from non-existence, as an approximation for the restoration of bodies, with a subtle and hidden wisdom. That is, it is possible that God sends rain upon the very persons of human bodies, which becomes a cause of their being formed as complete bodies as they were in their origins, just as a tree grows from the kernel of its root. The argument for resurrection was completed at His saying ﴿Or are We the ones who bring it down?﴾.

His saying ﴿Is it you who brought it down from the cloud﴾ is made into an argument, dependent upon the bringing down of water from the cloud, in the manner of describing it by its bringing down, rather than by its creation fit for drinking, because its bringing down is what yields benefit from it; for this reason it is described by His saying ﴿which you drink﴾. It is followed by His saying ﴿If We willed, We could make it salty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 70], so there arises between the two sentences an implicit correspondence (ihtibak), as if it were said: Is it you who created it sweet and fit for drinking and brought it down from the cloud? If We willed, We would have made it salty, and kept it in its cloud, or sent it down upon the seas or the wastelands, and you would not have benefited from it.

His saying ﴿Is it you who brought it down from the cloud﴾ is made into an argument, dependent upon the bringing down of water from the cloud, in the manner of describing it by its bringing down, rather than by its creation fit for drinking, because its bringing down is what yields benefit from it; for this reason it is described by His saying ﴿which you drink﴾. It is followed by His saying ﴿If We willed, We could make it salty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 70], so there arises between the two sentences an implicit correspondence (ihtibak), as if it were said: Is it you who created it sweet and fit for drinking and brought it down from the cloud? If We willed, We would have made it salty, and kept it in its cloud, or sent it down upon the seas or the wastelands, and you would not have benefited from it.

[Page 325]

﴿If We willed, We would have made it salty; so why do you not give thanks?﴾ Its placement is like the placement of the clause ﴿If We willed, We would have made it debris﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 65]. The meaning is: If We willed, We would make it unbeneficial to you. This is an argument that He is able to annul the water's capacity for benefit after the form of water exists in it. Its parallel is His saying ﴿We have decreed death among you﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 60] and His saying ﴿If We willed, We would have made it debris﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 65].

From this completing clause, he moves on to a reminder of favour with His words ﴿so why do you not give thanks?﴾, urging them to give thanks and to reject disbelief and association (shirk).

The lam that normally enters the answer (jawab) of the past affirmative "law" (if) has been omitted, because it is an extra lam (lam za'ida) that serves only to emphasise. Its omission was therefore a form of concision (ijaz) in the speech.

Shaykh Muhammad ibn Sa'id al-Hajari al-Tunisi mentioned, in his gloss on al-Ashmuni's commentary on the Alfiyya of Ibn Malik (a famous versified work on Arabic grammar), entitled "Zawahir al-Kawakib," citing the book "al-Burhan fi I'jaz al-Qur'an" (The Proof of the Inimitability of the Qur'an). This title was given to two books: one by Kamal al-Din Muhammad, known as Ibn al-Zamalkani, and the second by Ibn Abi al-Isba'. He said: If it is asked, why is the verb emphasised with the lam in the case of the crop but not in the case of the water? I say: Because the crop, its growth and its drying after freshness until it becomes debris, may be thought to be the work of the farmer, or due to the watering with water, and its drying due to the lack of watering. So He, glory be to Him, informed that He is the true doer of that, and that He is able to make it debris while it is growing, if He willed. As for the sending down of water from the sky, it cannot be imagined that anyone other than God, exalted is He, has power over it. End of quotation.

The omission of this lam is rare, except when the "law" clause and its condition form a relative clause (silat al-mawsul), in which case the omission of this lam is frequent because of the length of the clause. This is what Ibn Malik firmly stated in his "al-Tashil," and al-Radi followed him, as in God's saying ﴿And let those fear who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would fear for them﴾ [al-Nisa': 9]. Al-Muradi and al-Damamini, in their two commentaries, said that this is not known except from the author (Ibn Malik). Al-Radi said: Likewise, when the condition is lengthened with its appendages, as in God's saying ﴿And if every tree on the earth were pens, and the sea [were ink] replenished by seven more seas after it, the words of God would not be exhausted﴾ [Luqman: 26]. That is, in other than these cases the omission of the lam is rare, but it has been repeated in the Qur'an in several places, of which this verse is one. Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) has a discussion on the rule governing the omission of this lam, which is not complete.

[Page 326]

The verse is like its predecessor in the arrangement of the discourse (nazm al-kalam).

The connection between moving from the argument from the creation of water to the argument from the creation of fire is the same as the connection previously made when moving to the creation of water from the argument from the creation of crops and trees, for fire comes out of trees when struck, and it is kindled and ignited by means of trees.

This argument is meant to bring closer the manner of revival for the Resurrection, in that striking (for fire) is a bringing forth, and the firestick by which fire is kindled comes out of the sticks used for striking, while they are dead.

In His saying ﴿the fire that you kindle﴾ there is an embedding (idmaj, the incorporation of one theme within another) of the favour (imtinan) into the argument, through what preceded in His saying ﴿Have you considered the water that you drink?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 68].

It is also a description of the intended object of the proof, which is the fire that is struck from the firestick, not the blazing fire. The pronoun in "shajaratuha" (its tree) refers to the fire.

The tree of fire is the kind of tree that contains a tinder (hurraq), that is, that from which fire is struck. The trees of fire are many, among them al-markh (with fatha then sukun), al-'afar (with fatha on the 'ayn), al-'ushar (with damma then fatha), and al-kalkh (with fatha then sukun). Among the proverbs is: "In every tree there is fire, and al-markh and al-'afar have excelled," meaning they have produced more fire.

Tuwarun is the present form of awra al-zand, when one strikes the firestick with a similar piece to draw fire from it. They would place a stick of fire-wood and strike it from its upper end with another similar stick, so the fire comes out from the lower stick. The upper stick is called zand (with fatha on the zay and sukun on the nun) or zinad (with kasra on the zay), and the lower one is called zandah, with the feminine ending at its end. They likened the upper stick to the stallion (fahl) and the lower stick to the female camel (tarugah). Dhu al-Rummah followed this meaning in describing the striking of fire, saying, in the manner of riddles:

"And a fragment like the eye of a rooster, I alternated with my companion in its father, and we prepared for its place a socket ∗∗∗ of a well-known one, which does not let the stallion reach its mother, if we do not hold its ends by force."

The returning pronoun to the relative pronoun is omitted, because the object pronoun is often omitted from the relative clause. Its full form is: "allati tuwarunaha" (that you strike it).

The transitive use of tuwarun with the pronoun of the fire is by way of an implied noun, meaning "you strike its tree," as indicated by His saying ﴿Is it you who produced its tree?﴾. This omission is widespread in speech, and they say awra al-nar just as they say awra al-zand.

The clause ﴿Is it you who produced its tree?﴾ and what follows is an explanation (bayan) of the clause ﴿Have you considered the fire?﴾ and what follows, as was mentioned before in His saying ﴿Do you create it, or are We the creators?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 59].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 56, verse 73:

Page 327
﴿We have made it a reminder and a provision for the wayfarers.﴾
The clause is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the clause ﴿Or are We the producers of it?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 72], meaning: the creation of the Fire was for benefits and wisdoms, among them that it be a reminder for people, by which they recall the Fire of Jahannam and compare its burning with the burning of Jahannam, which they know to be more severe than their fire.

Al-mata' (provision): that which is enjoyed, i.e., benefited from for a period of time. It was mentioned in His saying ﴿Say: The enjoyment of this world is little﴾ [al-Nisa': 77] in Surah al-Nisa'.

Al-muqwi (the wayfarer, or one in need): the one who enters the qiwa' (with a fatha on the qaf and a long vowel), which is the barren desert. Al-muqwi is also applied to the hungry, because his stomach has become empty (aqwat), i.e., devoid of food, since both verbs are derived from qawa, which means emptiness. The emptiness of the belly is called qiwa' and qiwan. Thus the choice of this descriptor in this verse is to combine both meanings: the fire is a provision for travellers, who use it for light in their resting places, for warmth in the cold, and whom a wayfarer sees at night in the desert so that he is guided to the place of lodging and comes to them; and it is a provision for the hungry, who cook their food with it both at home and while travelling. This is an incorporation of the blessing (imdaj fi al-imtinan) within the argument (fi khilal al-istidlal). These two descriptors were chosen because the need of their possessors for the fire is greater than the need of others.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 56, verse 74:

﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ ordered (rattaba) upon what preceded of the speech containing the proofs of the greatness of divine power, and upon examples to bring closer the resurrection whose report they denied, and upon the sublime blessings embedded within that, that Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to exalt Him with a special exaltation, following what those sublime attributes that preceded pour upon him of a renewed remembrance, the exaltation being after it a kind of remembrance of the majesty of His essence and gratitude for His bounties. For acts of worship have occasions in which they are more perfect than in other than them, so that they have from excellence what makes their reward abundant. The Messenger ﷺ does not leave off glorifying his Lord and reflecting on the greatness of His station, but because glorifying and reflecting differ, the renewal of the soul's attention makes each state of reflection have features that give it particular qualities and increase its reward.

Page 328

So the sentence is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the sentence ﴿Say: Indeed, the former and the latter will surely be gathered﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 49] up to His saying ﴿and a provision for the desert dwellers﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 73], and it is a tadhyil (concluding appendix).

Al-tasbih (glorification) means tanzih (declaring Allah free of imperfection), and it has already been discussed at His saying ﴿while we glorify You with Your praise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The name of the Lord is that which indicates His essence and the totality of His attributes, and it is the Name of Majesty (ism al-jalalah), meaning that one says: "Subhan Allah." So tasbih is an utterance related to words.

Since speech is designed to indicate what is in the soul, glorifying the Name entails declaring its Named One free of imperfection, and it also entails that the glorification be by utterance together with belief, not mere belief, because when glorification is attached to the utterance of a name, it is determined that it is verbal glorification, i.e., say a speech that carries the meaning of tanzih, and attach it to the name of your Lord. Thus every speech that indicates the tanzih of Allah falls under this command, but imitating the wording of the Qur'an is more preferable and more comprehensive, by saying: "Subhan Allah." This is supported by what 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: that when His saying ﴿So glorify with the praise of your Lord and seek His forgiveness﴾ [al-Nasr: 3] was revealed, "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say in his prostration: 'Subhanaka Allahumma Rabbana wa bihamdika, Allahumma ighfir li,' interpreting the Qur'an," i.e., he interpreted it by applying its wording.

The letter ba' entering upon "ism" is extra, for emphasizing adhesion, meaning the connection of the verb to its object. This is because the command to glorify came right after mentioning several matters that call for it, as indicated by the fa' of sequence, so it was fitting to strengthen and urge it. This is unlike His saying ﴿Glorify the name of your Most High Lord﴾ [al-A'la: 1], since it occurs at the beginning of its sentence, like His saying ﴿O you who believe, remember Allah with much remembrance and glorify Him morning and evening﴾ [al-Ahzab: 41].

This command includes the Muslims, by the indication that the Qur'an is recited to them and that what the command branches from is not knowledge restricted to the Prophet ﷺ. Since he was commanded to glorify because of it, likewise whoever among the Muslims knows it.

The meaning: if you know what We have sent down of proofs and remember what blessings are in that, then declare Allah free of imperfection and magnify Him with the utmost of your ability.

Page 329

The word "al-'Azim" is suitable to be made an attribute of "Rabbika" (your Lord), and He is Mighty in the sense that all perfection is established for Him; this is a widespread metaphor closely linked to the literal meaning. It is also suitable to be an attribute of "ism" (name), the Name being mighty with a metaphorical greatness due to its blessing and the greatness of the One named by it.

[Page 330]

This is a consequence (*tafri'*, a logical branching) of the statement ﴿Say: Indeed, the former and the later peoples will surely be gathered﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 49]. It indicates an address from God Most High directed at those who deny resurrection, who say: "When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised?" From this, the discourse moves to praising the Qur'an. Since they denied resurrection, and since affirming resurrection was among the most important things the Qur'an brought, and since its affirmation of resurrection, which they considered impossible, was one of the things that incited them to deny the Qur'an, in addition to their denial of it in other matters that it brought, namely the nullification of their polytheism and their falsehoods, then once the proof had been established against their error in their denial, the truthfulness of what the Qur'an had informed them of became clear, and so its truthfulness was established. For this reason the context became ready for praising its status.

The *fa'* (the conjunctive particle "then") is for the branching of the oath upon what preceded it, namely the proofs for the occurrence of resurrection. The statement ﴿Say: Indeed, the former and the later peoples will surely be gathered﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 49] is an announcement of the Day of Resurrection and a warning to them of it, while they had denied it. Because it seemed impossible in their limited view, they denied the Qur'an and denied the one who brought it. So He branched, upon establishing the occurrence of resurrection and the warning of it, the establishment that the Qur'an is free of defects, that it is a revelation from God, and that the one who brought it is a messenger conveying from God.

The branching of the oath is a branching in meaning with respect to the object sworn upon, and it is also a verbal branching with respect to the act of swearing, if they say to you: "He swore by the positions of the stars."

The branching of an oath upon what precedes it with *fa'* has come in mere mention, in the words of Zuhayr:

*So I swore by the House around which walked men whom Quraysh and Jurhum had built,*

after the verses of erotic prelude (*nasib*) from his mu'allaqah, and there is no connection between the erotic prelude and what branches from it, the oath. He only intended that what follows the *fa'* is the purpose of the poem, and that he preceded it with the erotic prelude to rouse the listener. By this, the difference in composition between the verse and Zuhayr's line becomes evident.

*La uqsimu* (﴿لا أُقْسِمُ﴾): in the sense of *uqsimu*, and *la* is additional for emphasis. Its original function is negation, indicating that the speaker does not venture to swear by what he swears by, out of fear of the evil consequence of lying in an oath.

It also carries the sense that he does not need to swear, because the matter is clearly established. Since this usage became common, it came to mean the emphasis of the statement, and so it equals an oath. This is shown by His words following it: ﴿And indeed it is an oath, if you knew, a great one﴾. This second aspect is the more appropriate one, given what has occurred similarly in the Qur'an.

On both readings, it is an embedding (*idmaj*) to praise the status of what, if He were swearing, He would swear by. On the second reading, His words ﴿and indeed it is an oath﴾ mean: "and indeed what is mentioned is a great thing by which swearers swear." The application of the word *qasam* (oath) to it is from the use of a verbal noun to mean the object, like *al-khalq* (creation) meaning the created thing.

From Sa'id ibn Jubayr and some exegetes: they made *la* a separate particle, not part of the verb *uqsimu*, standing as a response to an implied statement that is indicated by what follows it, namely ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾, in reply to their claims about the Qur'an: that it is poetry, or magic, or the fables of the ancients, or the speech of a soothsayer. They made His words *uqsimu* a resumption (*isti'naf*). According to this reading, the meaning of the speech together with the *fa'* of branching upon the proofs for the possibility of resurrection that have become manifest is: "What you claim about the Qur'an is not as you assert; rather it is a noble Qur'an, etc."

*Mawaqi' al-nujum* (﴿مَواقِعِ النُّجُومِ﴾) is the plural of *mawqi'*, which may be the place of falling, that is, the locations where they fall, whether fixed stars or wandering stars. *Al-wuqu'* is used for falling, that is, setting, so the positions of the stars are the places of their setting. This agrees with His words Most High ﴿By the star when it sets﴾ [al-Najm: 1]. Swearing by this is among what is included in His words Most High ﴿So I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 40]. The positions of the stars, in this sense, are made an object of oath because those places, at the time the stars set at them, remind one of the wonderful order established for the movement of the heavenly bodies, which does not fail or deviate every night, and they remind one of the greatness of the heavenly bodies and their alternation one after another. That is a great matter, which makes swearing by it appropriate, and the swearing by it returns to swearing by its Originator.

*Al-wuqu'* is also used for alighting in a place. It is said: "The camels *waqa'at*," when they knelt, and "the sheep *waqa'at*" in their pens. From this comes the name *al-waqi'ah* for an event, as was mentioned earlier. So *al-mawaqi'* are the places of their alighting and the lines of their courses. This is close to His words ﴿By the sky of the constellations﴾ [al-Buruj: 1].

*Al-mawaqi'* are the orbits of the stars, precisely regulated in their motion across the horizon of the sky. Likewise their constellations and their stations.

Mentioning the positions of the stars in both senses is a praise of them and an exaltation of their matter, because their conditions indicate the subtleties of God's wisdom in the arrangement of their motion and the wonders of His power in subjecting them.

It is also possible that *mawaqi'* is the plural of *mawqi'*, which is the mimi verbal noun (a noun of place or time formed from the root) of *al-wuqu'*.

Some exegetes interpreted *al-nujum* as the plural of *najm*, which means a portion of wealth or other things, as one says: "the installments (*nujum*) of blood-money and fines." They interpreted *al-nujum*, that is, groups of verses, which descend from the Qur'an. This is from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah. Thus it returns to an oath by the Qur'an in its literal sense, in the manner mentioned earlier in His words Most High ﴿By the Clear Book﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 2] ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 3].

The sentence ﴿And indeed it is an oath, if you knew, a great one﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraD*) between the oath and its answer.

The pronoun in ﴿innahu﴾ refers either to the oath mentioned in ﴿I do not swear by the positions of the stars﴾, or it refers to the positions of the stars, taking them as "what is mentioned," so that it is an oath in the sense of "the thing sworn by," as you have understood a moment ago.

It is also possible that it refers to the thing sworn to, namely what is contained in the answer of the oath, His words ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾.

The clause ﴿if you knew﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between the described and its description, and it is a parenthesis within a parenthesis.

The knowledge that the counterfactual *law* (conditional of impossibility) requires to be absent from them, if you make the pronoun in ﴿innahu﴾ refer to the oath, is the detailed knowledge of the conditions of the positions of the stars. For the polytheists are not free of a general, varying knowledge that in those positions there is a lesson for observers. Or that general knowledge is treated as if it were nonexistent, because by their disbelief they did not act in accordance with what that knowledge requires of the Oneness of God. So if they knew what the conditions of the positions of the stars contain of the connections to God's attributes, they would know that they are sacred positions by which none swears except one who is truthful in his oath. But they are far removed from this knowledge, for the majesty of the sworn object is among what restrains the swearer from lying in his oath. The evidence that they lacked knowledge of its greatness is that they did not perceive the indication of that for the Oneness of God in divinity, so they ascribed to Him partners who created nothing of that, nor anything approaching it. This is a sign that they did not perceive the proofs contained within that, until the creator of what is in those positions and the non-creator became equal to them.

As for if you make the pronoun in ﴿And indeed it is an oath﴾ refer to the object sworn to, then the meaning is: "If you knew that, you would not need an oath."

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) recited *bi-mawaqi'* in the plural form, with a fatha on the *waw* and an *alif* after it. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf recited *bi-mawqi'* with a sukun on the *waw* and without an *alif* after it, in the singular form, as a mimi verbal noun, that is, "by their setting," or it is a noun for the direction of their setting, like His words "Lord of the East and the West."

The object of *ta'lamun* (you know) is omitted, indicated by the context: "if you knew His greatness," that is, the proofs of His greatness. You may also treat the verb *ta'lamun* as if it were intransitive, that is: "if you had knowledge, but you do not have the attribute of knowledge."

The pronoun in ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾ refers to something not mentioned in the speech, because it is known and present to them.

*Al-Qur'an* is the read speech, that is, the recited, repeated speech. That is, it is speech by which one is admonished, a locus of reflection and recitation. This has been mentioned earlier at His words Most High ﴿And you are not engaged in any matter, nor do you recite from it any Qur'an﴾ [Yunus: 61] in Surah Yunus.

*Al-karim* means precious and elevated within its kind, as was mentioned earlier at His words Most High ﴿Indeed, there has been delivered to me a noble letter﴾ [al-Naml: 29] in Surah al-Naml.

This is a preference of the Qur'an over the individual members of its genre of divine books, such as the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Book of Luqman. Its superiority over them is that it surpassed them in fully covering the aims of religion, the conditions of livelihood and the hereafter, and establishing beliefs through proofs from creation, and in thoroughly refuting falsehood with a refutation that no earlier book contained the like of, especially in matters of belief; and in the clarity of its meanings, in the abundance of its indication with the scarcity of its words, in its eloquence, in the beauty of its verses and the beauty of their placement for the ear. All of this is among the effects of what God intended by the universality of guidance through it, and its suitability for every nation and every age. So this is a description of the Qur'an as elevated above all books, a truth which the opponent cannot find a way to challenge.

After the Qur'an was described as *karim* (noble), it was described a second time as ﴿in a Book well-guarded﴾. This is certainly a description of honor, so neither the word *kitab* (book) nor the description *maknun* (well-guarded) is intended literally, since taking them literally would not confer honor. Therefore the particle *fi* (in) is for figurative location.

The "well-guarded Book" is a metaphor for the agreement of the words and meanings of the Qur'an with what is in God's knowledge, His will, and His command to the angel to convey it to the Messenger (ﷺ). These are matters hidden from us. Therefore He described the Book as *maknun*, derived from *iktinan*, which means concealment, that is, hidden from the gaze of people. So it is a matter unseen, whose reality none knows except God.

The essential meaning of this verse is: the Qur'an that reached them and that they heard from the Prophet (ﷺ) is in accordance with what God intended to inform people of, and what His power has determined the creation of its inimitable composition, so that it may complete the description that it is the speech of God Most High and that no human made it.

A parallel to this locative particle is His words Most High ﴿And not a leaf falls but He knows it﴾ [al-An'am: 59], up to His words ﴿except that it is in a clear Book﴾ [al-An'am: 59] in Surah al-An'am, and His words ﴿And no one is granted long life nor is any of his life shortened except that it is in a Book﴾ [Fatir: 11]. That is: except as it proceeds according to what God knew and what His decree has determined. Likewise His words here ﴿in a Book well-guarded﴾. So the particle of location is borrowed for the meaning of correspondence to what is with God, likening that correspondence to the union of the contained with the container. Close to this is His words Most High ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scriptures﴾ [al-A'la: 18] ﴿the scriptures of Abraham and Moses﴾ [al-A'la: 19]. This is better than considering metaphor in ascribing the attribute of being in a well-guarded Book to a noble Qur'an by way of rational metaphor (*majaz 'aqli*), on the ground that the real basis of this metaphor is describing a counterpart and match of the Qur'an, since the counterpart is connected to its counterpart.

The word *kitab* is borrowed for a matter that is established and fixed, which does not accept change. Thus there is harmony between the borrowing of the locative particle for the meaning of correspondence and the borrowing of *kitab* for what is established and fixed, the meaning being that the meanings of this Qur'an agree with what is with God from the objects of His knowledge, the objects of His will and power, and that its words agree with what God commanded to be created of speech expressing those meanings in the most eloquent manner. Close to this borrowing is the verse of Bishr ibn Abi Khazim, or al-Tirimmah:

*We found in the Book of the Banu Tamim*
*the most deserving of horses to be spurred, the borrowed one.*

The Banu Tamim have no book, but he applied the word *kitab* to what was established of their customs and their knowledge.

The sentence ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾ is a second description of *kitab* (Book).

"And the purified ones" (al-mutahharun): the angels. What is meant is the purity of the soul, which is purification (zaka'). This is the view of the majority of the exegetes. In the Muwatta', Malik said: "The best I have heard concerning this verse, ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾, is that it is like this verse in (Surah) 'Abasa and He Frowned, the saying of God, blessed and exalted be He: ﴿Nay, verily it is a reminder﴾ [80:11] ﴿So whoever wills may remember it﴾ [80:12] ﴿In scrolls held in honour﴾ [80:13] ﴿Exalted, purified﴾ [80:14] ﴿By the hands of scribes﴾ [80:15] ﴿Noble and dutiful﴾ [80:16]." End quote. He means that the purified ones are the noble, dutiful scribes, not the people who purify themselves.

The meaning of "touch" (massa) is "take hold of." In a hadith, "massa min tayyibah" means he took (some) of perfume. The word "massa" is also used for "association" and "perusal." Yazid ibn al-Hakam al-Kilabi said:

∗∗∗ "We have touched (massa) from the fathers something, so each of us
is toward a lineage in his people, not lowering it."

Al-Marzuqi, in his commentary on this verse from al-Hamasa, said: "massa" may mean "we attained and we tested," because touching with the hand is intended for testing. It may also mean "we sought." So the meaning is: the Book does not directly handle the transmission of what it contains for its conveyance except the angels.

The purpose of this is that the Qur'an is not, as the polytheists claim, the words of a soothsayer. They claim that the soothsayer receives from the jinn and devils what they steal of news from the heaven, according to their belief. Nor is it the words of a poet, since they claimed that every poet has a devil who dictates poetry to him. Nor is it "the legends of the ancients," for they mean by them the false tales with which the people of evening gatherings amuse themselves. God said: this Qur'an conforms to what is with God, which none witnesses except the purified angels.

The clause "a revelation from the Lord of the worlds" explains the clause "in a Book well-guarded, none touches it except the purified," so it follows as a description of the Qur'an, meaning: its reaching you was by a revelation from God, that is, the angels brought it down.

In the sense of the structure of this verse is God's saying: ﴿Nor is it the word of a poet; little do you believe﴾ [69:41] ﴿nor the word of a soothsayer; little do you remember﴾ [69:42] ﴿a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [69:43].

Since this noble rank of the Qur'an is established, it is fitting that its recitation and its writing be honored. For this reason, it is among what is commanded that none touch the written Qur'an except one who is purified, imitating the state of the angels in handling the Qur'an, such that the one holding the Qur'an is in a state of religious purity. This is the meaning that the legislation of purification for one who wishes to pray points to, like the hadith "the one praying is conversing with his Lord."

Traditions indicate this, the clearest of which is what Malik narrated in the Muwatta' as a mursal report: that in the letter which the Messenger of God ﷺ wrote to the kings (aqyal) of Dhu Ru'ayn, Ma'afir and Hamadhan, and sent with 'Amr ibn Hazm, was: "None touches the Qur'an except one who is pure." Al-Manawi said: its chain is sound, and al-Suyuti placed it in the rank of hasan.

In the books of biography it is reported that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, before he embraced Islam, entered upon his sister, the wife of Sa'id ibn Zayd, and found her reading the Qur'an from a page on which Surah Ta-Ha was written. He asked for the page to read it, and she said to him: "None touches it except the purified." So he stood up, performed ghusl, read the surah, and embraced Islam. This verse, therefore, is not evidence for the ruling on people touching the Qur'an with their hands; but God's mention of it does not exclude the intention that people be compared to the angels in that they do not touch the Qur'an except when they are pure, as the angels are, that is, to the extent possible of human purity.

Thus it is established that the command to purify oneself for one who holds a written part of the Qur'an was settled among the Muslims from the early period of Islam in Makkah.

The jurists differed only over the implication of this command, whether obligatory or recommended. The majority held it obligatory that the one holding written Qur'an be in a state of wudu', and this is the view of 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Sa'd, Sa'id, 'Ata', al-Zuhri, Malik, al-Shafi'i, and it is a narration from Abu Hanifa. A group said that this is a command of recommendation, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, and it is narrated from Abu Hanifa, and it is the view of Ahmad and Dawud al-Zahiri.

Malik said in the Muwatta': "No one carries the mushaf, neither by its strap nor on a cushion, except while pure, out of honor for the Qur'an and magnifying it." In the narration of Ibn al-Qasim from the Kitab al-Wudu' of al-'Utbiyya, in the sixth question, Malik was asked about a tablet on which the Qur'an is written: may it be touched without wudu'? He said: as for children who are learning, I see no harm in it. He was asked: what about a man learning from it? He said: I hope it is lenient. It was said to Ibn al-Qasim: what about a teacher who shapes children's tablets while not in wudu'? He said: I consider that lenient. Ibn Rushd said in al-Bayan wa al-Tahsil: because of the hardship that would befall them in that, and this would be a cause for prohibiting their learning it; this is the reason for the leniency for children. Al-Baji indicated in al-Muntaqa that the permission to touch the Qur'an for the learner and the teacher is for the sake of the necessity of learning.

They considered this a ruling for what is written with the Qur'an with the intention that it be a mushaf, or part of a mushaf, or a tablet of the Qur'an; and they did not consider it applicable to verses of the Qur'an written by way of quotation, citation, or argument. Among this is what is written on dinars and dirhams, and on rings.

The meaning of purity according to those who hold it obligatory is the minor purification, that is, wudu'. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Sha'bi said: it is permissible to touch the Qur'an with the major purification even if the minor one is not present.

Among what is connected to this issue is the question of a non-purified person reciting the Qur'an. This is not apparently covered by the verse, but since the prohibition against touching the mushaf for one not purified may be because touching is a contact with the written Qur'an, the prohibition on pronouncing the words of the Qur'an may be established by the understanding of agreement (mafhum al-muwafaqa), equal or stronger, since uttering is a contact like the contact of holding the written text or stronger. I suppose this is the source of their disagreement over reciting the Qur'an for one who is not purified. The consensus of the scholars that one who is not in wudu' may recite the Qur'an, despite their disagreement over touching the mushaf for one not in wudu', indicates that touching the mushaf in their view is a stronger contact than pronouncing the verses of the Qur'an.

Malik, Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i said: it is not permissible for one in janabah to recite the Qur'an, but it is permissible for one not in wudu'. I say: among the Muslims in the era of the Companions the practice spread that one who is junub does not recite the Qur'an, and no fatwa to that effect was reported from them. Ahmad and Dawud said: reciting the Qur'an is permissible for one in janabah. Malik allowed the recitation of a small portion of it, such as a verse or two, and none of the scholars required wudu' of the one reciting the Qur'an.

There is disagreement concerning its recitation by a menstruating or post-natal woman. On this, Malik has two narrations, and I suppose that the narration of permissibility takes into account that the lapse of the validity of their purity lasts a long time, and this was the reason for the leniency.
