This is a consequence (*tafri'*, a logical branching) of the statement ﴿Say: Indeed, the former and the later peoples will surely be gathered﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 49]. It indicates an address from God Most High directed at those who deny resurrection, who say: "When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised?" From this, the discourse moves to praising the Qur'an. Since they denied resurrection, and since affirming resurrection was among the most important things the Qur'an brought, and since its affirmation of resurrection, which they considered impossible, was one of the things that incited them to deny the Qur'an, in addition to their denial of it in other matters that it brought, namely the nullification of their polytheism and their falsehoods, then once the proof had been established against their error in their denial, the truthfulness of what the Qur'an had informed them of became clear, and so its truthfulness was established. For this reason the context became ready for praising its status.

The *fa'* (the conjunctive particle "then") is for the branching of the oath upon what preceded it, namely the proofs for the occurrence of resurrection. The statement ﴿Say: Indeed, the former and the later peoples will surely be gathered﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 49] is an announcement of the Day of Resurrection and a warning to them of it, while they had denied it. Because it seemed impossible in their limited view, they denied the Qur'an and denied the one who brought it. So He branched, upon establishing the occurrence of resurrection and the warning of it, the establishment that the Qur'an is free of defects, that it is a revelation from God, and that the one who brought it is a messenger conveying from God.

The branching of the oath is a branching in meaning with respect to the object sworn upon, and it is also a verbal branching with respect to the act of swearing, if they say to you: "He swore by the positions of the stars."

The branching of an oath upon what precedes it with *fa'* has come in mere mention, in the words of Zuhayr:

*So I swore by the House around which walked men whom Quraysh and Jurhum had built,*

after the verses of erotic prelude (*nasib*) from his mu'allaqah, and there is no connection between the erotic prelude and what branches from it, the oath. He only intended that what follows the *fa'* is the purpose of the poem, and that he preceded it with the erotic prelude to rouse the listener. By this, the difference in composition between the verse and Zuhayr's line becomes evident.

*La uqsimu* (﴿لا أُقْسِمُ﴾): in the sense of *uqsimu*, and *la* is additional for emphasis. Its original function is negation, indicating that the speaker does not venture to swear by what he swears by, out of fear of the evil consequence of lying in an oath.

It also carries the sense that he does not need to swear, because the matter is clearly established. Since this usage became common, it came to mean the emphasis of the statement, and so it equals an oath. This is shown by His words following it: ﴿And indeed it is an oath, if you knew, a great one﴾. This second aspect is the more appropriate one, given what has occurred similarly in the Qur'an.

On both readings, it is an embedding (*idmaj*) to praise the status of what, if He were swearing, He would swear by. On the second reading, His words ﴿and indeed it is an oath﴾ mean: "and indeed what is mentioned is a great thing by which swearers swear." The application of the word *qasam* (oath) to it is from the use of a verbal noun to mean the object, like *al-khalq* (creation) meaning the created thing.

From Sa'id ibn Jubayr and some exegetes: they made *la* a separate particle, not part of the verb *uqsimu*, standing as a response to an implied statement that is indicated by what follows it, namely ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾, in reply to their claims about the Qur'an: that it is poetry, or magic, or the fables of the ancients, or the speech of a soothsayer. They made His words *uqsimu* a resumption (*isti'naf*). According to this reading, the meaning of the speech together with the *fa'* of branching upon the proofs for the possibility of resurrection that have become manifest is: "What you claim about the Qur'an is not as you assert; rather it is a noble Qur'an, etc."

*Mawaqi' al-nujum* (﴿مَواقِعِ النُّجُومِ﴾) is the plural of *mawqi'*, which may be the place of falling, that is, the locations where they fall, whether fixed stars or wandering stars. *Al-wuqu'* is used for falling, that is, setting, so the positions of the stars are the places of their setting. This agrees with His words Most High ﴿By the star when it sets﴾ [al-Najm: 1]. Swearing by this is among what is included in His words Most High ﴿So I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 40]. The positions of the stars, in this sense, are made an object of oath because those places, at the time the stars set at them, remind one of the wonderful order established for the movement of the heavenly bodies, which does not fail or deviate every night, and they remind one of the greatness of the heavenly bodies and their alternation one after another. That is a great matter, which makes swearing by it appropriate, and the swearing by it returns to swearing by its Originator.

*Al-wuqu'* is also used for alighting in a place. It is said: "The camels *waqa'at*," when they knelt, and "the sheep *waqa'at*" in their pens. From this comes the name *al-waqi'ah* for an event, as was mentioned earlier. So *al-mawaqi'* are the places of their alighting and the lines of their courses. This is close to His words ﴿By the sky of the constellations﴾ [al-Buruj: 1].

*Al-mawaqi'* are the orbits of the stars, precisely regulated in their motion across the horizon of the sky. Likewise their constellations and their stations.

Mentioning the positions of the stars in both senses is a praise of them and an exaltation of their matter, because their conditions indicate the subtleties of God's wisdom in the arrangement of their motion and the wonders of His power in subjecting them.

It is also possible that *mawaqi'* is the plural of *mawqi'*, which is the mimi verbal noun (a noun of place or time formed from the root) of *al-wuqu'*.

Some exegetes interpreted *al-nujum* as the plural of *najm*, which means a portion of wealth or other things, as one says: "the installments (*nujum*) of blood-money and fines." They interpreted *al-nujum*, that is, groups of verses, which descend from the Qur'an. This is from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah. Thus it returns to an oath by the Qur'an in its literal sense, in the manner mentioned earlier in His words Most High ﴿By the Clear Book﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 2] ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 3].

The sentence ﴿And indeed it is an oath, if you knew, a great one﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraD*) between the oath and its answer.

The pronoun in ﴿innahu﴾ refers either to the oath mentioned in ﴿I do not swear by the positions of the stars﴾, or it refers to the positions of the stars, taking them as "what is mentioned," so that it is an oath in the sense of "the thing sworn by," as you have understood a moment ago.

It is also possible that it refers to the thing sworn to, namely what is contained in the answer of the oath, His words ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾.

The clause ﴿if you knew﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between the described and its description, and it is a parenthesis within a parenthesis.

The knowledge that the counterfactual *law* (conditional of impossibility) requires to be absent from them, if you make the pronoun in ﴿innahu﴾ refer to the oath, is the detailed knowledge of the conditions of the positions of the stars. For the polytheists are not free of a general, varying knowledge that in those positions there is a lesson for observers. Or that general knowledge is treated as if it were nonexistent, because by their disbelief they did not act in accordance with what that knowledge requires of the Oneness of God. So if they knew what the conditions of the positions of the stars contain of the connections to God's attributes, they would know that they are sacred positions by which none swears except one who is truthful in his oath. But they are far removed from this knowledge, for the majesty of the sworn object is among what restrains the swearer from lying in his oath. The evidence that they lacked knowledge of its greatness is that they did not perceive the indication of that for the Oneness of God in divinity, so they ascribed to Him partners who created nothing of that, nor anything approaching it. This is a sign that they did not perceive the proofs contained within that, until the creator of what is in those positions and the non-creator became equal to them.

As for if you make the pronoun in ﴿And indeed it is an oath﴾ refer to the object sworn to, then the meaning is: "If you knew that, you would not need an oath."

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) recited *bi-mawaqi'* in the plural form, with a fatha on the *waw* and an *alif* after it. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf recited *bi-mawqi'* with a sukun on the *waw* and without an *alif* after it, in the singular form, as a mimi verbal noun, that is, "by their setting," or it is a noun for the direction of their setting, like His words "Lord of the East and the West."

The object of *ta'lamun* (you know) is omitted, indicated by the context: "if you knew His greatness," that is, the proofs of His greatness. You may also treat the verb *ta'lamun* as if it were intransitive, that is: "if you had knowledge, but you do not have the attribute of knowledge."

The pronoun in ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾ refers to something not mentioned in the speech, because it is known and present to them.

*Al-Qur'an* is the read speech, that is, the recited, repeated speech. That is, it is speech by which one is admonished, a locus of reflection and recitation. This has been mentioned earlier at His words Most High ﴿And you are not engaged in any matter, nor do you recite from it any Qur'an﴾ [Yunus: 61] in Surah Yunus.

*Al-karim* means precious and elevated within its kind, as was mentioned earlier at His words Most High ﴿Indeed, there has been delivered to me a noble letter﴾ [al-Naml: 29] in Surah al-Naml.

This is a preference of the Qur'an over the individual members of its genre of divine books, such as the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Book of Luqman. Its superiority over them is that it surpassed them in fully covering the aims of religion, the conditions of livelihood and the hereafter, and establishing beliefs through proofs from creation, and in thoroughly refuting falsehood with a refutation that no earlier book contained the like of, especially in matters of belief; and in the clarity of its meanings, in the abundance of its indication with the scarcity of its words, in its eloquence, in the beauty of its verses and the beauty of their placement for the ear. All of this is among the effects of what God intended by the universality of guidance through it, and its suitability for every nation and every age. So this is a description of the Qur'an as elevated above all books, a truth which the opponent cannot find a way to challenge.

After the Qur'an was described as *karim* (noble), it was described a second time as ﴿in a Book well-guarded﴾. This is certainly a description of honor, so neither the word *kitab* (book) nor the description *maknun* (well-guarded) is intended literally, since taking them literally would not confer honor. Therefore the particle *fi* (in) is for figurative location.

The "well-guarded Book" is a metaphor for the agreement of the words and meanings of the Qur'an with what is in God's knowledge, His will, and His command to the angel to convey it to the Messenger (ﷺ). These are matters hidden from us. Therefore He described the Book as *maknun*, derived from *iktinan*, which means concealment, that is, hidden from the gaze of people. So it is a matter unseen, whose reality none knows except God.

The essential meaning of this verse is: the Qur'an that reached them and that they heard from the Prophet (ﷺ) is in accordance with what God intended to inform people of, and what His power has determined the creation of its inimitable composition, so that it may complete the description that it is the speech of God Most High and that no human made it.

A parallel to this locative particle is His words Most High ﴿And not a leaf falls but He knows it﴾ [al-An'am: 59], up to His words ﴿except that it is in a clear Book﴾ [al-An'am: 59] in Surah al-An'am, and His words ﴿And no one is granted long life nor is any of his life shortened except that it is in a Book﴾ [Fatir: 11]. The consensus of the scholars that one who is not in wudu' may recite the Qur'an, despite their disagreement over touching the mushaf for one not in wudu', indicates that touching the mushaf in their view is a stronger contact than pronouncing the verses of the Qur'an.

I say: among the Muslims in the era of the Companions the practice spread that one who is junub does not recite the Qur'an, and no fatwa to that effect was reported from them. Ahmad and Dawud said: reciting the Qur'an is permissible for one in janabah. On this, Malik has two narrations, and I suppose that the narration of permissibility takes into account that the lapse of the validity of their purity lasts a long time, and this was the reason for the leniency.

This is a consequence (*tafri'*, a logical branching) of the statement ﴿Say: Indeed, the former and the later peoples will surely be gathered﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 49]. It indicates an address from God Most High directed at those who deny resurrection, who say: "When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised?" From this, the discourse moves to praising the Qur'an. Since they denied resurrection, and since affirming resurrection was among the most important things the Qur'an brought, and since its affirmation of resurrection, which they considered impossible, was one of the things that incited them to deny the Qur'an, in addition to their denial of it in other matters that it brought, namely the nullification of their polytheism and their falsehoods, then once the proof had been established against their error in their denial, the truthfulness of what the Qur'an had informed them of became clear, and so its truthfulness was established. For this reason the context became ready for praising its status.

The *fa'* (the conjunctive particle "then") is for the branching of the oath upon what preceded it, namely the proofs for the occurrence of resurrection. The statement ﴿Say: Indeed, the former and the later peoples will surely be gathered﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 49] is an announcement of the Day of Resurrection and a warning to them of it, while they had denied it. Because it seemed impossible in their limited view, they denied the Qur'an and denied the one who brought it. So He branched, upon establishing the occurrence of resurrection and the warning of it, the establishment that the Qur'an is free of defects, that it is a revelation from God, and that the one who brought it is a messenger conveying from God.

The branching of the oath is a branching in meaning with respect to the object sworn upon, and it is also a verbal branching with respect to the act of swearing, if they say to you: "He swore by the positions of the stars."

The branching of an oath upon what precedes it with *fa'* has come in mere mention, in the words of Zuhayr:

*So I swore by the House around which walked men whom Quraysh and Jurhum had built,*

after the verses of erotic prelude (*nasib*) from his mu'allaqah, and there is no connection between the erotic prelude and what branches from it, the oath. He only intended that what follows the *fa'* is the purpose of the poem, and that he preceded it with the erotic prelude to rouse the listener. By this, the difference in composition between the verse and Zuhayr's line becomes evident.

*La uqsimu* (﴿لا أُقْسِمُ﴾): in the sense of *uqsimu*, and *la* is additional for emphasis. Its original function is negation, indicating that the speaker does not venture to swear by what he swears by, out of fear of the evil consequence of lying in an oath.

It also carries the sense that he does not need to swear, because the matter is clearly established. Since this usage became common, it came to mean the emphasis of the statement, and so it equals an oath. This is shown by His words following it: ﴿And indeed it is an oath, if you knew, a great one﴾. This second aspect is the more appropriate one, given what has occurred similarly in the Qur'an.

On both readings, it is an embedding (*idmaj*) to praise the status of what, if He were swearing, He would swear by. On the second reading, His words ﴿and indeed it is an oath﴾ mean: "and indeed what is mentioned is a great thing by which swearers swear." The application of the word *qasam* (oath) to it is from the use of a verbal noun to mean the object, like *al-khalq* (creation) meaning the created thing.

From Sa'id ibn Jubayr and some exegetes: they made *la* a separate particle, not part of the verb *uqsimu*, standing as a response to an implied statement that is indicated by what follows it, namely ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾, in reply to their claims about the Qur'an: that it is poetry, or magic, or the fables of the ancients, or the speech of a soothsayer. They made His words *uqsimu* a resumption (*isti'naf*). According to this reading, the meaning of the speech together with the *fa'* of branching upon the proofs for the possibility of resurrection that have become manifest is: "What you claim about the Qur'an is not as you assert; rather it is a noble Qur'an, etc."

*Mawaqi' al-nujum* (﴿مَواقِعِ النُّجُومِ﴾) is the plural of *mawqi'*, which may be the place of falling, that is, the locations where they fall, whether fixed stars or wandering stars. *Al-wuqu'* is used for falling, that is, setting, so the positions of the stars are the places of their setting. This agrees with His words Most High ﴿By the star when it sets﴾ [al-Najm: 1]. Swearing by this is among what is included in His words Most High ﴿So I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 40]. The positions of the stars, in this sense, are made an object of oath because those places, at the time the stars set at them, remind one of the wonderful order established for the movement of the heavenly bodies, which does not fail or deviate every night, and they remind one of the greatness of the heavenly bodies and their alternation one after another. That is a great matter, which makes swearing by it appropriate, and the swearing by it returns to swearing by its Originator.

*Al-wuqu'* is also used for alighting in a place. It is said: "The camels *waqa'at*," when they knelt, and "the sheep *waqa'at*" in their pens. From this comes the name *al-waqi'ah* for an event, as was mentioned earlier. So *al-mawaqi'* are the places of their alighting and the lines of their courses. This is close to His words ﴿By the sky of the constellations﴾ [al-Buruj: 1].

*Al-mawaqi'* are the orbits of the stars, precisely regulated in their motion across the horizon of the sky. Likewise their constellations and their stations.

Mentioning the positions of the stars in both senses is a praise of them and an exaltation of their matter, because their conditions indicate the subtleties of God's wisdom in the arrangement of their motion and the wonders of His power in subjecting them.

It is also possible that *mawaqi'* is the plural of *mawqi'*, which is the mimi verbal noun (a noun of place or time formed from the root) of *al-wuqu'*.

Some exegetes interpreted *al-nujum* as the plural of *najm*, which means a portion of wealth or other things, as one says: "the installments (*nujum*) of blood-money and fines." They interpreted *al-nujum*, that is, groups of verses, which descend from the Qur'an. This is from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah. Thus it returns to an oath by the Qur'an in its literal sense, in the manner mentioned earlier in His words Most High ﴿By the Clear Book﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 2] ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 3].

The sentence ﴿And indeed it is an oath, if you knew, a great one﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraD*) between the oath and its answer.

The pronoun in ﴿innahu﴾ refers either to the oath mentioned in ﴿I do not swear by the positions of the stars﴾, or it refers to the positions of the stars, taking them as "what is mentioned," so that it is an oath in the sense of "the thing sworn by," as you have understood a moment ago.

It is also possible that it refers to the thing sworn to, namely what is contained in the answer of the oath, His words ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾.

The clause ﴿if you knew﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between the described and its description, and it is a parenthesis within a parenthesis.

The knowledge that the counterfactual *law* (conditional of impossibility) requires to be absent from them, if you make the pronoun in ﴿innahu﴾ refer to the oath, is the detailed knowledge of the conditions of the positions of the stars. For the polytheists are not free of a general, varying knowledge that in those positions there is a lesson for observers. Or that general knowledge is treated as if it were nonexistent, because by their disbelief they did not act in accordance with what that knowledge requires of the Oneness of God. So if they knew what the conditions of the positions of the stars contain of the connections to God's attributes, they would know that they are sacred positions by which none swears except one who is truthful in his oath. But they are far removed from this knowledge, for the majesty of the sworn object is among what restrains the swearer from lying in his oath. The evidence that they lacked knowledge of its greatness is that they did not perceive the indication of that for the Oneness of God in divinity, so they ascribed to Him partners who created nothing of that, nor anything approaching it. This is a sign that they did not perceive the proofs contained within that, until the creator of what is in those positions and the non-creator became equal to them.

As for if you make the pronoun in ﴿And indeed it is an oath﴾ refer to the object sworn to, then the meaning is: "If you knew that, you would not need an oath."

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) recited *bi-mawaqi'* in the plural form, with a fatha on the *waw* and an *alif* after it. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf recited *bi-mawqi'* with a sukun on the *waw* and without an *alif* after it, in the singular form, as a mimi verbal noun, that is, "by their setting," or it is a noun for the direction of their setting, like His words "Lord of the East and the West."

The object of *ta'lamun* (you know) is omitted, indicated by the context: "if you knew His greatness," that is, the proofs of His greatness. You may also treat the verb *ta'lamun* as if it were intransitive, that is: "if you had knowledge, but you do not have the attribute of knowledge."

The pronoun in ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾ refers to something not mentioned in the speech, because it is known and present to them.

*Al-Qur'an* is the read speech, that is, the recited, repeated speech. That is, it is speech by which one is admonished, a locus of reflection and recitation. This has been mentioned earlier at His words Most High ﴿And you are not engaged in any matter, nor do you recite from it any Qur'an﴾ [Yunus: 61] in Surah Yunus.

*Al-karim* means precious and elevated within its kind, as was mentioned earlier at His words Most High ﴿Indeed, there has been delivered to me a noble letter﴾ [al-Naml: 29] in Surah al-Naml.

This is a preference of the Qur'an over the individual members of its genre of divine books, such as the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Book of Luqman. Its superiority over them is that it surpassed them in fully covering the aims of religion, the conditions of livelihood and the hereafter, and establishing beliefs through proofs from creation, and in thoroughly refuting falsehood with a refutation that no earlier book contained the like of, especially in matters of belief; and in the clarity of its meanings, in the abundance of its indication with the scarcity of its words, in its eloquence, in the beauty of its verses and the beauty of their placement for the ear. All of this is among the effects of what God intended by the universality of guidance through it, and its suitability for every nation and every age. So this is a description of the Qur'an as elevated above all books, a truth which the opponent cannot find a way to challenge.

After the Qur'an was described as *karim* (noble), it was described a second time as ﴿in a Book well-guarded﴾. This is certainly a description of honor, so neither the word *kitab* (book) nor the description *maknun* (well-guarded) is intended literally, since taking them literally would not confer honor. Therefore the particle *fi* (in) is for figurative location.

The "well-guarded Book" is a metaphor for the agreement of the words and meanings of the Qur'an with what is in God's knowledge, His will, and His command to the angel to convey it to the Messenger (ﷺ). These are matters hidden from us. Therefore He described the Book as *maknun*, derived from *iktinan*, which means concealment, that is, hidden from the gaze of people. So it is a matter unseen, whose reality none knows except God.

The essential meaning of this verse is: the Qur'an that reached them and that they heard from the Prophet (ﷺ) is in accordance with what God intended to inform people of, and what His power has determined the creation of its inimitable composition, so that it may complete the description that it is the speech of God Most High and that no human made it.

A parallel to this locative particle is His words Most High ﴿And not a leaf falls but He knows it﴾ [al-An'am: 59], up to His words ﴿except that it is in a clear Book﴾ [al-An'am: 59] in Surah al-An'am, and His words ﴿And no one is granted long life nor is any of his life shortened except that it is in a Book﴾ [Fatir: 11]. That is: except as it proceeds according to what God knew and what His decree has determined. Likewise His words here ﴿in a Book well-guarded﴾. So the particle of location is borrowed for the meaning of correspondence to what is with God, likening that correspondence to the union of the contained with the container. Close to this is His words Most High ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scriptures﴾ [al-A'la: 18] ﴿the scriptures of Abraham and Moses﴾ [al-A'la: 19]. This is better than considering metaphor in ascribing the attribute of being in a well-guarded Book to a noble Qur'an by way of rational metaphor (*majaz 'aqli*), on the ground that the real basis of this metaphor is describing a counterpart and match of the Qur'an, since the counterpart is connected to its counterpart.

The word *kitab* is borrowed for a matter that is established and fixed, which does not accept change. Thus there is harmony between the borrowing of the locative particle for the meaning of correspondence and the borrowing of *kitab* for what is established and fixed, the meaning being that the meanings of this Qur'an agree with what is with God from the objects of His knowledge, the objects of His will and power, and that its words agree with what God commanded to be created of speech expressing those meanings in the most eloquent manner. Close to this borrowing is the verse of Bishr ibn Abi Khazim, or al-Tirimmah:

*We found in the Book of the Banu Tamim*
*the most deserving of horses to be spurred, the borrowed one.*

The Banu Tamim have no book, but he applied the word *kitab* to what was established of their customs and their knowledge.

The sentence ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾ is a second description of *kitab* (Book).

"And the purified ones" (al-mutahharun): the angels. What is meant is the purity of the soul, which is purification (zaka'). This is the view of the majority of the exegetes. In the Muwatta', Malik said: "The best I have heard concerning this verse, ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾, is that it is like this verse in (Surah) 'Abasa and He Frowned, the saying of God, blessed and exalted be He: ﴿Nay, verily it is a reminder﴾ [80:11] ﴿So whoever wills may remember it﴾ [80:12] ﴿In scrolls held in honour﴾ [80:13] ﴿Exalted, purified﴾ [80:14] ﴿By the hands of scribes﴾ [80:15] ﴿Noble and dutiful﴾ [80:16]." End quote. He means that the purified ones are the noble, dutiful scribes, not the people who purify themselves.

The meaning of "touch" (massa) is "take hold of." In a hadith, "massa min tayyibah" means he took (some) of perfume. The word "massa" is also used for "association" and "perusal." Yazid ibn al-Hakam al-Kilabi said:

∗∗∗ "We have touched (massa) from the fathers something, so each of us
is toward a lineage in his people, not lowering it."

Al-Marzuqi, in his commentary on this verse from al-Hamasa, said: "massa" may mean "we attained and we tested," because touching with the hand is intended for testing. It may also mean "we sought." So the meaning is: the Book does not directly handle the transmission of what it contains for its conveyance except the angels.

The purpose of this is that the Qur'an is not, as the polytheists claim, the words of a soothsayer. They claim that the soothsayer receives from the jinn and devils what they steal of news from the heaven, according to their belief. Nor is it the words of a poet, since they claimed that every poet has a devil who dictates poetry to him. Nor is it "the legends of the ancients," for they mean by them the false tales with which the people of evening gatherings amuse themselves. God said: this Qur'an conforms to what is with God, which none witnesses except the purified angels.

The clause "a revelation from the Lord of the worlds" explains the clause "in a Book well-guarded, none touches it except the purified," so it follows as a description of the Qur'an, meaning: its reaching you was by a revelation from God, that is, the angels brought it down.

In the sense of the structure of this verse is God's saying: ﴿Nor is it the word of a poet; little do you believe﴾ [69:41] ﴿nor the word of a soothsayer; little do you remember﴾ [69:42] ﴿a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [69:43].

Since this noble rank of the Qur'an is established, it is fitting that its recitation and its writing be honored. For this reason, it is among what is commanded that none touch the written Qur'an except one who is purified, imitating the state of the angels in handling the Qur'an, such that the one holding the Qur'an is in a state of religious purity. This is the meaning that the legislation of purification for one who wishes to pray points to, like the hadith "the one praying is conversing with his Lord."

Traditions indicate this, the clearest of which is what Malik narrated in the Muwatta' as a mursal report: that in the letter which the Messenger of God ﷺ wrote to the kings (aqyal) of Dhu Ru'ayn, Ma'afir and Hamadhan, and sent with 'Amr ibn Hazm, was: "None touches the Qur'an except one who is pure." Al-Manawi said: its chain is sound, and al-Suyuti placed it in the rank of hasan.

In the books of biography it is reported that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, before he embraced Islam, entered upon his sister, the wife of Sa'id ibn Zayd, and found her reading the Qur'an from a page on which Surah Ta-Ha was written. He asked for the page to read it, and she said to him: "None touches it except the purified." So he stood up, performed ghusl, read the surah, and embraced Islam. This verse, therefore, is not evidence for the ruling on people touching the Qur'an with their hands; but God's mention of it does not exclude the intention that people be compared to the angels in that they do not touch the Qur'an except when they are pure, as the angels are, that is, to the extent possible of human purity.

Thus it is established that the command to purify oneself for one who holds a written part of the Qur'an was settled among the Muslims from the early period of Islam in Makkah.

The jurists differed only over the implication of this command, whether obligatory or recommended. The majority held it obligatory that the one holding written Qur'an be in a state of wudu', and this is the view of 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Sa'd, Sa'id, 'Ata', al-Zuhri, Malik, al-Shafi'i, and it is a narration from Abu Hanifa. A group said that this is a command of recommendation, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, and it is narrated from Abu Hanifa, and it is the view of Ahmad and Dawud al-Zahiri.

Malik said in the Muwatta': "No one carries the mushaf, neither by its strap nor on a cushion, except while pure, out of honor for the Qur'an and magnifying it." In the narration of Ibn al-Qasim from the Kitab al-Wudu' of al-'Utbiyya, in the sixth question, Malik was asked about a tablet on which the Qur'an is written: may it be touched without wudu'? He said: as for children who are learning, I see no harm in it. He was asked: what about a man learning from it? He said: I hope it is lenient. It was said to Ibn al-Qasim: what about a teacher who shapes children's tablets while not in wudu'? He said: I consider that lenient. Ibn Rushd said in al-Bayan wa al-Tahsil: because of the hardship that would befall them in that, and this would be a cause for prohibiting their learning it; this is the reason for the leniency for children. Al-Baji indicated in al-Muntaqa that the permission to touch the Qur'an for the learner and the teacher is for the sake of the necessity of learning.

They considered this a ruling for what is written with the Qur'an with the intention that it be a mushaf, or part of a mushaf, or a tablet of the Qur'an; and they did not consider it applicable to verses of the Qur'an written by way of quotation, citation, or argument. Among this is what is written on dinars and dirhams, and on rings.

This is not apparently covered by the verse, but since the prohibition against touching the mushaf for one not purified may be because touching is a contact with the written Qur'an, the prohibition on pronouncing the words of the Qur'an may be established by the understanding of agreement (mafhum al-muwafaqa), equal or stronger, since uttering is a contact like the contact of holding the written text or stronger. I suppose this is the source of their disagreement over reciting the Qur'an for one who is not purified. The consensus of the scholars that one who is not in wudu' may recite the Qur'an, despite their disagreement over touching the mushaf for one not in wudu', indicates that touching the mushaf in their view is a stronger contact than pronouncing the verses of the Qur'an.

Mentioning the positions of the stars in both senses is a praise of them and an exaltation of their matter, because their conditions indicate the subtleties of God's wisdom in the arrangement of their motion and the wonders of His power in subjecting them.

It is also possible that *mawaqi'* is the plural of *mawqi'*, which is the mimi verbal noun (a noun of place or time formed from the root) of *al-wuqu'*.

Some exegetes interpreted *al-nujum* as the plural of *najm*, which means a portion of wealth or other things, as one says: "the installments (*nujum*) of blood-money and fines." They interpreted *al-nujum*, that is, groups of verses, which descend from the Qur'an. This is from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah. Thus it returns to an oath by the Qur'an in its literal sense, in the manner mentioned earlier in His words Most High ﴿By the Clear Book﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 2] ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 3].

The sentence ﴿And indeed it is an oath, if you knew, a great one﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraD*) between the oath and its answer.

The pronoun in ﴿innahu﴾ refers either to the oath mentioned in ﴿I do not swear by the positions of the stars﴾, or it refers to the positions of the stars, taking them as "what is mentioned," so that it is an oath in the sense of "the thing sworn by," as you have understood a moment ago.

It is also possible that it refers to the thing sworn to, namely what is contained in the answer of the oath, His words ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾.

The clause ﴿if you knew﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between the described and its description, and it is a parenthesis within a parenthesis.

The knowledge that the counterfactual *law* (conditional of impossibility) requires to be absent from them, if you make the pronoun in ﴿innahu﴾ refer to the oath, is the detailed knowledge of the conditions of the positions of the stars. For the polytheists are not free of a general, varying knowledge that in those positions there is a lesson for observers. Or that general knowledge is treated as if it were nonexistent, because by their disbelief they did not act in accordance with what that knowledge requires of the Oneness of God. So if they knew what the conditions of the positions of the stars contain of the connections to God's attributes, they would know that they are sacred positions by which none swears except one who is truthful in his oath. But they are far removed from this knowledge, for the majesty of the sworn object is among what restrains the swearer from lying in his oath. The evidence that they lacked knowledge of its greatness is that they did not perceive the indication of that for the Oneness of God in divinity, so they ascribed to Him partners who created nothing of that, nor anything approaching it. This is a sign that they did not perceive the proofs contained within that, until the creator of what is in those positions and the non-creator became equal to them.

As for if you make the pronoun in ﴿And indeed it is an oath﴾ refer to the object sworn to, then the meaning is: "If you knew that, you would not need an oath."

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) recited *bi-mawaqi'* in the plural form, with a fatha on the *waw* and an *alif* after it. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf recited *bi-mawqi'* with a sukun on the *waw* and without an *alif* after it, in the singular form, as a mimi verbal noun, that is, "by their setting," or it is a noun for the direction of their setting, like His words "Lord of the East and the West."

The object of *ta'lamun* (you know) is omitted, indicated by the context: "if you knew His greatness," that is, the proofs of His greatness. You may also treat the verb *ta'lamun* as if it were intransitive, that is: "if you had knowledge, but you do not have the attribute of knowledge."

The pronoun in ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾ refers to something not mentioned in the speech, because it is known and present to them.

*Al-Qur'an* is the read speech, that is, the recited, repeated speech. That is, it is speech by which one is admonished, a locus of reflection and recitation. This has been mentioned earlier at His words Most High ﴿And you are not engaged in any matter, nor do you recite from it any Qur'an﴾ [Yunus: 61] in Surah Yunus.

*Al-karim* means precious and elevated within its kind, as was mentioned earlier at His words Most High ﴿Indeed, there has been delivered to me a noble letter﴾ [al-Naml: 29] in Surah al-Naml.

This is a preference of the Qur'an over the individual members of its genre of divine books, such as the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Book of Luqman. Its superiority over them is that it surpassed them in fully covering the aims of religion, the conditions of livelihood and the hereafter, and establishing beliefs through proofs from creation, and in thoroughly refuting falsehood with a refutation that no earlier book contained the like of, especially in matters of belief; and in the clarity of its meanings, in the abundance of its indication with the scarcity of its words, in its eloquence, in the beauty of its verses and the beauty of their placement for the ear. All of this is among the effects of what God intended by the universality of guidance through it, and its suitability for every nation and every age. So this is a description of the Qur'an as elevated above all books, a truth which the opponent cannot find a way to challenge.

After the Qur'an was described as *karim* (noble), it was described a second time as ﴿in a Book well-guarded﴾. This is certainly a description of honor, so neither the word *kitab* (book) nor the description *maknun* (well-guarded) is intended literally, since taking them literally would not confer honor. Therefore the particle *fi* (in) is for figurative location.

The "well-guarded Book" is a metaphor for the agreement of the words and meanings of the Qur'an with what is in God's knowledge, His will, and His command to the angel to convey it to the Messenger (ﷺ). These are matters hidden from us. Therefore He described the Book as *maknun*, derived from *iktinan*, which means concealment, that is, hidden from the gaze of people. So it is a matter unseen, whose reality none knows except God.

The essential meaning of this verse is: the Qur'an that reached them and that they heard from the Prophet (ﷺ) is in accordance with what God intended to inform people of, and what His power has determined the creation of its inimitable composition, so that it may complete the description that it is the speech of God Most High and that no human made it.

A parallel to this locative particle is His words Most High ﴿And not a leaf falls but He knows it﴾ [al-An'am: 59], up to His words ﴿except that it is in a clear Book﴾ [al-An'am: 59] in Surah al-An'am, and His words ﴿And no one is granted long life nor is any of his life shortened except that it is in a Book﴾ [Fatir: 11]. That is: except as it proceeds according to what God knew and what His decree has determined. Likewise His words here ﴿in a Book well-guarded﴾. So the particle of location is borrowed for the meaning of correspondence to what is with God, likening that correspondence to the union of the contained with the container. Close to this is His words Most High ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scriptures﴾ [al-A'la: 18] ﴿the scriptures of Abraham and Moses﴾ [al-A'la: 19]. This is better than considering metaphor in ascribing the attribute of being in a well-guarded Book to a noble Qur'an by way of rational metaphor (*majaz 'aqli*), on the ground that the real basis of this metaphor is describing a counterpart and match of the Qur'an, since the counterpart is connected to its counterpart.

The word *kitab* is borrowed for a matter that is established and fixed, which does not accept change. Thus there is harmony between the borrowing of the locative particle for the meaning of correspondence and the borrowing of *kitab* for what is established and fixed, the meaning being that the meanings of this Qur'an agree with what is with God from the objects of His knowledge, the objects of His will and power, and that its words agree with what God commanded to be created of speech expressing those meanings in the most eloquent manner. Close to this borrowing is the verse of Bishr ibn Abi Khazim, or al-Tirimmah:

*We found in the Book of the Banu Tamim*
*the most deserving of horses to be spurred, the borrowed one.*

The Banu Tamim have no book, but he applied the word *kitab* to what was established of their customs and their knowledge.

The sentence ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾ is a second description of *kitab* (Book).

"And the purified ones" (al-mutahharun): the angels. What is meant is the purity of the soul, which is purification (zaka'). This is the view of the majority of the exegetes. In the Muwatta', Malik said: "The best I have heard concerning this verse, ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾, is that it is like this verse in (Surah) 'Abasa and He Frowned, the saying of God, blessed and exalted be He: ﴿Nay, verily it is a reminder﴾ [80:11] ﴿So whoever wills may remember it﴾ [80:12] ﴿In scrolls held in honour﴾ [80:13] ﴿Exalted, purified﴾ [80:14] ﴿By the hands of scribes﴾ [80:15] ﴿Noble and dutiful﴾ [80:16]." End quote. He means that the purified ones are the noble, dutiful scribes, not the people who purify themselves.

The meaning of "touch" (massa) is "take hold of." In a hadith, "massa min tayyibah" means he took (some) of perfume. The word "massa" is also used for "association" and "perusal." Yazid ibn al-Hakam al-Kilabi said:

∗∗∗ "We have touched (massa) from the fathers something, so each of us
is toward a lineage in his people, not lowering it."

Al-Marzuqi, in his commentary on this verse from al-Hamasa, said: "massa" may mean "we attained and we tested," because touching with the hand is intended for testing. It may also mean "we sought." So the meaning is: the Book does not directly handle the transmission of what it contains for its conveyance except the angels.

The purpose of this is that the Qur'an is not, as the polytheists claim, the words of a soothsayer. They claim that the soothsayer receives from the jinn and devils what they steal of news from the heaven, according to their belief. Nor is it the words of a poet, since they claimed that every poet has a devil who dictates poetry to him. Nor is it "the legends of the ancients," for they mean by them the false tales with which the people of evening gatherings amuse themselves. God said: this Qur'an conforms to what is with God, which none witnesses except the purified angels.

The clause "a revelation from the Lord of the worlds" explains the clause "in a Book well-guarded, none touches it except the purified," so it follows as a description of the Qur'an, meaning: its reaching you was by a revelation from God, that is, the angels brought it down.

In the sense of the structure of this verse is God's saying: ﴿Nor is it the word of a poet; little do you believe﴾ [69:41] ﴿nor the word of a soothsayer; little do you remember﴾ [69:42] ﴿a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [69:43].

Since this noble rank of the Qur'an is established, it is fitting that its recitation and its writing be honored. For this reason, it is among what is commanded that none touch the written Qur'an except one who is purified, imitating the state of the angels in handling the Qur'an, such that the one holding the Qur'an is in a state of religious purity. This is the meaning that the legislation of purification for one who wishes to pray points to, like the hadith "the one praying is conversing with his Lord."

Traditions indicate this, the clearest of which is what Malik narrated in the Muwatta' as a mursal report: that in the letter which the Messenger of God ﷺ wrote to the kings (aqyal) of Dhu Ru'ayn, Ma'afir and Hamadhan, and sent with 'Amr ibn Hazm, was: "None touches the Qur'an except one who is pure." Al-Manawi said: its chain is sound, and al-Suyuti placed it in the rank of hasan.

In the books of biography it is reported that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, before he embraced Islam, entered upon his sister, the wife of Sa'id ibn Zayd, and found her reading the Qur'an from a page on which Surah Ta-Ha was written. He asked for the page to read it, and she said to him: "None touches it except the purified." So he stood up, performed ghusl, read the surah, and embraced Islam. This verse, therefore, is not evidence for the ruling on people touching the Qur'an with their hands; but God's mention of it does not exclude the intention that people be compared to the angels in that they do not touch the Qur'an except when they are pure, as the angels are, that is, to the extent possible of human purity.

Thus it is established that the command to purify oneself for one who holds a written part of the Qur'an was settled among the Muslims from the early period of Islam in Makkah.

The jurists differed only over the implication of this command, whether obligatory or recommended. The majority held it obligatory that the one holding written Qur'an be in a state of wudu', and this is the view of 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Sa'd, Sa'id, 'Ata', al-Zuhri, Malik, al-Shafi'i, and it is a narration from Abu Hanifa. A group said that this is a command of recommendation, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, and it is narrated from Abu Hanifa, and it is the view of Ahmad and Dawud al-Zahiri.

Malik said in the Muwatta': "No one carries the mushaf, neither by its strap nor on a cushion, except while pure, out of honor for the Qur'an and magnifying it." In the narration of Ibn al-Qasim from the Kitab al-Wudu' of al-'Utbiyya, in the sixth question, Malik was asked about a tablet on which the Qur'an is written: may it be touched without wudu'? He said: as for children who are learning, I see no harm in it. He was asked: what about a man learning from it? He said: I hope it is lenient. It was said to Ibn al-Qasim: what about a teacher who shapes children's tablets while not in wudu'? He said: I consider that lenient. Ibn Rushd said in al-Bayan wa al-Tahsil: because of the hardship that would befall them in that, and this would be a cause for prohibiting their learning it; this is the reason for the leniency for children. Al-Baji indicated in al-Muntaqa that the permission to touch the Qur'an for the learner and the teacher is for the sake of the necessity of learning.

They considered this a ruling for what is written with the Qur'an with the intention that it be a mushaf, or part of a mushaf, or a tablet of the Qur'an; and they did not consider it applicable to verses of the Qur'an written by way of quotation, citation, or argument. Among this is what is written on dinars and dirhams, and on rings.

The meaning of purity according to those who hold it obligatory is the minor purification, that is, wudu'. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Sha'bi said: it is permissible to touch the Qur'an with the major purification even if the minor one is not present.

Among what is connected to this issue is the question of a non-purified person reciting the Qur'an. This is not apparently covered by the verse, but since the prohibition against touching the mushaf for one not purified may be because touching is a contact with the written Qur'an, the prohibition on pronouncing the words of the Qur'an may be established by the understanding of agreement (mafhum al-muwafaqa), equal or stronger, since uttering is a contact like the contact of holding the written text or stronger. I suppose this is the source of their disagreement over reciting the Qur'an for one who is not purified. The consensus of the scholars that one who is not in wudu' may recite the Qur'an, despite their disagreement over touching the mushaf for one not in wudu', indicates that touching the mushaf in their view is a stronger contact than pronouncing the verses of the Qur'an.

Malik, Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i said: it is not permissible for one in janabah to recite the Qur'an, but it is permissible for one not in wudu'. I say: among the Muslims in the era of the Companions the practice spread that one who is junub does not recite the Qur'an, and no fatwa to that effect was reported from them. Ahmad and Dawud said: reciting the Qur'an is permissible for one in janabah. Malik allowed the recitation of a small portion of it, such as a verse or two, and none of the scholars required wudu' of the one reciting the Qur'an.

There is disagreement concerning its recitation by a menstruating or post-natal woman. On this, Malik has two narrations, and I suppose that the narration of permissibility takes into account that the lapse of the validity of their purity lasts a long time, and this was the reason for the leniency.

This is a consequence (*tafri'*, a logical branching) of the statement ﴿Say: Indeed, the former and the later peoples will surely be gathered﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 49]. It indicates an address from God Most High directed at those who deny resurrection, who say: "When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised?" From this, the discourse moves to praising the Qur'an. Since they denied resurrection, and since affirming resurrection was among the most important things the Qur'an brought, and since its affirmation of resurrection, which they considered impossible, was one of the things that incited them to deny the Qur'an, in addition to their denial of it in other matters that it brought, namely the nullification of their polytheism and their falsehoods, then once the proof had been established against their error in their denial, the truthfulness of what the Qur'an had informed them of became clear, and so its truthfulness was established. For this reason the context became ready for praising its status.

The *fa'* (the conjunctive particle "then") is for the branching of the oath upon what preceded it, namely the proofs for the occurrence of resurrection. The statement ﴿Say: Indeed, the former and the later peoples will surely be gathered﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 49] is an announcement of the Day of Resurrection and a warning to them of it, while they had denied it. Because it seemed impossible in their limited view, they denied the Qur'an and denied the one who brought it. So He branched, upon establishing the occurrence of resurrection and the warning of it, the establishment that the Qur'an is free of defects, that it is a revelation from God, and that the one who brought it is a messenger conveying from God.

The branching of the oath is a branching in meaning with respect to the object sworn upon, and it is also a verbal branching with respect to the act of swearing, if they say to you: "He swore by the positions of the stars."

The branching of an oath upon what precedes it with *fa'* has come in mere mention, in the words of Zuhayr:

*So I swore by the House around which walked men whom Quraysh and Jurhum had built,*

after the verses of erotic prelude (*nasib*) from his mu'allaqah, and there is no connection between the erotic prelude and what branches from it, the oath. He only intended that what follows the *fa'* is the purpose of the poem, and that he preceded it with the erotic prelude to rouse the listener. By this, the difference in composition between the verse and Zuhayr's line becomes evident.

*La uqsimu* (﴿لا أُقْسِمُ﴾): in the sense of *uqsimu*, and *la* is additional for emphasis. Its original function is negation, indicating that the speaker does not venture to swear by what he swears by, out of fear of the evil consequence of lying in an oath.

It also carries the sense that he does not need to swear, because the matter is clearly established. Since this usage became common, it came to mean the emphasis of the statement, and so it equals an oath. This is shown by His words following it: ﴿And indeed it is an oath, if you knew, a great one﴾. This second aspect is the more appropriate one, given what has occurred similarly in the Qur'an.

On both readings, it is an embedding (*idmaj*) to praise the status of what, if He were swearing, He would swear by. On the second reading, His words ﴿and indeed it is an oath﴾ mean: "and indeed what is mentioned is a great thing by which swearers swear." The application of the word *qasam* (oath) to it is from the use of a verbal noun to mean the object, like *al-khalq* (creation) meaning the created thing.

From Sa'id ibn Jubayr and some exegetes: they made *la* a separate particle, not part of the verb *uqsimu*, standing as a response to an implied statement that is indicated by what follows it, namely ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾, in reply to their claims about the Qur'an: that it is poetry, or magic, or the fables of the ancients, or the speech of a soothsayer. They made His words *uqsimu* a resumption (*isti'naf*). According to this reading, the meaning of the speech together with the *fa'* of branching upon the proofs for the possibility of resurrection that have become manifest is: "What you claim about the Qur'an is not as you assert; rather it is a noble Qur'an, etc."

The word *kitab* is borrowed for a matter that is established and fixed, which does not accept change. Thus there is harmony between the borrowing of the locative particle for the meaning of correspondence and the borrowing of *kitab* for what is established and fixed, the meaning being that the meanings of this Qur'an agree with what is with God from the objects of His knowledge, the objects of His will and power, and that its words agree with what God commanded to be created of speech expressing those meanings in the most eloquent manner. Close to this borrowing is the verse of Bishr ibn Abi Khazim, or al-Tirimmah:

*We found in the Book of the Banu Tamim*
*the most deserving of horses to be spurred, the borrowed one.*

The Banu Tamim have no book, but he applied the word *kitab* to what was established of their customs and their knowledge.

The sentence ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾ is a second description of *kitab* (Book).

"And the purified ones" (al-mutahharun): the angels. What is meant is the purity of the soul, which is purification (zaka'). This is the view of the majority of the exegetes. In the Muwatta', Malik said: "The best I have heard concerning this verse, ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾, is that it is like this verse in (Surah) 'Abasa and He Frowned, the saying of God, blessed and exalted be He: ﴿Nay, verily it is a reminder﴾ [80:11] ﴿So whoever wills may remember it﴾ [80:12] ﴿In scrolls held in honour﴾ [80:13] ﴿Exalted, purified﴾ [80:14] ﴿By the hands of scribes﴾ [80:15] ﴿Noble and dutiful﴾ [80:16]." End quote. He means that the purified ones are the noble, dutiful scribes, not the people who purify themselves.

The meaning of "touch" (massa) is "take hold of." In a hadith, "massa min tayyibah" means he took (some) of perfume. The word "massa" is also used for "association" and "perusal." Yazid ibn al-Hakam al-Kilabi said:

∗∗∗ "We have touched (massa) from the fathers something, so each of us
is toward a lineage in his people, not lowering it."

Al-Marzuqi, in his commentary on this verse from al-Hamasa, said: "massa" may mean "we attained and we tested," because touching with the hand is intended for testing. It may also mean "we sought." So the meaning is: the Book does not directly handle the transmission of what it contains for its conveyance except the angels.

The purpose of this is that the Qur'an is not, as the polytheists claim, the words of a soothsayer. They claim that the soothsayer receives from the jinn and devils what they steal of news from the heaven, according to their belief. Nor is it the words of a poet, since they claimed that every poet has a devil who dictates poetry to him. Nor is it "the legends of the ancients," for they mean by them the false tales with which the people of evening gatherings amuse themselves. God said: this Qur'an conforms to what is with God, which none witnesses except the purified angels.

The clause "a revelation from the Lord of the worlds" explains the clause "in a Book well-guarded, none touches it except the purified," so it follows as a description of the Qur'an, meaning: its reaching you was by a revelation from God, that is, the angels brought it down.

In the sense of the structure of this verse is God's saying: ﴿Nor is it the word of a poet; little do you believe﴾ [69:41] ﴿nor the word of a soothsayer; little do you remember﴾ [69:42] ﴿a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [69:43].

Since this noble rank of the Qur'an is established, it is fitting that its recitation and its writing be honored. For this reason, it is among what is commanded that none touch the written Qur'an except one who is purified, imitating the state of the angels in handling the Qur'an, such that the one holding the Qur'an is in a state of religious purity. This is the meaning that the legislation of purification for one who wishes to pray points to, like the hadith "the one praying is conversing with his Lord."

Traditions indicate this, the clearest of which is what Malik narrated in the Muwatta' as a mursal report: that in the letter which the Messenger of God ﷺ wrote to the kings (aqyal) of Dhu Ru'ayn, Ma'afir and Hamadhan, and sent with 'Amr ibn Hazm, was: "None touches the Qur'an except one who is pure." Al-Manawi said: its chain is sound, and al-Suyuti placed it in the rank of hasan.

In the books of biography it is reported that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, before he embraced Islam, entered upon his sister, the wife of Sa'id ibn Zayd, and found her reading the Qur'an from a page on which Surah Ta-Ha was written. He asked for the page to read it, and she said to him: "None touches it except the purified." So he stood up, performed ghusl, read the surah, and embraced Islam. This verse, therefore, is not evidence for the ruling on people touching the Qur'an with their hands; but God's mention of it does not exclude the intention that people be compared to the angels in that they do not touch the Qur'an except when they are pure, as the angels are, that is, to the extent possible of human purity.

Thus it is established that the command to purify oneself for one who holds a written part of the Qur'an was settled among the Muslims from the early period of Islam in Makkah.

The jurists differed only over the implication of this command, whether obligatory or recommended. The majority held it obligatory that the one holding written Qur'an be in a state of wudu', and this is the view of 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Sa'd, Sa'id, 'Ata', al-Zuhri, Malik, al-Shafi'i, and it is a narration from Abu Hanifa. A group said that this is a command of recommendation, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, and it is narrated from Abu Hanifa, and it is the view of Ahmad and Dawud al-Zahiri.

Malik said in the Muwatta': "No one carries the mushaf, neither by its strap nor on a cushion, except while pure, out of honor for the Qur'an and magnifying it." In the narration of Ibn al-Qasim from the Kitab al-Wudu' of al-'Utbiyya, in the sixth question, Malik was asked about a tablet on which the Qur'an is written: may it be touched without wudu'? He said: as for children who are learning, I see no harm in it. He was asked: what about a man learning from it? He said: I hope it is lenient. It was said to Ibn al-Qasim: what about a teacher who shapes children's tablets while not in wudu'? He said: I consider that lenient. Ibn Rushd said in al-Bayan wa al-Tahsil: because of the hardship that would befall them in that, and this would be a cause for prohibiting their learning it; this is the reason for the leniency for children. Al-Baji indicated in al-Muntaqa that the permission to touch the Qur'an for the learner and the teacher is for the sake of the necessity of learning.

They considered this a ruling for what is written with the Qur'an with the intention that it be a mushaf, or part of a mushaf, or a tablet of the Qur'an; and they did not consider it applicable to verses of the Qur'an written by way of quotation, citation, or argument. Among this is what is written on dinars and dirhams, and on rings.

The meaning of purity according to those who hold it obligatory is the minor purification, that is, wudu'. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Sha'bi said: it is permissible to touch the Qur'an with the major purification even if the minor one is not present.

Among what is connected to this issue is the question of a non-purified person reciting the Qur'an. This is not apparently covered by the verse, but since the prohibition against touching the mushaf for one not purified may be because touching is a contact with the written Qur'an, the prohibition on pronouncing the words of the Qur'an may be established by the understanding of agreement (mafhum al-muwafaqa), equal or stronger, since uttering is a contact like the contact of holding the written text or stronger. I suppose this is the source of their disagreement over reciting the Qur'an for one who is not purified. The consensus of the scholars that one who is not in wudu' may recite the Qur'an, despite their disagreement over touching the mushaf for one not in wudu', indicates that touching the mushaf in their view is a stronger contact than pronouncing the verses of the Qur'an.

Malik, Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i said: it is not permissible for one in janabah to recite the Qur'an, but it is permissible for one not in wudu'. I say: among the Muslims in the era of the Companions the practice spread that one who is junub does not recite the Qur'an, and no fatwa to that effect was reported from them. Ahmad and Dawud said: reciting the Qur'an is permissible for one in janabah. Malik allowed the recitation of a small portion of it, such as a verse or two, and none of the scholars required wudu' of the one reciting the Qur'an.

There is disagreement concerning its recitation by a menstruating or post-natal woman. On this, Malik has two narrations, and I suppose that the narration of permissibility takes into account that the lapse of the validity of their purity lasts a long time, and this was the reason for the leniency.

This is a consequence (*tafri'*, a logical branching) of the statement ﴿Say: Indeed, the former and the later peoples will surely be gathered﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 49]. It indicates an address from God Most High directed at those who deny resurrection, who say: "When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised?" From this, the discourse moves to praising the Qur'an. Since they denied resurrection, and since affirming resurrection was among the most important things the Qur'an brought, and since its affirmation of resurrection, which they considered impossible, was one of the things that incited them to deny the Qur'an, in addition to their denial of it in other matters that it brought, namely the nullification of their polytheism and their falsehoods, then once the proof had been established against their error in their denial, the truthfulness of what the Qur'an had informed them of became clear, and so its truthfulness was established. For this reason the context became ready for praising its status.

The *fa'* (the conjunctive particle "then") is for the branching of the oath upon what preceded it, namely the proofs for the occurrence of resurrection. The statement ﴿Say: Indeed, the former and the later peoples will surely be gathered﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 49] is an announcement of the Day of Resurrection and a warning to them of it, while they had denied it. Because it seemed impossible in their limited view, they denied the Qur'an and denied the one who brought it. So He branched, upon establishing the occurrence of resurrection and the warning of it, the establishment that the Qur'an is free of defects, that it is a revelation from God, and that the one who brought it is a messenger conveying from God.

The branching of the oath is a branching in meaning with respect to the object sworn upon, and it is also a verbal branching with respect to the act of swearing, if they say to you: "He swore by the positions of the stars."

The branching of an oath upon what precedes it with *fa'* has come in mere mention, in the words of Zuhayr:

*So I swore by the House around which walked men whom Quraysh and Jurhum had built,*

after the verses of erotic prelude (*nasib*) from his mu'allaqah, and there is no connection between the erotic prelude and what branches from it, the oath. He only intended that what follows the *fa'* is the purpose of the poem, and that he preceded it with the erotic prelude to rouse the listener. By this, the difference in composition between the verse and Zuhayr's line becomes evident.

*La uqsimu* (﴿لا أُقْسِمُ﴾): in the sense of *uqsimu*, and *la* is additional for emphasis. Its original function is negation, indicating that the speaker does not venture to swear by what he swears by, out of fear of the evil consequence of lying in an oath.

It also carries the sense that he does not need to swear, because the matter is clearly established. Since this usage became common, it came to mean the emphasis of the statement, and so it equals an oath. This is shown by His words following it: ﴿And indeed it is an oath, if you knew, a great one﴾. This second aspect is the more appropriate one, given what has occurred similarly in the Qur'an.

On both readings, it is an embedding (*idmaj*) to praise the status of what, if He were swearing, He would swear by. On the second reading, His words ﴿and indeed it is an oath﴾ mean: "and indeed what is mentioned is a great thing by which swearers swear." The application of the word *qasam* (oath) to it is from the use of a verbal noun to mean the object, like *al-khalq* (creation) meaning the created thing.

From Sa'id ibn Jubayr and some exegetes: they made *la* a separate particle, not part of the verb *uqsimu*, standing as a response to an implied statement that is indicated by what follows it, namely ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾, in reply to their claims about the Qur'an: that it is poetry, or magic, or the fables of the ancients, or the speech of a soothsayer. They made His words *uqsimu* a resumption (*isti'naf*). According to this reading, the meaning of the speech together with the *fa'* of branching upon the proofs for the possibility of resurrection that have become manifest is: "What you claim about the Qur'an is not as you assert; rather it is a noble Qur'an, etc."

*Mawaqi' al-nujum* (﴿مَواقِعِ النُّجُومِ﴾) is the plural of *mawqi'*, which may be the place of falling, that is, the locations where they fall, whether fixed stars or wandering stars. *Al-wuqu'* is used for falling, that is, setting, so the positions of the stars are the places of their setting. This agrees with His words Most High ﴿By the star when it sets﴾ [al-Najm: 1]. Swearing by this is among what is included in His words Most High ﴿So I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 40]. The positions of the stars, in this sense, are made an object of oath because those places, at the time the stars set at them, remind one of the wonderful order established for the movement of the heavenly bodies, which does not fail or deviate every night, and they remind one of the greatness of the heavenly bodies and their alternation one after another. That is a great matter, which makes swearing by it appropriate, and the swearing by it returns to swearing by its Originator.

*Al-wuqu'* is also used for alighting in a place. It is said: "The camels *waqa'at*," when they knelt, and "the sheep *waqa'at*" in their pens. From this comes the name *al-waqi'ah* for an event, as was mentioned earlier. So *al-mawaqi'* are the places of their alighting and the lines of their courses. This is close to His words ﴿By the sky of the constellations﴾ [al-Buruj: 1].

*Al-mawaqi'* are the orbits of the stars, precisely regulated in their motion across the horizon of the sky. Likewise their constellations and their stations.

Mentioning the positions of the stars in both senses is a praise of them and an exaltation of their matter, because their conditions indicate the subtleties of God's wisdom in the arrangement of their motion and the wonders of His power in subjecting them.

It is also possible that *mawaqi'* is the plural of *mawqi'*, which is the mimi verbal noun (a noun of place or time formed from the root) of *al-wuqu'*.

Some exegetes interpreted *al-nujum* as the plural of *najm*, which means a portion of wealth or other things, as one says: "the installments (*nujum*) of blood-money and fines." They interpreted *al-nujum*, that is, groups of verses, which descend from the Qur'an. This is from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah. Thus it returns to an oath by the Qur'an in its literal sense, in the manner mentioned earlier in His words Most High ﴿By the Clear Book﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 2] ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 3].

The sentence ﴿And indeed it is an oath, if you knew, a great one﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraD*) between the oath and its answer.

The pronoun in ﴿innahu﴾ refers either to the oath mentioned in ﴿I do not swear by the positions of the stars﴾, or it refers to the positions of the stars, taking them as "what is mentioned," so that it is an oath in the sense of "the thing sworn by," as you have understood a moment ago.

It is also possible that it refers to the thing sworn to, namely what is contained in the answer of the oath, His words ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾.

The clause ﴿if you knew﴾ is a parenthetical insertion between the described and its description, and it is a parenthesis within a parenthesis.

The knowledge that the counterfactual *law* (conditional of impossibility) requires to be absent from them, if you make the pronoun in ﴿innahu﴾ refer to the oath, is the detailed knowledge of the conditions of the positions of the stars. For the polytheists are not free of a general, varying knowledge that in those positions there is a lesson for observers. Or that general knowledge is treated as if it were nonexistent, because by their disbelief they did not act in accordance with what that knowledge requires of the Oneness of God. So if they knew what the conditions of the positions of the stars contain of the connections to God's attributes, they would know that they are sacred positions by which none swears except one who is truthful in his oath. But they are far removed from this knowledge, for the majesty of the sworn object is among what restrains the swearer from lying in his oath. The evidence that they lacked knowledge of its greatness is that they did not perceive the indication of that for the Oneness of God in divinity, so they ascribed to Him partners who created nothing of that, nor anything approaching it. This is a sign that they did not perceive the proofs contained within that, until the creator of what is in those positions and the non-creator became equal to them.

As for if you make the pronoun in ﴿And indeed it is an oath﴾ refer to the object sworn to, then the meaning is: "If you knew that, you would not need an oath."

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) recited *bi-mawaqi'* in the plural form, with a fatha on the *waw* and an *alif* after it. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf recited *bi-mawqi'* with a sukun on the *waw* and without an *alif* after it, in the singular form, as a mimi verbal noun, that is, "by their setting," or it is a noun for the direction of their setting, like His words "Lord of the East and the West."

The object of *ta'lamun* (you know) is omitted, indicated by the context: "if you knew His greatness," that is, the proofs of His greatness. You may also treat the verb *ta'lamun* as if it were intransitive, that is: "if you had knowledge, but you do not have the attribute of knowledge."

The pronoun in ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾ refers to something not mentioned in the speech, because it is known and present to them.

*Al-Qur'an* is the read speech, that is, the recited, repeated speech. That is, it is speech by which one is admonished, a locus of reflection and recitation. This has been mentioned earlier at His words Most High ﴿And you are not engaged in any matter, nor do you recite from it any Qur'an﴾ [Yunus: 61] in Surah Yunus.

*Al-karim* means precious and elevated within its kind, as was mentioned earlier at His words Most High ﴿Indeed, there has been delivered to me a noble letter﴾ [al-Naml: 29] in Surah al-Naml.

This is a preference of the Qur'an over the individual members of its genre of divine books, such as the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Book of Luqman. Its superiority over them is that it surpassed them in fully covering the aims of religion, the conditions of livelihood and the hereafter, and establishing beliefs through proofs from creation, and in thoroughly refuting falsehood with a refutation that no earlier book contained the like of, especially in matters of belief; and in the clarity of its meanings, in the abundance of its indication with the scarcity of its words, in its eloquence, in the beauty of its verses and the beauty of their placement for the ear. All of this is among the effects of what God intended by the universality of guidance through it, and its suitability for every nation and every age. So this is a description of the Qur'an as elevated above all books, a truth which the opponent cannot find a way to challenge.

After the Qur'an was described as *karim* (noble), it was described a second time as ﴿in a Book well-guarded﴾. This is certainly a description of honor, so neither the word *kitab* (book) nor the description *maknun* (well-guarded) is intended literally, since taking them literally would not confer honor. Therefore the particle *fi* (in) is for figurative location.

The "well-guarded Book" is a metaphor for the agreement of the words and meanings of the Qur'an with what is in God's knowledge, His will, and His command to the angel to convey it to the Messenger (ﷺ). These are matters hidden from us. Therefore He described the Book as *maknun*, derived from *iktinan*, which means concealment, that is, hidden from the gaze of people. So it is a matter unseen, whose reality none knows except God.

The essential meaning of this verse is: the Qur'an that reached them and that they heard from the Prophet (ﷺ) is in accordance with what God intended to inform people of, and what His power has determined the creation of its inimitable composition, so that it may complete the description that it is the speech of God Most High and that no human made it.
