They considered this a ruling for what is written with the Qur'an with the intention that it be a mushaf, or part of a mushaf, or a tablet of the Qur'an; and they did not consider it applicable to verses of the Qur'an written by way of quotation, citation, or argument. Among this is what is written on dinars and dirhams, and on rings.

The meaning of purity according to those who hold it obligatory is the minor purification, that is, wudu'. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Sha'bi said: it is permissible to touch the Qur'an with the major purification even if the minor one is not present.

Among what is connected to this issue is the question of a non-purified person reciting the Qur'an. This is not apparently covered by the verse, but since the prohibition against touching the mushaf for one not purified may be because touching is a contact with the written Qur'an, the prohibition on pronouncing the words of the Qur'an may be established by the understanding of agreement (mafhum al-muwafaqa), equal or stronger, since uttering is a contact like the contact of holding the written text or stronger. I suppose this is the source of their disagreement over reciting the Qur'an for one who is not purified. The consensus of the scholars that one who is not in wudu' may recite the Qur'an, despite their disagreement over touching the mushaf for one not in wudu', indicates that touching the mushaf in their view is a stronger contact than pronouncing the verses of the Qur'an.

Malik, Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i said: it is not permissible for one in janabah to recite the Qur'an, but it is permissible for one not in wudu'. I say: among the Muslims in the era of the Companions the practice spread that one who is junub does not recite the Qur'an, and no fatwa to that effect was reported from them. Ahmad and Dawud said: reciting the Qur'an is permissible for one in janabah. Malik allowed the recitation of a small portion of it, such as a verse or two, and none of the scholars required wudu' of the one reciting the Qur'an.

There is disagreement concerning its recitation by a menstruating or post-natal woman. On this, Malik has two narrations, and I suppose that the narration of permissibility takes into account that the lapse of the validity of their purity lasts a long time, and this was the reason for the leniency.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 56, verse 81:

﴿Then is it with this discourse that you are being complacent (mudhinun)?﴾

The fa' (فاء) is a consequential particle (tafri') upon what the preceding speech was brought for, namely its purpose of extolling the Qur'an's status, which is the sense conveyed by "bi-hadhha" (with this), or upon the establishment of resurrection and recompense, which encompasses most of the surah, and extolling the Qur'an was among its consequences.

The exegetes, with the exception of al-Fakhr (al-Razi), agreed that the demonstrative noun (ism al-isharah) and its clarification by the phrase ﴿Then is it with this discourse﴾ refer to the Qur'an, owing to the transition from extolling its status to rebuking those who deny it. Thus the consequence (tafri') is upon His saying ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 77], and so on.

Page 338
By "al-hadith" (the discourse) is meant God's report about the Qur'an, and the use of "hadith" to mean the Qur'an occurs in the Qur'an itself, such as His saying in Surah al-Qalam: ﴿So leave Me with those who deny this discourse﴾ [al-Qalam: 44], and His saying in Surah al-Najm: ﴿Is it at this discourse that you marvel?﴾ [al-Najm: 59].
The shift from the pronoun to the demonstrative in ﴿Then is it with this discourse﴾, rather than saying "Then is it with it that you are complacent," takes the speech out of the expected form, so that the demonstrative gives an added extolling of the Qur'an.

As for al-Fakhr, he took the demonstrative in ﴿Then is it with this discourse﴾ to refer to what they had said earlier, in His saying ﴿And they used to say: "When we are dead and have become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected? And our forefathers too?"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 47–48], and God answered them with His saying ﴿Say: Indeed, the former and the latter﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 49], and so on. He explained that all of that is a report from God, by His saying ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 77]. Then he returned to their speech and said: "Then is it with this discourse that you talk about that you are being complacent toward your companions?" End of quote. This is in the sense of His saying: ﴿And he said: "You have taken only idols instead of God as a means of affection among yourselves in the worldly life"﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 25].

This is indeed a good statement, but if "al-hadith" were taken to mean everything that preceded from the beginning of the surah, both principal and consequential, that is, this speech that has struck your ears, it would be better. The application of "al-hadith" to the report of resurrection is clearer, because "hadith" refers to a report that has become a topic of talk among the people.

The definiteness of "al-hadith" in both explanations is the definiteness of previous reference (ta'rif al-'ahd).

Al-mudhin: the one who shows the opposite of what he conceals. It is said: adhan and dahana. It has also been explained as laxity and failure to act with resolve, and it has been explained as denial.

The interrogative, on all the explanations, is used for rebuke, meaning: your speech should be nothing but complacency, just as one says to someone who utters falsehood: "Are you mocking?" That is, the proof of the Qur'an's truthfulness has been so firmly established that no denier denies it except that he himself does not believe he is denying it, since knowledge of what proof has established cannot be removed from oneself by its possessor. So your persistence in denial after that is nothing but complacency toward your people, fearing that if you affirm this discourse your leadership will vanish. This is in the sense of His saying ﴿For they do not deny you, but the wrongdoers deny the signs of God﴾ [al-An'am: 33].

Page 339
And according to the explanation of mudhinun as softening (al-ilanah), the meaning is: do not be lax regarding this discourse; ponder it and take up its following immediately.

If mudhinun is explained as "you lie," the meaning is clear.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase is for emphasis.

The nominal construction in ﴿you are mudhinun﴾ is used because the established matter is a settled, continuous complacency.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 56, verse 82:

﴿And you make your provision that you deny⁠﴾

If we proceed according to what the commentators have explained, this sentence is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the sentence ﴿Is it this discourse that you are scornful of?﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 81]. It is the conjoining of one sentence to another, so it falls within the scope of the interrogation (istifham) and is independent in its meaning.

The meaning is: "Do you make your provision that you deny?" This is a consequence of what was included in the argument from the formation of human offspring, the creation of grain, the water in the clouds, and the fire from the firesticks. For in all of that there is the presence of the constituents of sustenance, which is provision (rizq), and offspring is also a provision; one says "So-and-so was provided (ruziqa) a son," because provision applies to beneficial giving. Labid said:

*Ruziqat marabiʿa al-nujumi wa ṣābahā / wadquhu al-rawaʿidi jawduhā fa-rihāmuhā*

That is, it was given. And God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿I do not want provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me⁠﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 57], so He conjoined feeding to provision, and conjunction requires difference.

The interrogative understood after the conjunctive particle is reproachful (inkari). Since denial cannot be made into provision, the implication of the context requires an omitted element, so the commentators estimated it: "the thanks for your provision," or something similar, meaning: "You make the thanks of God for His provision to you into denying His power to restore life," because they turned away from thanking God for what He had bestowed upon them, so they belittled His power to restore bodies, and they attributed the crops to themselves, and they claimed that the rain is sent down by the stars called the anwaʾ. Therefore Ibn ʿAbbas said: "It was revealed concerning their saying: 'We have been given rain by the anwaʾ of such-and-such.'" That is, because they say it out of belief in the effect of the anwaʾ in creating rain, so the meaning of Ibn ʿAbbas's words "We have been given rain by the nawʾ of such-and-such" is that it is intended within the meaning of the verse.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "The commentators agreed that the verse is a rebuke to those who say, concerning the rain that God sends down as provision: 'This is by the nawʾ of such-and-such.'" End.

This points to what is narrated in the Muwatta' from Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) led us in the dawn prayer at al-Hudaybiyah following a rain. When the Prophet (ﷺ) finished, he turned to the people and said: 'Do you know what your Lord said?' They said: 'God and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'He said: Among My servants, there has become one who believes in Me and one who disbelieves. As for the one who said: We have been given rain by the grace of God and His mercy, he is one who believes in Me and disbelieves in the star. As for the one who said: We have been given rain by the nawʾ of such-and-such and the nawʾ of such-and-such, he is one who disbelieves in Me and believes in the star.'" There is no addition in it, and then this verse was revealed. Had its revelation been on that day, the Companion present on that day would have said so.

In Sahih Muslim, from Ibn ʿAbbas, it occurs that he said: "The people were given rain during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Among the people there has become one thankful and among them one disbelieving.' They said: 'This is the mercy of God.' And some of them said: 'The nawʾ of such-and-such and the nawʾ of such-and-such has spoken truly.' He said: Then it was revealed: ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars⁠﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 75] until He reached ﴿And you make your provision that you deny⁠﴾."

So he added, beyond what is in the hadith of Zayd ibn Khalid, his statement "then it was revealed, 'So I swear...' etc."

The narrator's addition is disputed as to whether it is accepted unconditionally, or on condition that the gathering is not unified, or on condition that the one narrating it is not of the sort who would ordinarily fail to notice such an addition. These are positions of the imams of hadith and the principles of jurisprudence. Ibn ʿAbbas was not of the age of those who narrate at the time this surah was revealed in Makkah, so his saying "then it was revealed" is perhaps his own interpretation, for he meant that the people were given rain in Makkah in the early days of Islam, and the believers said a thing and the polytheists said a thing, so the verse ﴿And you make your provision that you deny⁠﴾ was revealed as a rebuke to the polytheists among them for a belief of those beliefs which God denounced in them. And what occurred at al-Hudaybiyah was another rain, because the surah was revealed before the Hijrah. It is not reported that this verse was appended to the surah after the surah's revelation.

Perhaps the narrator from him did not express his words well, so that by his saying "then it was revealed, 'So I swear by the positions of the stars'" he gave the impression that Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited, 'So I swear by the positions of the stars'," or a phrase similar to that. Such an illusion has been repeated in reports on the occasions of revelation. This is reinforced by the form ﴿you deny⁠﴾, because their saying "We have been given rain by the nawʾ of such-and-such" contains no denial of anything. That is why Ibn ʿAtiyyah needed to interpret it by saying: "For God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We sent down from the sky blessed water, and We caused to grow thereby gardens and the grain of harvest⁠﴾ [Qaf: 9] ﴿and tall palm trees with spathes stacked⁠﴾ [Qaf: 10] ﴿as provision for the servants⁠﴾ [Qaf: 11]. So this is the meaning of ﴿that you deny⁠﴾, that is, you deny this report."

What al-Razi pursued is another direction: he made the meaning of ﴿And you make your provision that you deny⁠﴾ a completion of the scorn (idhhan) in God's words ﴿Is it this discourse that you are scornful of?⁠﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 81]. He said: that is, you fear that if you believe in the Qur'an and prevent your weak ones from disbelief, what you gain through them will be lost to you from your earnings, so you make your provision that you deny the Messenger, that is, the conjunction is upon "scornful" (mudhinun) as the conjunction of a verb upon a noun resembling it, and it is of the kind of conjoining of single words, meaning: "You are scornful and making your provision that you deny." So this denial is part of the scorn: they know the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ), but they display his denial to preserve their interests. It is like God's words ﴿For they do not deny you, but the wrongdoers deny the signs of God⁠﴾ [al-An'am: 33]. On this reading, His words ﴿that you deny⁠﴾ are parsed as in the genitive with an omitted preposition bi- (with), and the estimate is: "And you make your provision with that you deny," that is, you make in exchange for it that you deny the Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 56, verse 83–87:

[Page 342]
﴿Why then, when it [the soul] reaches the throat, and you are at that time looking on — and We are nearer to him than you, but you do not see — why then, if you are not to be recompensed, do you not return it, if you are truthful?﴾

The implication of the particle of consequence (fa') is that the speech that follows it arises from what precedes it, according to its order. Since the preceding speech was the establishing of proofs that God is able to restore life to people after death, and this was followed by the statement that those proofs confirm what the Qur'an affirms regarding the resurrection, and it criticized them for having the proof made clear to them while they remained arrogant about it and displayed denial, although they were certain of it inwardly, and all of this returns to reasoning from the strength of God's power to bring into existence beings that human perceptions cannot reach, the discourse moved on to proving the resurrection by an argument they have no escape from acknowledging the force of.

So the consequence is upon the clause ﴿And you have certainly known the first creation, so why do you not remember?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 62]. It means that their inability to return the soul when it departs the body alerts them that this departure is decreed within the order of creation and that it is for a wisdom.

The meaning of the speech is therefore: God has informed you that He recompenses people for their deeds, and for this reason He revives them after their death in order to carry out the recompense upon them. He has indicated this to you by the forcible extraction of their souls from them. If what you claim were true, that you will not be recompensed after death, the souls would remain in their bodies, since there would be no benefit in extracting them after depositing them within, were it not for the wisdom of transferring them to a second life, so that their recompense for their deeds in the first life may be carried out.

This is like the argument for God's exclusive divinity, that in the existence of beings there are created signs that they are made by God, Exalted is He. This is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly, and their shadows at morning and evening﴾ [al-Ra'd: 15]. The basis of this meaning returns to the fact that this is an argument by the requirement of divine wisdom in the state of the creation of man, for the placing of souls in bodies is an action of God's action, and He is the All-Wise. Therefore He did not extract the souls from the bodies after depositing them there for a period, except because extracting them is what wisdom requires, and that is confined to their being subjected to reckoning for what they earned during the period of the worldly life.

[Page 343]
This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Did you suppose that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115]. God, Exalted is He, made the worldly life and the terms (ājal) periods for action, and made the Hereafter the abode of recompense for deeds. For this reason He established the order of this world upon the principle of the ending of the terms of people's lives.

As for the death of those who are near the age of responsibility and below it, and the death of animals, that is an incidental matter following from the operation of formation upon living bodies according to the uniform order of formation; likewise what befalls them of destructive accidents, which is required by the conflict of the requirements of order and the formation of temperaments, of health and sickness, of peace and aggression.

There remains the difficulty of making ﴿turjiʻūnahā﴾ part of the response to the conditional (in), since the inability of them to prevent the souls from leaving does not necessarily entail that their departure is for the carrying out of reckoning.

What removes this difficulty is the necessity of interpreting ﴿turjiʻūnahā﴾ as meaning "you attempt to return it." That is: your not attempting to return it since the earliest ages is evidence of your acceptance of the impossibility of returning it, and this is only because it must depart from the life of deeds to the life of recompense.

The original construction of this sentence is: "If you are truthful in claiming that you are not to be recompensed, then why do you not attempt, at every dying person, when the soul reaches the throat, to return it to its places in the parts of his body? What turned you away from attempting that except the necessary knowledge that the soul is going, without doubt." When you understand this, the arrangement of the verse becomes clear, which was composed in a wondrous manner of concision, and within its proof was incorporated what completes the inimitability.

The ﴿lawlā﴾ is a particle of exhortation used in the sense of incapacitation, because the one being exhorted, if he does not do what he is urged to do, has shown his incapacity. The verb upon which he is urged is ﴿turjiʻūnahā﴾, that is, "you attempt its return."

﴿Idhā balaghat﴾ is an adverbial phrase governed by ﴿turjiʻūnahā﴾ and placed before it for its emphasis and to create suspense toward the verb of urging.

The hidden pronoun in ﴿balaghat﴾ refers to a concept understood from the context, since it is evident that what reaches the throat is the soul; it has been omitted for brevity, like His saying: ﴿until it [the sun] was hidden by the veil﴾ [Sad: 32], that is, the sun.

The ﴿al-﴾ in ﴿al-ḥulqūm﴾ is for generic reference (al-ʻahd al-jinsī).

The clause ﴿and you are at that time looking on﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿balaghat﴾, and the object of ﴿tanẓurūn﴾ is omitted; its estimate is: "you look upon its companion," that is, the companion of the soul, by the indication of His following saying ﴿and We are nearer to him﴾. The benefit of this circumstance is to establish that God diverted them from attempting to return it, despite their great grief at the death of the dear ones.

The clause ﴿and We are nearer to him than you﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the omitted object of ﴿tanẓurūn﴾, or it is a parenthetical clause and the waw is parenthetical.

In either case, it is a precaution to clarify that there is a presence nearer than their presence at the dying person, which is the presence of disposing of his inward states.

The nearness of God is nearness of knowledge and power, in the manner of His saying "and your Lord came," or the nearness of His angels sent to execute His command concerning life and death, in the manner of His saying ﴿And We had certainly brought them a Book﴾ [al-A'raf: 52], that is, Gabriel brought them a book. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿until, when Our messengers come to them to take them in death﴾ [al-A'raf: 37].

The clause ﴿but you do not see﴾ is parenthetical between the clause ﴿and We are nearer to him than you﴾ and the clause ﴿why then, if you are not to be recompensed﴾. The second ﴿fa-lawlā﴾ is a verbal emphasis of its earlier counterpart, repeated so that the clause ﴿turjiʻūnahā﴾ may be built upon it, because of the length of the separation.

The clause ﴿in kuntum ghayra madīnīn﴾ is parenthetical, or a circumstantial clause from the waw in ﴿turjiʻūnahā﴾.

The response to the conditional (in) is omitted, indicated by the verb ﴿turjiʻūnahā﴾. Ibn ʻAṭiyyah said: "His saying ﴿turjiʻūnahā﴾ takes the place of the responses and explanations that the exhortations require, and ﴿idhā﴾ in His saying ﴿fa-lawlā idhā balaghat﴾ and the repeated ﴿in﴾, and the bearing of some speech upon other speech, is concision or abbreviated expressions." End of quotation.

The clause ﴿in kuntum ṣādiqīn﴾ is an explanation of the clause ﴿in kuntum ghayra madīnīn﴾. On the first interpretation of the meaning of madīnīn, the reason for repeating this condition, although it is derived from His saying ﴿in kuntum ghayra madīnīn﴾, is to allude to the supposition of the condition in ﴿in kuntum ghayra madīnīn﴾ with respect to what is actually the case, while the condition in ﴿in kuntum ṣādiqīn﴾ is a supposition and assumption with no actual occurrence, namely the denial of resurrection. On the second interpretation, the saying ﴿in kuntum ṣādiqīn﴾ returns to what the exhortation implied, and the position of the consequence particle is in the sense that the seizing of souls is for delaying them until the Day of Recompense; that is, "if you are truthful in denying resurrection and recompense."

The feminine pronoun in ﴿turjiʻūnahā﴾ refers to the soul, indicated by the feminine ending in ﴿balaghat al-ḥulqūm﴾.

The sense of the contrastive particle in ﴿but you do not see﴾ returns to His saying ﴿and We are nearer to him than you﴾, to remove the misapprehension of a speaker who asks: how can He be nearer to the dying person than the visitors surrounding him, who see one another? The answer is that they are veiled from seeing God's command.

The clause ﴿but you do not see﴾ is parenthetical, and the waw is parenthetical. The object of ﴿tubṣirūn﴾ is omitted, indicated by His saying ﴿and We are nearer to him﴾.

The meaning of madīnīn is "those recompensed for their deeds." On this meaning, the majority of the earlier exegetes took it: Ibn ʻAbbas, Mujahid, Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Hasan, and Qatadah; and the majority of later exegetes take it generally so. al-Farra' and al-Zamakhshari interpreted madīnīn as "slaves of God," from their saying: "the sultan subjugated (dāna) the subjects," when he governed them, meaning "not those who are owned (marbūbīn)," and this is far from the context.

Know that His saying ﴿in kuntum ghayra madīnīn﴾ is a supposition and assumption, and the ﴿in﴾ in it has the status of ﴿law﴾, meaning: "if you were not to be recompensed," that is, not to be repaid for deeds.

The verb of ﴿in kuntum ghayra madīnīn﴾ is attributed to the addressees by the pronoun of address, rather than saying "if people were not recompensed," because the addressees are those for whose denial of resurrection this speech was brought. The meaning is: "If you yourselves and people were not to be recompensed, the souls would not have been extracted from the bodies, since no benefit would result from separating those two companions, were it not for a lofty purpose, namely placing each soul in what befits it from the world of eternity as recompense for deeds. For this reason the word ﴿ghayra madīnīn﴾ was preferred over saying 'ghayr mab'ūthīn' or 'ghayr mu'ādīn'; although denying indebtedness does not necessarily entail denying resurrection, since it is possible that there is a resurrection without recompense, that is not claimed, for it would be vain."

So His saying ﴿in kuntum ghayra madīnīn﴾ is an allusion that the purpose of setting forth this proof is to nullify their denial of resurrection, which is for the wisdom of recompense.

Among the implications of this speech is that it indicates an allusion to the wisdom of death with respect to humans, since it serves to release souls from this transient life filled with falsehood to the true eternal life in which the states of souls proceed in accordance with their conduct in the worldly life, as His saying, Exalted is He, indicated: ﴿Did you suppose that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115]. It implies that were it not that you are to be recompensed, We would not have extracted the souls from their bodies after placing them in them, and We would have left them, because the human soul is not like the animal soul. Thus the verse contains two proofs: one by the strict composition itself, and the other by its implications, to which His saying ﴿in kuntum ghayra madīnīn﴾ alludes. The first purpose is the one appended by His saying ﴿in kuntum ṣādiqīn﴾.

This is the interpretation of the verse which encompasses the fullest of its meanings in indication, implication, and consequences. In the Kashshaf, the verse's direction was described as aiming at nullifying what the Dahriyyah believe, namely those who say "we die and live, and nothing destroys us but time," because they denied being servants of God. The meaning of madīnīn was taken as "owned by God," and al-Farra' interpreted it accordingly. Ibn ʻAṭiyyah said: it is the most correct thing said about the meaning of the word here, and whoever expresses it as "recompensed" or "held to account" is uneasy here. And I say: in his speech there is clear scrutiny.

al-Zamakhshari made the consequence (tafrī') of the verse upon what was related of their earlier speech, based on the premise that what was related of their statements about the constellations and denial leads to the doctrine of negation of the Creator (ta'til), so he argued against them with a proof that entails the existence of the Creator. All of this is far from the direction of the verse, because the Dahriyyah are not adopted by all of the Arabs; rather, it is the creed of a few small groups among them, and it is far from the customary usage of its terms and from the arrangement of its argumentation.

As for the death of those who are near the age of responsibility and below it, and the death of animals, that is an incidental matter following from the operation of formation upon living bodies according to the uniform order of formation; likewise what befalls them of destructive accidents, which is required by the conflict of the requirements of order and the formation of temperaments, of health and sickness, of peace and aggression.

There remains the difficulty of making ﴿turjiʻūnahā﴾ part of the response to the conditional (in), since the inability of them to prevent the souls from leaving does not necessarily entail that their departure is for the carrying out of reckoning.

What removes this difficulty is the necessity of interpreting ﴿turjiʻūnahā﴾ as meaning "you attempt to return it." That is: your not attempting to return it since the earliest ages is evidence of your acceptance of the impossibility of returning it, and this is only because it must depart from the life of deeds to the life of recompense.

The original construction of this sentence is: "If you are truthful in claiming that you are not to be recompensed, then why do you not attempt, at every dying person, when the soul reaches the throat, to return it to its places in the parts of his body? What turned you away from attempting that except the necessary knowledge that the soul is going, without doubt." When you understand this, the arrangement of the verse becomes clear, which was composed in a wondrous manner of concision, and within its proof was incorporated what completes the inimitability.

The ﴿lawlā﴾ is a particle of exhortation used in the sense of incapacitation, because the one being exhorted, if he does not do what he is urged to do, has shown his incapacity. The verb upon which he is urged is ﴿turjiʻūnahā﴾, that is, "you attempt its return."

﴿Idhā balaghat﴾ is an adverbial phrase governed by ﴿turjiʻūnahā﴾ and placed before it for its emphasis and to create suspense toward the verb of urging.

The hidden pronoun in ﴿balaghat﴾ refers to a concept understood from the context, since it is evident that what reaches the throat is the soul; it has been omitted for brevity, like His saying: ﴿until it [the sun] was hidden by the veil﴾ [Sad: 32], that is, the sun.

The ﴿al-﴾ in ﴿al-ḥulqūm﴾ is for generic reference (al-ʻahd al-jinsī).

The clause ﴿and you are at that time looking on﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿balaghat﴾, and the object of ﴿tanẓurūn﴾ is omitted; its estimate is: "you look upon its companion," that is, the companion of the soul, by the indication of His following saying ﴿and We are nearer to him﴾. The benefit of this circumstance is to establish that God diverted them from attempting to return it, despite their great grief at the death of the dear ones.

The clause ﴿and We are nearer to him than you﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the omitted object of ﴿tanẓurūn﴾, or it is a parenthetical clause and the waw is parenthetical.

In either case, it is a precaution to clarify that there is a presence nearer than their presence at the dying person, which is the presence of disposing of his inward states.

The nearness of God is nearness of knowledge and power, in the manner of His saying "and your Lord came," or the nearness of His angels sent to execute His command concerning life and death, in the manner of His saying ﴿And We had certainly brought them a Book﴾ [al-A'raf: 52], that is, Gabriel brought them a book. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿until, when Our messengers come to them to take them in death﴾ [al-A'raf: 37].

The clause ﴿but you do not see﴾ is parenthetical between the clause ﴿and We are nearer to him than you﴾ and the clause ﴿why then, if you are not to be recompensed﴾. The second ﴿fa-lawlā﴾ is a verbal emphasis of its earlier counterpart, repeated so that the clause ﴿turjiʻūnahā﴾ may be built upon it, because of the length of the separation.

The clause ﴿in kuntum ghayra madīnīn﴾ is parenthetical, or a circumstantial clause from the waw in ﴿turjiʻūnahā﴾.

The response to the conditional (in) is omitted, indicated by the verb ﴿turjiʻūnahā﴾. Ibn ʻAṭiyyah said: "His saying ﴿turjiʻūnahā﴾ takes the place of the responses and explanations that the exhortations require, and ﴿idhā﴾ in His saying ﴿fa-lawlā idhā balaghat﴾ and the repeated ﴿in﴾, and the bearing of some speech upon other speech, is concision or abbreviated expressions." End of quotation.

The clause ﴿in kuntum ṣādiqīn﴾ is an explanation of the clause ﴿in kuntum ghayra madīnīn﴾. On the first interpretation of the meaning of madīnīn, the reason for repeating this condition, although it is derived from His saying ﴿in kuntum ghayra madīnīn﴾, is to allude to the supposition of the condition in ﴿in kuntum ghayra madīnīn﴾ with respect to what is actually the case, while the condition in ﴿in kuntum ṣādiqīn﴾ is a supposition and assumption with no actual occurrence, namely the denial of resurrection. On the second interpretation, the saying ﴿in kuntum ṣādiqīn﴾ returns to what the exhortation implied, and the position of the consequence particle is in the sense that the seizing of souls is for delaying them until the Day of Recompense; that is, "if you are truthful in denying resurrection and recompense."

The feminine pronoun in ﴿turjiʻūnahā﴾ refers to the soul, indicated by the feminine ending in ﴿balaghat al-ḥulqūm﴾.

The sense of the contrastive particle in ﴿but you do not see﴾ returns to His saying ﴿and We are nearer to him than you﴾, to remove the misapprehension of a speaker who asks: how can He be nearer to the dying person than the visitors surrounding him, who see one another? The answer is that they are veiled from seeing God's command.

The meaning of madīnīn is "those recompensed for their deeds." On this meaning, the majority of the earlier exegetes took it: Ibn ʻAbbas, Mujahid, Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Hasan, and Qatadah; and the majority of later exegetes take it generally so. al-Farra' and al-Zamakhshari interpreted madīnīn as "slaves of God," from their saying: "the sultan subjugated (dāna) the subjects," when he governed them, meaning "not those who are owned (marbūbīn)," and this is far from the context.

Know that His saying ﴿in kuntum ghayra madīnīn﴾ is a supposition and assumption, and the ﴿in﴾ in it has the status of ﴿law﴾, meaning: "if you were not to be recompensed," that is, not to be repaid for deeds.

The meaning is: "If you yourselves and people were not to be recompensed, the souls would not have been extracted from the bodies, since no benefit would result from separating those two companions, were it not for a lofty purpose, namely placing each soul in what befits it from the world of eternity as recompense for deeds. The first purpose is the one appended by His saying ﴿in kuntum ṣādiqīn﴾.

This is the interpretation of the verse which encompasses the fullest of its meanings in indication, implication, and consequences. In the Kashshaf, the verse's direction was described as aiming at nullifying what the Dahriyyah believe, namely those who say "we die and live, and nothing destroys us but time," because they denied being servants of God. The meaning of madīnīn was taken as "owned by God," and al-Farra' interpreted it accordingly. And I say: in his speech there is clear scrutiny.

All of this is far from the direction of the verse, because the Dahriyyah are not adopted by all of the Arabs; rather, it is the creed of a few small groups among them, and it is far from the customary usage of its terms and from the arrangement of its argumentation.

The implication of the particle of consequence (fa') is that the speech that follows it arises from what precedes it, according to its order. Since the preceding speech was the establishing of proofs that God is able to restore life to people after death, and this was followed by the statement that those proofs confirm what the Qur'an affirms regarding the resurrection, and it criticized them for having the proof made clear to them while they remained arrogant about it and displayed denial, although they were certain of it inwardly, and all of this returns to reasoning from the strength of God's power to bring into existence beings that human perceptions cannot reach, the discourse moved on to proving the resurrection by an argument they have no escape from acknowledging the force of.

So the consequence is upon the clause ﴿And you have certainly known the first creation, so why do you not remember?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 62]. It means that their inability to return the soul when it departs the body alerts them that this departure is decreed within the order of creation and that it is for a wisdom.

The meaning of the speech is therefore: God has informed you that He recompenses people for their deeds, and for this reason He revives them after their death in order to carry out the recompense upon them. He has indicated this to you by the forcible extraction of their souls from them. End of quotation.

Know that His saying ﴿in kuntum ghayra madīnīn﴾ is a supposition and assumption, and the ﴿in﴾ in it has the status of ﴿law﴾, meaning: "if you were not to be recompensed," that is, not to be repaid for deeds.

The verb of ﴿in kuntum ghayra madīnīn﴾ is attributed to the addressees by the pronoun of address, rather than saying "if people were not recompensed," because the addressees are those for whose denial of resurrection this speech was brought. For this reason the word ﴿ghayra madīnīn﴾ was preferred over saying 'ghayr mab'ūthīn' or 'ghayr mu'ādīn'; although denying indebtedness does not necessarily entail denying resurrection, since it is possible that there is a resurrection without recompense, that is not claimed, for it would be vain."

So His saying ﴿in kuntum ghayra madīnīn﴾ is an allusion that the purpose of setting forth this proof is to nullify their denial of resurrection, which is for the wisdom of recompense.

Among the implications of this speech is that it indicates an allusion to the wisdom of death with respect to humans, since it serves to release souls from this transient life filled with falsehood to the true eternal life in which the states of souls proceed in accordance with their conduct in the worldly life, as His saying, Exalted is He, indicated: ﴿Did you suppose that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115]. It implies that were it not that you are to be recompensed, We would not have extracted the souls from their bodies after placing them in them, and We would have left them, because the human soul is not like the animal soul. Thus the verse contains two proofs: one by the strict composition itself, and the other by its implications, to which His saying ﴿in kuntum ghayra madīnīn﴾ alludes. The first purpose is the one appended by His saying ﴿in kuntum ṣādiqīn﴾.

This is the interpretation of the verse which encompasses the fullest of its meanings in indication, implication, and consequences. In the Kashshaf, the verse's direction was described as aiming at nullifying what the Dahriyyah believe, namely those who say "we die and live, and nothing destroys us but time," because they denied being servants of God. The meaning of madīnīn was taken as "owned by God," and al-Farra' interpreted it accordingly. Ibn ʻAṭiyyah said: it is the most correct thing said about the meaning of the word here, and whoever expresses it as "recompensed" or "held to account" is uneasy here. And I say: in his speech there is clear scrutiny.

al-Zamakhshari made the consequence (tafrī') of the verse upon what was related of their earlier speech, based on the premise that what was related of their statements about the constellations and denial leads to the doctrine of negation of the Creator (ta'til), so he argued against them with a proof that entails the existence of the Creator. All of this is far from the direction of the verse, because the Dahriyyah are not adopted by all of the Arabs; rather, it is the creed of a few small groups among them, and it is far from the customary usage of its terms and from the arrangement of its argumentation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 56, verse 83–87:

[Page 342]
﴿Why then, when it [the soul] reaches the throat, and you are at that time looking on — and We are nearer to him than you, but you do not see — why then, if you are not to be recompensed, do you not return it, if you are truthful?﴾

The implication of the particle of consequence (fa') is that the speech that follows it arises from what precedes it, according to its order. Since the preceding speech was the establishing of proofs that God is able to restore life to people after death, and this was followed by the statement that those proofs confirm what the Qur'an affirms regarding the resurrection, and it criticized them for having the proof made clear to them while they remained arrogant about it and displayed denial, although they were certain of it inwardly, and all of this returns to reasoning from the strength of God's power to bring into existence beings that human perceptions cannot reach, the discourse moved on to proving the resurrection by an argument they have no escape from acknowledging the force of.

So the consequence is upon the clause ﴿And you have certainly known the first creation, so why do you not remember?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 62]. It means that their inability to return the soul when it departs the body alerts them that this departure is decreed within the order of creation and that it is for a wisdom.

The meaning of the speech is therefore: God has informed you that He recompenses people for their deeds, and for this reason He revives them after their death in order to carry out the recompense upon them. He has indicated this to you by the forcible extraction of their souls from them. If what you claim were true, that you will not be recompensed after death, the souls would remain in their bodies, since there would be no benefit in extracting them after depositing them within, were it not for the wisdom of transferring them to a second life, so that their recompense for their deeds in the first life may be carried out.

This is like the argument for God's exclusive divinity, that in the existence of beings there are created signs that they are made by God, Exalted is He. This is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly, and their shadows at morning and evening﴾ [al-Ra'd: 15]. The basis of this meaning returns to the fact that this is an argument by the requirement of divine wisdom in the state of the creation of man, for the placing of souls in bodies is an action of God's action, and He is the All-Wise. Therefore He did not extract the souls from the bodies after depositing them there for a period, except because extracting them is what wisdom requires, and that is confined to their being subjected to reckoning for what they earned during the period of the worldly life.

This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Did you suppose that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115]. God, Exalted is He, made the worldly life and the terms (ājal) periods for action, and made the Hereafter the abode of recompense for deeds. For this reason He established the order of this world upon the principle of the ending of the terms of people's lives.

As for the death of those who are near the age of responsibility and below it, and the death of animals, that is an incidental matter following from the operation of formation upon living bodies according to the uniform order of formation; likewise what befalls them of destructive accidents, which is required by the conflict of the requirements of order and the formation of temperaments, of health and sickness, of peace and aggression.

That is: your not attempting to return it since the earliest ages is evidence of your acceptance of the impossibility of returning it, and this is only because it must depart from the life of deeds to the life of recompense.

The original construction of this sentence is: "If you are truthful in claiming that you are not to be recompensed, then why do you not attempt, at every dying person, when the soul reaches the throat, to return it to its places in the parts of his body? When you understand this, the arrangement of the verse becomes clear, which was composed in a wondrous manner of concision, and within its proof was incorporated what completes the inimitability.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 56, verses 88–94:

Page 347

﴿But if he is of those brought near (to Allah), then rest and provision and a Garden of delight.﴾ ﴿And if he is of the companions of the right, then peace be upon you from the companions of the right.﴾ ﴿But if he is of the deniers, the astray, then a welcome of boiling water, and burning in Hellfire.﴾ When the discourse had, in its entirety, established that the human being, the possessor of the soul, is destined for recompense, he branched from this a general summary of the states of recompense among the ranks of people, as a summary of what had been detailed earlier with His saying ﴿And you were three kinds﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 7] up to His saying ﴿neither cool nor generous﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 44], so that this would serve as a concluding summary (fadhlaka) for the surah and a return of its end to its beginning.

The pronoun in "in kana" (if he is) refers back to what the pronoun in "ilayhi" refers to in His saying ﴿and We are nearer to him than you﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 85].

Al-muqarrabun (those brought near) are the foremost (al-sabiqun) whose mention preceded in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 10] ﴿those are the ones brought near﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 11]. The companions of the right have already been mentioned. The deniers, the astray, are the companions of the left, whose mention preceded.

For each of these categories a recompense has been mentioned that was not mentioned for it earlier, so that it may be added to what was prepared for it earlier, in accordance with the Qur'anic method of distributing the narrative.

Al-rawh (rest/ease): with a fatha on the ra' in the reading of the majority, meaning rest, i.e., "fa-rawhun lahu," that is, he is in rest and delight. It was mentioned in His saying ﴿and do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾ [Yusuf: 87] in Surah Yusuf. Ruways transmitted from Ya'qub a reading with a damma on the ra'. This reading has been related from 'A'isha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), in (the collections of) Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i; that is, the two readings are both related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The well-known reading is related through mass transmission (mutawatir), and the other is related both through mass transmission and through single chains (ahad), and both are intended.

The meaning of the verse according to the reading with a damma on the ra' is: his soul (rawh) is accompanied by al-rayhan, which is fragrance, and a Garden of delight. It has also been reported in another hadith that "the soul of the believer departs good (fragrant)." It has been said that rawh with a damma was used to refer to mercy, because whoever is in the mercy of Allah is truly living, possessing a soul. As for whoever is in punishment, his life is less than death, so He, exalted is He, said ﴿neither dies therein nor lives﴾ [Ta-Ha: 74], that is, because he wishes for death but does not find it.

Al-rayhan: a plant whose leaves and twigs have a pleasant scent, very green, with which the nations used to adorn gatherings of drinking. Al-Hariri said: "At times he drains the jars, and at other times he inhales the rayhan." The kings of the Arabs used to adopt it; al-Nabigha said:

They are greeted with rayhan on the day of al-sabasib.

It was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿And the grain having husk and rayhan﴾ [al-Rahman: 12] in Surat al-Rahman. Specifying it by mention before mentioning the Garden which contains it is an indication of their honour with Allah, like His saying ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, (saying) "Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured. And excellent is the final attainment of the Home."﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23].

The clause ﴿fa-rawhun wa rayhan﴾ is the response (jawab) of "amma," which carries the meaning of "whatever may be the case." He separated "ma," which implicitly carries the sense of a conditional noun, and the conditional verb, and the response, with another condition, namely ﴿if he is of those brought near﴾, because the usage has been consistent in requiring a separation between "amma" and its response by a separator, out of dislike for the response particle's (fa') being joined to the conditional particle; since they committed to omitting the conditional verb, they placed in its stead a separator, whatever it was.

The response of the conditional "in" is omitted, the response of "amma" having taken its place. Likewise His saying ﴿then peace be upon you from the companions of the right﴾.

Al-salam: a noun for safety from what is disliked, and it is also applied to greeting; the lam in His saying "laka" is for specification. The statement is a general summary, to honour them, to elevate their rank and to note their deliverance from troubles, so that the listener's mind may go in every direction.

The exegetes differed concerning His saying ﴿then peace be upon you from the companions of the right﴾. It has been said: the kaf of address is directed to an unspecified person, that is, to everyone who hears this report. The meaning: the safety attained by the companions of the right gladdens whoever hears of their affair. This is like saying "nahika bihi" and "hasbuka bihi" (it is enough for you), and "min" is initial (ibtida'iyya), and the expression has gone in the manner of a proverb, so part of it was elided; its original form is: "for them is safety, a safety that gladdens whoever hears of it."

It has been said: the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the explanation of the meaning is as preceded, because the Prophet (ﷺ) is gladdened by what the people of Islam attain of honour with Allah, and they are among those included by the expression "companions of the right." It has been said: the statement is with an elided verb, that is, it is said to him: "Peace be upon you," that is, the angels say to him.

"Min ashab al-yamin" is the predicate of an elided subject, that is, "you are of the companions of the right," and "min" on this view is partitive; thus it is good tidings to the addressee at resurrection, in the manner of His saying ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, (saying) "Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured. And excellent is the final attainment of the Home."﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23].

It has been said: the kaf is address to one who is among the companions of the right, in the manner of iltifat (shift of address). The apparent requirement would be to say "fa-salamun lahu," but he shifted to address to evoke that noble state, that is, "the companions of the right greet him," in the manner of His saying ﴿and their greeting therein is peace﴾ [Yunus: 10], that is, they hasten to greet him with peace. This is a metonymy for his being of their rank, and "min" on this view is initial.

These are the interpretations of this verse, from whose totality is derived the meaning of elevation and honour.

The deniers, the astray: they are the companions of the left in the earlier category of the three kinds.

The description of denial is here placed before the description of error, the reverse of what preceded in His saying ﴿Then indeed you, O astray deniers﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 51], in consideration of the cause of the punishment they received, which is denial, because the discourse here concerns a punishment whose time has come and when the time for caution against it has passed; so the cause of their punishment is made clear and they are reminded of what brought them into its cause, so that the pain of regret may befall them.

Al-nuzul: what is offered to a guest as hospitality; its application here is sarcasm, as preceded shortly in this surah, like His saying ﴿This is their welcome on the Day of Judgement﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 56].

Page 350

Al-tasliyah: the verbal noun of the intensive "sallahu," meaning he burned and roasted it. It is said: "sallal-lahma tasliyatan" when he roasted the meat. Here it is from speech directed in a manner that gives the impression to him that roasted meat is cooked for him in his hospitality, in the manner of sarcasm, that is, he is burned by it.

Al-jahim: it is applied to a blazing fire, and it is applied as a proper name to Jahannam, the abode of the punishment of the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 56, verse 95:

﴿Indeed, this is the certain truth.﴾ It is a concluding affirmation (tadhyil) covering all the affirmed meanings contained in the surah.

The reference to that is by interpreting "what has been mentioned" as the establishing of truth and the nullifying of falsehood.

Al-haqq (the truth): what is established and firm. Al-yaqin (certainty): what is known with decisive conviction that does not accept doubt.

The idafa (genitive construction) of "haqq" to "al-yaqin" is an idafa of the attribute to the thing described, meaning: "Indeed, this is the true certainty." This is because when a thing is perfect in its kind, it is described as "the truth of that kind," as in the hadith, "I will surely send with you a trustworthy man, a truly trustworthy one" (la-ab'athanna ma'akum aminan haqqa amin). So the meaning is: what We have related to you in this surah is certainty, the true certainty, just as one says, "Zayd is the scholar, a true scholar." The outcome of this description is the emphasis of certainty; it is thus like mentioning a synonym of the thing, and the idafa of two synonyms conveys the sense of emphasis. Therefore they explained it as meaning: this is the certainty of certainty and the correctness of correctness; we mean: it is the ultimate correctness. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is the best of what has been said about it."

It is also permissible for the idafa to be explicative (bayaniyya) in the sense of "min" (of), while its underlying meaning is in the sense of "li" (belonging to), with the estimate: "Indeed, this is the truth of the certain matter." A parallel to this construction will come in surah al-Haqqa, and I will explain there what goes beyond what I have mentioned here, so refer to it there.

This concluding affirmation contains four emphatic particles: (inna) "indeed," the lam of initial emphasis (lam al-ibtida'), the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), and the idafa of two near-synonyms.

[p. 351]

﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty.﴾ This is a consequence of the affirmation that what has been mentioned is indeed certainty (al-yaqin), since what has been mentioned contains the great attributes of God, His wondrous creation, His wisdom and His justice. It also gives good news to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community of degrees of honour and safety according to the ranks of their stations, and of the blessing of salvation from the evil end that the polytheists will meet. Therefore it was fitting that he be commanded to glorify God with a glorification that befits His greatness. Tasbih (glorification) is praise, so it includes praise for His blessing and for what He guided to of the paths of good. The detailed discussion of its counterpart in this surah has already passed.

In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful. Surat al-Hadid (The Iron). This surah has been called "Surat al-Hadid" since the time of the Companions. It is reported in the hadith of the conversion of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, in al-Tabarani and al-Bazzar, that ʿUmar entered upon his sister before he embraced Islam, and there was a sheet (ṣaḥifa) with the beginning of Surat al-Hadid in it. He read it until he reached ﴿Believe in God and His Messenger, and spend of that in which He has made you successors﴾ [al-Hadid: 7], and he embraced Islam. Likewise it has been named so in the codices (al-maṣāhif) and in the books of Sunnah (the prophetic tradition), because the word "al-hadid" occurs in it in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We sent down iron, wherein is great might﴾ [al-Hadid: 25].

Although this word is mentioned in Surat al-Kahf in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Bring me blocks of iron﴾ [al-Kahf: 96], and that surah precedes Surat al-Hadid in revelation according to the preferred view, it was not named by it, because it was named by the name al-Kahf due to the attention given to the story of the People of the Cave. Also, the iron mentioned here is intended to be the iron of weapons: swords, coats of mail and helmets, to honour it as a sign of the wisdom of God in creating its substance and inspiring people to make it, so that benefits may be obtained through it for supporting the religion and repelling transgressors, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿In it is great might and benefits for people, and that God may know who helps Him and His messengers in the unseen﴾ [al-Hadid: 25].

Regarding whether this surah is Medinan or Meccan, there is a strong disagreement that has not occurred in regard to any other surah. The majority said: it is Medinan. Ibn ʿAtiyya related from al-Naqqash that this is the consensus of the exegetes (mufassirun). It has also been said that its opening is Meccan, because of what Muslim in his Sahih, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah related from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, that he said: "There was no time between our conversion and God's rebuke to us with this verse, ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of God?﴾ [al-Hadid: 16], up to His saying, ﴿and many of them are defiant transgressors﴾ [al-Hadid: 16], except four years." Ibn Masʿud was among the first of people to embrace Islam, so this verse would be Meccan.

This is opposed by what al-Tabarani (Ibn Mardawayh) related from Anas and Ibn ʿAbbas: that the revelation of this verse was thirteen or fourteen years after the beginning of the revelation of the Qur'an. So one resorts to reconciling the two reports or to giving preference. The report of Muslim and others from Ibn Masʿud is sounder in chain (asanad), and the statement of Ibn Masʿud is given preference over what has been related from Anas and Ibn ʿAbbas, because he was earlier in embracing Islam and more knowledgeable about the revelation of the Qur'an. You have already known just now that the opening of this surah was being recited before the conversion of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "Its opening resembles being Meccan, and God knows best. There is no disagreement that in it there is Medinan Qur'an." (End of quotation.)

It has been related that its revelation was on a Tuesday, relying on a weak hadith related by al-Tabarani from Ibn ʿUmar, and related by al-Daylami from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah.

I say: what appears is that its opening is Meccan, as Ibn ʿAtiyya perceived, and that this extends to His saying: ﴿Indeed God is to you Kind and Merciful﴾ [al-Hadid: 9]; and that what follows is partly revealed in Medina, as its meanings require, such as the recounting of the statements of the hypocrites; and partly revealed in Mecca, such as the verse ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe﴾ [al-Hadid: 16] and so on, as in the hadith of Muslim. It is likely that the end of the surah, His saying: ﴿Indeed God is Strong and Mighty﴾ [al-Hadid: 25], was revealed in Medina and was appended to this surah by the directive (tawqif) of the Prophet (ﷺ) within it or at its end.

I say: in it is the verse ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest﴾ [al-Hadid: 10], and whether the intended "conquest" in that verse is the conquest of Mecca or the conquest of al-Hudaybiya, [either way], it was called "the conquest," and by it Surat al-Fath was named. Therefore it is definite that it is Medinan, so there should be no disagreement that the majority of the surah is Medinan.

It has been related that its revelation was on Tuesday, relying on a weak hadith related by al-Tabarani from Ibn ʿUmar, and related by al-Daylami from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah.

The surah has been counted as the ninety-fifth in the order of revelation of the surahs, following the view of the majority that it is Medinan. They said: it was revealed after Surat al-Zalzala and before Surat al-Qital. If the statement of Ibn Masʿud is taken into account, that it was revealed four years after the Prophetic mission (al-baʿtha), then this counting does not hold. The reason is that what is taken into account is the place of the revelation of the surah, not the revelation of its end, so its position in counting the revelation of the surah becomes problematic.

[p. 355]
According to the statement of Ibn Masʿud, the beginning of its revelation would be at the end of the fourth year of the Prophetic mission, so it would be among the earliest surahs in revelation, revealed before Surat al-Hijr and Ta-Ha and after Ghafir. The correct view is that most of its verses were revealed after Surat al-Zalzala.

Its verses were counted by the people of Medina, Mecca and Syria as twenty-eight, and by the people of Basra and Kufa as twenty-nine.

With regard to its virtue, along with other surahs that begin with glorification (al-musabbihat), there is what Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i related from al-ʿIrbad ibn Sariya: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite the musabbihat before he slept, and he would say: 'In them there is a verse better than a thousand verses.'" Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a good, strange hadith."

Ibn Kathir thought that the verse referred to in the hadith of al-ʿIrbad is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden, and He is Knowing of all things﴾ [al-Hadid: 3], because of what has been reported in the narrations about the frequency with which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) mentioned it.

The themes that this surah includes are: reminding of the majesty of God, His great attributes, the vastness of His power and dominion, the comprehensiveness of His disposal of affairs, the necessity of His existence, the vastness of His knowledge; and the command to believe in His existence and in what His Messenger (ﷺ) brought, and in the clear signs revealed to him.

Drawing attention to the guidance and path of salvation in the Qur'an, and reminding of God's mercy and compassion towards His creation.

Exhorting spending in the way of God, and that wealth is a fleeting possession, of which nothing remains for its owner except the reward of what he spent of it seeking God's good pleasure.

Transition to what God has prepared for the believing men and women on the Day of Resurrection of good, and the opposite of that for the hypocritical men and women.

[p. 356]
Warning the Muslims against falling into the abyss of hardness of heart, into which the People of the Book before them fell, through neglecting the guidance that came to them, until their hearts hardened and that led many of them to defiance.

Reminding of the Resurrection.

Calling to paying little heed to the transient life.

Commanding patience in calamities, and drawing attention to the wisdom of sending messengers and books to establish people's affairs upon general justice.

Alluding to the virtue of jihad in the way of God.

Comparing the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) with the missions of Noah and Abraham (peace be upon them both), in that among their descendants are both the guided and the defiant.

That God followed the two of them with other messengers, among them Jesus (peace be upon him), who was the last messenger sent with a law before Islam, and that his followers were upon the way of those who preceded them, some of them believers and some of them disbelievers.

Then he urged the Muslims to make their faith sincere, obliquely referring to the hypocrites, and promised them a good end, and that God has preferred them over the nations, because bounty is in His hand; He gives it to whom He wills.
